Golak Chandra Roy ------ Appellant
vs.
Niva Rani Guha Roy ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
In this Lawazima matter we are called upon to decide as to whether in this First Miscellaneous Appeal which arises out of an application for revocation of a Probate an advalorum court fee is to be paid on the memo of appeal or not. 

2. The respondent filed Probate Case No. 6/82 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. The Probate Case was allowed on 16.9.82. Thereafter the present appellant filed the revocation Case No. 147/82 for revocation of the Probate granted in that Probate proceeding. This revocation case was dismissed as not maintainable. Against that order the present First Miscellaneous Appeal has been filed by the appellant before this court.

 3. It appears from the order of the Registrar of this Court dated 5.4.88 that he has directed the appellant to pay advalorem Court fee of Tk. 8350.00 on or before 8.4.88 in default to place the matter before this Court for favour of orders.

 4. From the order sheet it appears that the ad-valorem court fee has been directed to be paid by treating the order of the court below as decree. Further it has been opined that as per Rule 773, (Civil Rules and Orders), the memo is to be treated as one filed against a regular suit and accordingly Article 11 of schedule I of the Court Fees Act, 1870 will apply and advalorum court fee is to be paid on the memo of appeal. 

5. At the out set it is to be stated that Chapter 34 of Civil Rules and Orders deals with periodical re- turns and statements submitted by the Civil Courts. In such submission the classification of cases are made as suits; appeals arising from decrees, Miscellaneous judicial cases, Miscellaneous non-judicial cases and Miscellaneous appeals. The statements of cases are filed by the Civil courts to the Supreme Court, High Court Division for the purpose of ascertaining the disposal of the various nature of cases by civil courts below. The suits and appeals from decrees arc classified in one group and the Miscellaneous judicial cases, Miscellaneous non-judicial cases and Miscellaneous appeals arc classified in another group only for the purpose of satisfaction of this court as to the disposal of the various nature of cases by the civil court below. Rule 773 speaks that an application for Probate or for letters of administration should be considered as a Miscellaneous judicial case until the date upon which it is contested and it will be treated as a suit from the day when it is contested. Thus as per Rule 773 when a case for Probate or for letters of administration is contested it be- comes a suit and when not contested it becomes a Miscellaneous judicial case for the purpose of judging the return of the civil court for ascertaining whether a suit or a Miscellaneous case has been disposed of by the court below. In a contested case a longer time is taken and the higher court will treat it as if a regular suit has been disposed of. Rule 773 is only for the limited purpose of Judging the disposal list and nothing beyond. Rule 773 (note II) also speaks that application for revocation of Probate and letters of administration should be treated in the same manner as an application for Probate or letters of administration. We have no hesitation in our mind that this classification is only for the limited purpose of submitting report to the higher court and as such from this it will be totally erroneous to hold that the order passed in a revocation proceeding is a decree. Herein we will consider some decisions to see the impact of an order in such a proceeding. In a case reported in A.I.R. 1928 Allahabad-51, Sulaiman, J observed that Probate is a Miscellaneous judicial case and in a Probate proceeding the applicant is called the petitioner. In that decision it has been observed as follows: 

"In which there is contention, the proceeding shall take, as nearly as may be, the form of a suit, according to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code, in which the petitioner for probate shall be the plaintiff, and the person who may have appeared as aforesaid to oppose the grant shall be the defendant. In our opinion this section, instead of helping the respondent, is really against him, for it clearly implies that the proceeding is not itself a suit but is to take, as nearly as may be, the form of a suit. If the proceeding were itself a suit, there would be no necessity to say that it should take the form of a suit when there is a contention".

6. In another decision reported in I.L.R. Bombey 33-256 it has been clearly held that the proceedings for Probate are not of a regular suit or that they shall be treated as such for all purposes. A Probate proceeding does not under the law, fall within the description of a regular suit and they shall take as nearly as may be the form of a suit, according to the Provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. This would show that Probate Proceeding does not, under the ordinary case, fall within the description of a regular suit. In that decision it has further been observed that the Legislature intended the difference to exist due to the special provision’s in the Court Fees Act (Act VII of 1870) for the valuation of Court fee in the case of an application for Probate as distinguished from a suit. 

7. In another case reported in 9IC.-538 it has been noted in clear language that one is not to pay ad valorem court fee on a memorandum of appeal against a probate proceeding. Their Lordships observed as follows :- 

"The court fee payable on a memorandum of appeal against an order in probate proceedings is governed by Article I of Schedule II of the Court Fees Act. Therefore, an advalorum stamp duty on the value of the e state need not be levied in such cases". 

8. We will further refer to the different provisions of the Court-fees Act to see whether the observation made in the note sheetic correct or not. In Article 11 of Schedule I it has been stated that Probate of a will or letters of administration when the amount or value of the property in respect of which the grant of probate or letters is made exceeds of Tk. 2, 000/- on such amount or value upto Tk. 10,000/- then two per centum (proper fees) is to be paid. Article 11 goes on speaking different valuations of the estate and proper fees which is to be given on the estate. This Article applies where stamp duty is pay- able on the amount or value of the property when Probate or letters of Administration is granted by a Court. This Article lays down the fee payable for the Probate of will or letters of administration and not the fee payable on an application in such grant which is provided for by Article 1 of Schedule II of the Court fees Act. Herein we will consider section 19 of the Court fees Act. Section 19(1) speaks of payment of court fees in respect probate and letters of administration. In that section it has only been stated that no order for probate or letters of ad- ministration can be granted unless a valuation of the property is given as set forth in the 3rd schedule and the court is satisfied with the fees mentioned in article No. II of the I Schedule has been paid on such valuation. That is to say that in a probate proceeding the valuation of the property must be given as contemplated in schedule III of the Court-fees Act. So that after a probate is granted necessary and proper fees can be realised under Article 11 of Schedule I of Court Fees Act. The application that is filed in a probate proceeding is in the nature of a Miscellaneous judicial case and for that court fee is to be paid as required for application or petition as contemplated in the Article I(a) of schedule II Court fees Act. The appeal that has been filed before this court is against an order and it is governed by Article 11 Schedule II namely, Memorandum of Appeal presented against an order to a High Court. The learned Advocate submits that he has paid court fee of taka 10/- which is required in such Memorandum of Appeal before this court. 

9. Thus we are of the opinion that no further court fee is to be paid on this memo of appeal. The court fee payable on a memorandum of appeal against an order in a probate proceeding according to us is governed by Article 11 of Schedule II of the Court Fees Act. The Office is directed to follow this observation hereinabove for such cases future guidance. 

End.

Vs.

case_source: Appeal against the decree of M.A. Jain. Subordinate Judge, 1st Court of Zilla Dhaka, dated the 20th day of February, 1982 passed in Tittle Suit No. 785 of 1980.
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J: This appeal by the plaintiffs is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka dated 20.2.1982 in Title suit No. 785 of 1980. The appellants as plaintiffs instituted the said Title Suit for declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 3 of 19 77 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is void, illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

2. The case of the plaintiffs was to the effect that the land measuring. 32 decimals of C.S. plot No. 1077 in khatian No. 209 of Monza Bania originally belonged to Behari Mistry Behari Lal Majumder who died leaving 2 sons Srenibashi Majumder and Naribashi Majumder who inherited the property in equal shares. By a registered deed of sale dated 23-5-73, Srenibashi sold 3 decimals of land to Mohsin Mona who in his turn by a registered deed of sale dated 23-7-75 sold the said decimals of land to the plaintiffs No. 3 by a registered deed of sale dated 18-12-72. Hari Bashi also sold 4 decimals of land to Sarifa Khatun by a registered sale of deed dated 12.12.72. Sarifa sold it to Abdul Jalil Mia on 31.1.79. Abdul Jalil Mia in his turn sold the same to the plaintiff No. 4 by a sale deed dated 29.2.80. Hari Basi again sold 4 decimals of land by a sale deed dated 12.12.72 to Cheman Nahar Begum and Md. Habibulla who in their turn sold the same to Abdul Khaleque and Md. Nabbo Khan by a sale deed dated 10.9.73 and Abdul Khaleque and Md. Nabbo Khan then sold the said 4 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 5 by a sale deed dated 26.9.74. Srenibashi sold 3 decimals of land by a sale deed dated 15.6.73 to Md. Shamsul Hoque who then sold it to plaintiff No. 6 by a sale deed dated 9.3.77. Thus the plaintiffs are owners in possession of the suit land measuring 18 decimal out of 32 decimals where they are living with their families by making constructions. Defendant No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 585 of 1974 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka against Md. Hanif and Sk. Abdul Majid for specific performance of Contract. The said suit was transferred to the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1977. The defendant No. 1 of the present suit obtained an exparte decree in the said title suit fraudulently and collusively beyond the knowledge of the plaintiffs. In Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1978, arising out of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 3 of 1977, a process server of the Court went to the suit property on 14.6.80 to deliver possession to the defendant No, 1 but due to the resistance put by the plaintiffs possession of the suit property could not be delivered to the defendant No. 1. Thereafter the plaintiffs have filed the present suit for declaration noted above.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1 who by filing a written statement denied the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit property and contended that the suit plot belonged to Sree Nibash Majumder and Hari Bashi Majumder and 7 others as a part of the property of an undivided Hindu family. These owners transferred the entire suit plot along with other ejmali properties to Md. Hanif by a sale deed dated 1.4.1968 through Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1968 arising out of decree passed in Title Suit No. 236 of 1967. Md. Han-if possessed and then entered into a contract on 18.7.70 with the defendant No. 1 through his lawful attorney for sale of the entire suit plot. As Md. Hanif failed to execute a sale deed the defendant No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 585 of 1974 against Md. Hanif and others for specific performance of Contract and the suit was transferred to the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1977. The suit was decreed in favour of the defendant No. 1 and thereafter, in Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1978, the defendant got a sale deed executed and registered through Court and got delivery of possession of the entire suit plot physically on 14.6. 80. The defendant also contended that the suit was barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

<u>4. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the facts and circumstances adduced in the case held that the suit has been brought for a declaration that the ex-parte Judgment and decree dated 27.7.77 passed in Title Suit No. 3 of 1977 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is void, illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs and is liable to be set aside. He further found that possession have been delivered through Court to the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs have failed to prove their possession therein by any independent witness and as such the present suit for declaration without any prayer for recovery of khas possession is not maintainable. Ho also found that the question of the plaintiffs in the suit property is seriously involved and without establishment of declaration of their title in the suit property, the plaintiffs cannot have any locus standi to challenge that decree. He also found that in the present suit, there was no prayer for establishment or declaration of the plaintiffs' title in the suit property. He also opined that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and that it is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. He therefore dismissed the suit. As against the said judgment and decree the plaintiffs preferred this appeal before this Court and contended that the plaintiffs were not a party and the decree is not binding upon the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree as prayed for. The present suit is a suit for declaration that the said ex-parte decree is void. He was within his competency in the said suit to get a declaration to that effect in View of the fact that he was not a party in the original suit. In order to obtain a decree to the effect that the decree was void the person seeking such a relief has to prove his title to the suit property. Unless be can prove his title to the suit property he cannot have the luxury of having a decree declared to be void, in the present case it is found that the defendants are in possession in the suit property by virtue of previous title suit. So in the facts and circumstances of the case the plaintiffs are not entitled to any such declaration as prayed for. They can file a properly constituted suit for declaration of their title as also for declaration that the decree with regard to the property was void. It does not require any declaration by the Court that a decree is not binding on a person who is not a party to the suit. If he wants to have such a declaration he is to prove his title to the suit property, otherwise he is not entitled to get such a declaration. In the present case the plaintiffs have not established their title. As such the learned Judge was right in holding that the suit was barred under the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In that view of the matter we find that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. In that view of the matter this appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

5. The appellant filed an application for allowing the appeal and sending back the case to the Court below in order to enable the plaintiff to amend their plaint but we do not find any reason to allow such prayer because of the fact that the plaintiff have not shown any formal defect in the plaint. Amendment in the plaint now will definitely change the nature and character of the suit and as such remained order cannot be made on an appeal of this nature. In that view of the matter the application for remanding the case to the Court below cannot be maintained and the same is therefore rejected.

M. A. Jalil, J. —I agree.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury, J.: This Rule which has been argued at a considerable length raises a short question relating to the execution of a decree for ejectment. In order to make the question intelligible a short statement of facts is necessary.

2. The opposite parties obtained a decree for eviction of their monthly tenant M/s. Jamil Auto Centre and its proprietor, Mustafa Jamil Ahmed, from a holding at Sir Syed Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. When the decree was in execution the writ for deli very of possession was once resisted by the judgment debtor. So there was an order by the executing court for effecting delivery of possession with the help of police. Accordingly, the bailiff, being accompanied by a contingent of police went to the locality, but this time also he failed to execute the writ. He reported that possession could not be delivered as the judgment debtors and their men resisted the execution of the writ for delivery of possession. Notwithstanding such a report the decree-holders made no application to the executing Court complaining of the resistance. However, the petitioners who are third parties to the decree came up with an application saying that they were in possession of the properties in question in their own right as allottees from the Government and, therefore, were not bound by the decree of ejectment obtained by the decree-holders. The application was described as one under Order 21, rule 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They also obtained an order for local inspection to ascertain the real position. On coming to know of the order the decree-holders preferred an application purporting to be under section 151 of the Code for vacating the order as also for dismissal of the application under rule 99 on the plea that the petitioners had no locus standi to file any independent application under rule 99.

3. After hearing the parties, the executing Court sustained the objection of the decree-holders, vacated the order for local inspection and dismissed the application of the petitioners under rule 99. Against the said order the petitioners have obtained the present rule they now contend that the decision is wrong.

<u>4. The determination of the question depends upon the construction of Order 21, rules 35, 36 and 97-100 of the Code. The point is, however, not res integra. In Usha Jain and others Vs. Manmohan Bajaj and others, AIR 1980 MP 146, a Full Bench of Madhya Pradesh High Court had the occasion to consider the entire scheme of Order 21 with reference to the relevant earlier decisions of other High Courts of the subcontinent. After a careful review thereof it laid down that no inquiry into the title or possession of a third party is contemplated at any rate at his instance either under rules 35 and 36 or rules 95 and 96 of Order 21 CPC when the decree-holder or the auction-purchaser applies for obtaining possession. Subsequently, when the decree-holder or auction- purchaser is met with obstruction or resistance in obtaining possession, one of the options open to him is to apply under rule 97 but that provision is merely permissible and not mandatory and it is open to the decree-holder/auction-purchaser to apply instead for a fresh warrant of possession. An enquiry at the instance of a third party in possession is contemplated only under Order 21 rule 100 after he was dispossessed and not before it. In arriving at the said conclusion that Bench quoted with approval the reasonings of an earlier decision of the court in Ramgulam Vs. Mahendra Kumar, 1972 MPLJ, 254, which have been expressed in the following words:</u>

<u>"Under r. 35 and 36 the Court's assistance is available by issue of a warrant for delivery of actual possession, joint possession or symbolical possession. Form of warrant for delivery of possession finds place in Form No. ll of Appendix E. It is noteworthy that this warrant in general terms directs the .bailiff to put the decree-holder in possession of the property and to remove any person bound by the decree who may refuse to vacate the same. The language of the form, which is in line with first clause of r. 35, indicates that the warrant issued under this provision is not issued to remove any particular individual from possession, but is issued in general terms to remove any person bound by the decree. It follows that the words. 'if necessary by removing any person bound by, the decree who refuses to vacate the property' which find place in Cl. (1) of r.35, do not contemplate any inquiry for finding out as to who is the particular person in possession or whether he is bound by the decree or refusing to vacate the property. The provision for issue of warrant in general terms negatives any such inquiry."</u>

"The third clause of r.35, which also deals with delivery of actual possession, enables the Court to direct the removal or opening of any lock or bolt or breaking open of any door or doing of any act of similar nature for putting the decree-holder in possession of any building or enclosure when the person in possession being bound by the decree does not afford free access. The words-where the person in possession bound by the decree does not afford free access-as used in this clause like the words 'by removing any person bound by the decree who refuses to vacate the property' as used in the first clause do not require any inquiry to be made to find out as to who is the particular person in possession or whether he is bound by the decree or affording free access. The third clause interpreted along with the first clause only contemplates of a general direction to be inserted in the warrant authorising the bailiff to do the acts mentioned in that clause for putting the decree-holder in possession of any building or enclosure where the person in possession being bound by the decree does not afford free access."

<u>"The second clause of r. 35 deals with the mode of delivery of possession when the decree being executed is one for joint possession. It only requires that a copy of warrant be affixed in some conspicuous place on the property and the substance of the decree be proclaimed by beat of drum or other customary mode at some convenient place. There is hardly anything in this clause which may furnish the basis for any inquiry."</u>

<u>"But when the decree to be executed is one for actual possession and the decree-holder chooses to apply for issuance of a warrant for' delivery of actual possession, the Court is not required to hold an inquiry whether the person in occupation is one bound by the decree and the duty of the Court is to issue a warrant under r. 35. A third party, meaning thereby a person who is not the judgment-debtor or a representative in interest of the judgment-debtor, has no locus standi at that stage to apply that the application of the decree holder for actual delivery of possession should be dismissed and that he be granted only constructive possession. An application of the judgment-debtor or his representative in interest stating that the decree for any reason is not executable in a particular mode will stand on a different footing as it will fall under s. 47 of the Civil PC and will be decided under that provision. But a third party cannot intervene at that stage and force an inquiry into his title or possession on an unwilling decree-holder for the simple reason that his case does not fall under s.47 and no inquiry into his title or possession is contemplated under rr.35 and 36 at any rate at his instance."</u>

<u>"Similar is the position when an auction-purchaser seeks the assistance of the Court for being put into possession under rr.95 and 96. These rules are worded in like manner as rr.35 and 36 and a third party cannot intervene to have his title or possession investigated under them."</u>

<u>"After a warrant for delivery of possession is issued in favour of a decree-holder or an auction-purchaser, he may be met with resistance or obstruction in obtaining possession and the warrant may be returned unexecuted. He will then have three courses open to him. He may accept that the person resisting or obstructing execution is a third party in possession who is not bound by the decree in which case he will have to institute a separate suit for possession within ordinary period of limitation for obtaining possession. He may proceed on the assumption that the resistance or obstruction is by the judgment-debtor or a person bound by the decree in which case he has to apply under r.97 for getting the title and nature of possession of the person obstructing or resisting investigation in execution proceedings. But he is not bound to apply under r. 97 and may ignore the obstruction or resistance and apply again for warrant of delivery of possession; See Nathu Harishankar Vs. Fatusa AIR 1933 Nag 369, Ganpati Singh Vs. Ramgopal Air 1941Nag. 322 and Official Trustee Vs. Monmothonath AIR 1953 Cal.399. It is also clear that if the decree-holder or the auction purchaser does not choose to apply under r. 97 neither the person obstructing or resisting execution, nor a person who may in future obstruct or resist execution can apply under that rule to have his title and possession investigated; See Jagannath Vs. Khaja Faijuddin AIR 1935 Nag 212 and Nanakchand Vs. Chaturbhuj 1964 MPLJ (Note) 126."</u>

<u>"Thus the provisions contained in rr. 97, 98 and 99 authorise an inquiry into the nature and character of the possession of a person who has obstructed or resisted the delivery of possession; but as already stated, the inquiry under these rules can be made only on the complaint of the decree-holder or auction-purchaser and not at the instance of the party in possession."</u>

<u>"An inquiry at the instance of a third party in possession is contemplated only after he is dispossessed in execution and applies under r.l00 complaining of such dispossession."</u>

5. The principle enunciated in that case was followed in Mohammad Shareef and others Vs. Bashir Ahmed and others, AIR 1983 MP 44, Harijan Wood Workers Production-Cum-Sales Co-operatives Society Ltd. Vs. Smt. Maya Wati and another, AIR 1985 Punjab and Hariana, 181.

6. To the same effect are also the decisions in Nittyananda Kanango Vs. Sm. Paw Devi, AIR 1952 Orissa (FB) 120, Ianki Mohan and another Vs. Dr. S. Samaddar and others, AIR 1962 Patna 403, Motamari Ramiah and others Vs. Kumari Malliah and others, AIR 1962 Andhra Pradesh 72 and Gopal Chandra Sadhukhen Vs. Sheikh Iamsed and another, AIR 1965 Cal. 51.

7. So far as this Court is concerned, a similar view has been expressed in Saleh Ahmed Vs. Md. Zakaria, 37 DLR 296. In that case one Saleh Ahmed obtained a decree for ejectment against one Md. Ilias Majhi. The decree was put into execution but while the decree-holder went to take possession through process of the Court he could not get possession due to resistance. So he filed an application to, get delivery of possession with the help of police. At that stage Md. Zakaria who happened to be a third party to the decree filed an application under Order 21 rule 99 of the Code for not allowing the decree -holder to execute the decree without determining his claim to the disputed property. The decree-holder opposed the application asserting that the provisions of Order 21 rule 99 have no application to the case. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the prayer of the third party. A question, therefore, arose as to whether the executing Court had jurisdiction to pass such an order at the instance of a third party. Abdul Jalil, J. speaking for a Division Bench answered it thus:

"Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate, has taken us through the provisions of Order 21, rules 99 and 100 wherefrom it appears that the executing Court may pass such order in case of resistance but that order must be on application filed by the decree-holder under Order 21, rule 97 of the same Code. The 3rd party cannot file such application but he may file an application if evicted under rule 100 of the said Order and the executing Court may investigate into the matter and restore the applicant in possession."

8. In our opinion the judicial authorities are thus unanimous that unless and until the decree-holder makes an application under Order 21 rule 97 of the Code, a person who is not a party to the decree has no locus standi to make any application under rule 99 for adjudication of his alleged claim of title or possession over the disputed property and if he makes such an application the same is liable to be dismissed as being not maintainable.

9. In the case before us, the decree-holder admittedly made no complaint under rule 97 alleging any resistance or obstruction by the petitioners in obtaining possession in execution of the decree. It was, therefore, not open to the petitioners who are third parties to make any independent application under rule 99 seeking adjudication of their alleged claim. Accordingly, we find that the impugned order suffers from no error of law.

<u>10. The only further question which has been argued is whether it was permissible for the executing Court to entertain the application in exercise of its power under section 151 of the Code. Precisely, this question was also agitated in the case of Saleh Ahmed Vs. Ilias Majhi (Supra). It was held in that case that there being a remedy open to a third party by way of a separate suit, there was no room for exercise of the inherent power. Similar view was also expressed in Janki Mohan and another Vs. Dr. S. Samaddar & others, Nittyananda Kanongo Vs. Sm. Pala Devi (Supra), and Ali Hossain Vs. Rajiquddin PLD 1977, Lahore 418. In that view of the matter the contention is overruled.</u>

11. For all these reasons I find no substance in this case.

12. The Rule is, accordingly, discharged with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
The petitioner obtained this Rule against the judgment and decree dated 26-10-81 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 60 of 1980 affirming those of the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Bhola dated 25-2-80 made in Title Suit No. 58 of 1968 dismissing the suit.

The facts giving rise to this Rule arises out of the circumstances which may, in brief, be stated as follows:-

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid Title Suit against the present opposite party Nos. 1-3 for declaration of title and recovery of possession after evicting the defendants-opposite parties from the suit land on the allegations, inter alia, that the plaintiff got settlement of suit land along with other lands measuring 3 acres from the Government under the Settlement Case No. 26251/50-60 by executing a kabuliyat on 12-6-66 and got possession therein from the Surveyor of the Government ; that the defendant opposite party wanted to purchase the suit land from the plaintiff but as the plaintiff did not agree to sell the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff from the land in suit in the first part of Magh 1374 BS constructing but and digging ditches and excavating tank in the suit land; that the defendants also threatened him to dispossess from the remaining vacant land.

3. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement and as additional written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint con-tending, inter alia, that he and the defendant No. 2 had been possessing suit plot Nos. 2129/ 2392 since 1360 BS. By constructing but and excavating tank therein, that the plaintiff in pursuance of a Salish held at his instance transferred the entire land to the defendants during pendency of the appeal against the part decree in this suit and executed a kabala in favour of the defendant No. 1, Waziullah on receipt of Taka 6,000 from him as the plaintiff had no possession in the suit land; that the defendant No. 1 also paid balance selami Taka 662 to the Government on 18-4-73 which was due from the plaintiff; that the said kabala was obtained in the name of his 'Fufata Bhai' Md Hanif ; that he had also established a Forkania Madrasha and a Mosque and excavated another tank measuring 100 x 80 cubits in the suit land; that the plaintiff by suppressing this fact of benami transaction and without impleading him as a party filed a Title Suit being Title Suit No. 605 of 1976 on 20-11-76 in the Court of Munsif against Hanif, his benamder, for reconveyance of the suit land without any basis as there was no contract for reconveyance between the plaintiff and the said Md Hanif; that the said agreement for reconveyance dated 10-10-70 was a forged one and the said decree made in TS No. 605 of 1976 was not binding on him as he was not a party to the suit; that the plaintiff had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and the plaintiff's suit was liable to be dismissed. Upon the pleadings of the parties the learned trial Court framed the following issues:-

1. Is the suit property valued and stamped?

2. Is the suit maintainable ?

3. Is the plaintiff entitled to get decree for khass possession in the suit land?

4. Has the plaintiff get right, title and interest in the suit land ?

5. To what relief if any is the plaintiff entitled ?

4. The learned Munsif considering the evidence on record dismissed the suit on contest with costs against the defendant No. 1 & exparte against the rest without costs by his aforesaid judgment & decree. The Plaintiff being aggrieved by the said judgment & decree of the learned Munsif preferred T Appeal No. 60 of 1980 in the court of District Judge, Bakergonj. The appeal of the plaintiff, however, was dismissed on contest against the defendant No. 1 with costs by the learned Sub-Judge.

5. In this Rule only question for determination by this court is, as contended by the learned Advocate for both the parties, whether the learned Munsif was justified in holding that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 605 of 1976 was binding on the defendant No. 1 or not and whether the lower Appellate Court rightly held that the decree obtained by the plaintiff in that suit was binding on the defendant No. 1 merely on the ground that a decree against the benamder is binding on the real owner without considering the circumstances of the case leading to the decree.

6. Mr Md Nizamul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, firstly, submitted that in the appeal preferred by the appellant as no cross objection was filed by the defendant the defendant was not entitled to urge as to whether the finding of the Trial Court as to fraud was correct or not. In reply to this Mr Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 submitted that the defendant without preferring cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure can urge the point. True, the defendant for urging such a point before the appellate court need not file cross-objection and without filing such cross objection under Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure he can urge the point. Thus the first contention for the petitioner fails.

7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner next submitted that in the Title Suit No. 605 of 1976 the question of fraud not having been taken specifically the courts below cannot consider that question and the learned Munsif was wrong in holding that the decree passed in that suit against Md Hanif was not binding upon the defendant on an erroneous view. He submitted, therefore, that the appellate court rightly held that there was no scope for considering the question of fraud by the trial Court and as such the lower appellate court correctly held that the decree on the estensible owner is binding on the real owner. Mr Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, submitted that the defendant need not file a separate suit for avoiding fraudulent decree and he can agitate this point in another collateral suit or proceeding. In support of his contention he relied upon the decision in the case of Rakhal Chandra Das vs Benecha Khatun reported in 24 DLR 63 Mr Ahmed submitted that he relied upon this decision only on the ground of fraud and not collusion. The learned Advocate for the petitioner very strenuously argued that the principle laid down in that case is not applicable in the present case inasmuch as there was no definite finding as to fraud in obtaining the decree in the present case but allegation was of non-service of notice.

Although in the present case the allegation of non-service of notice was made in the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure yet it appears from the written statement filed by the defendant that he also pleaded the fraud when he made statement to the effect that the plaintiff had the knowledge that the defendant was in possession of the disputed land and the defendant after purchase of the disputed land from the plaintiff himself established a Madrasha, excavated tank and also created other structures. The facts sufficiently indicate that the ostensible owner (Md Hanif) was not the real owner and the defendant No. 1 was the real owner of the disputed property who also paid the balance premium to the Government. In view of the aforesaid circumstances the plaintiff obtained the decree fraudulently in Title Suit No. 605 of 1976. No doubt it is now a settled principle of law that a decree on the estensible owner is binding on the real owner. But in this case there are certain special features to be considered to apply this principle of law in deciding the present case. In this case the plaintiff obtained the settlement from the Government but could not get possession as because the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the disputed land by erecting homestead, etc from before. Secondly, at the instance of the plaintiff himself a salish was held and in pursuance of that salish the plaintiff had to execute a kabala and transferred the land in suit in favour of the defendant No. 1 for consideration of Taka. 6,000; the defendant after purchase continued in possession of the disputed land by exercising the right of a real owner by further erecting hut, establishing Madrasha, Mosque and also excavating tank. It also appears from the finding of the learned Munsif that plaintiff did not adduce any other corroborative evidence to prove that Md Hanif paid him Taka 6,000.

<u>8. The learned trial Court also considering the evidence of DWs 1, 6, 7 and 8 came to the finding that the defendant No. 1 got the kabala in question out of his own fund and for his self-interest in the benami of Md Hanif who happens to be a Fufata Bhai of the defendant No. 1.</u>

<u>When a decree is obtained by a plaintiff practicing fraud it is not necessary to file a separate suit for avoiding such decree but the said decree can be impugned in another suit or proceeding by a person aggrieved by such fraudulent decree in view of the provision of section 44 of the Evidence Act.</u>

<u>Considering all these aspects I am inclined to hold that whether the plaintiff obtained decree in TS No. 605/76 by practicing fraud or not has to be decided with reference to the evidence on record of the case and this question can be gone into in the present suit. In this respect I would also like to add that the purchaser from a benamder is protected under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act provided he satisfied the conditions laid down in the said section. Section 41 runs as follows:—</u>

<u>"41. Transfer by estensible owner. —Where, with the consent, express or implied, of the persons interested in immovable property, a person is the estensible owner of such property, and transfers the same for consideration, the transfer shall not be voidable on the ground that the transferor was not authorised to make it; provided that the transferee, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had power to make the transfer, has acted in good faith".</u>

<u>9. From the reading of the language of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act it appears to me that it is incumbent on the transferee to show that he acted after taking reasonable care to ascertain as to whether the benamder (here Md Hanif) had power to make transfer and he acted in good faith in obtaining the deed of reconveyance from Md Hanif. In other words, the real owner can avoid the transfer by his benamder provided no reasonable care was taken by the transferee in getting the transfer from the benamder.</u>

<u>In this case the plaintiff himself transferred the land to the defendant who was althrough in possession and the plaintiff obtained a deed of reconveyance from Hanif knowing full well that Hanif was not in possession of the property which is also abundantly clear from the evidence of Hanif himself as noticed by the trial Court. These aspects need consideration by the court of appeal below, the last Court of fact, for the purpose of holding whether the decree obtained in the Title Suit No. 605 of 1976 was obtained fraudulently or not.</u>

<u>The learned Lower Appellate Court was not right in holding that a decree against the benamder is binding on the real owner by making a general observation to that effect without at all considering all these material aspects and the facts and circumstances of the present case. In view of the above discussion, I hold that the judgment of the Lower Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. I, therefore, set-aside the judgment and decree of the Lower Appellate Court and send back the appeal to that court for disposal in the light of the observations made above after considering the respective case of the parties with reference to the evidence on record.</u>

In the result, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman J: In this Rule the point raised seems to us of first impression and involves a complicated question of great public importance calling for interpretation of various Articles of our Constitution and different provisions of the statutory laws. And for the reasons we have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and Mr. A F Hassan Ariff, the learned Deputy Attorney-General who appeared to assist us on our request at a great length.

2. The question we are to resolve is: whether the Governor of Bangladesh Bank is under legal obligation to satisfy a decree made in suit by payment of decretal amount to the decree-holder out of the Consolidated Fund of the Republic kept in the Bangladesh Bank in obedience to an order of a Civil Court.

3. In order to answer this question the facts necessary to be stated are, in short, that a decree for Taka 2,15,374.00 was passed in Title Suit No. 8 of 1977 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in favour of Mrs. Rana Awan, the opposite party l(plaintiff). The petitioner, the Bangladesh Bank, was not a party to that suit. But by an order of the Court passed on March 3, 1991 the petitioner was directed to keep the decretal amount with it as the same had been attached in Money Execution Case No. 5 of 1979 for the satisfaction of the decree till further order. The said order was followed by an order dated April 27, 1991 passed under Or. 21, r. 56 CPC directing the petitioner Bank to deposit the attached decretal amount in the account of the learned Advocate of the decree-holder Mrs. Rana Awan. On receipt of this order the petitioner wrote to the judgment-debtors-opposite party on May 13, 1991 for payment of the money and informed the Court on May 15, 1991 about the step it took. Thereafter on July 13, 1991 the petitioner received a legal notice from the decree-holder-opposite party 1 for compliance with the Court's direction for payment of the amount. This notice was followed by a letter dated July 30, 1991 to the judgment debtors for the same purpose. The petitioner sent on September 14, 1991 a reply to the legal notice and thereafter filed an application on September 30, 1991 in the Court for recalling of the notices given under Or. 21, rr 52 and 56 CPC on the ground that such direction was required to be sent to the authorised person as contemplated under Article 85 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. The application was resisted by the opposite party-decree-holder by filing a written objection. The learned Subordinate Judge on contest, however, rejected the application by the impugned order dated 5.10.91. This Rule is directed against this order and is resisted by the opposite party 1 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition to which the petitioner also filed affidavit-in-reply.

4. Dr. M. Zahir first relying upon Article 85 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh submits that Article 85 provides for regulation of public money kept in the Consolidated Fund with the Bangladesh Bank and withdrawal of money from the Fund is to be regulated by an Act of Parliament or until such law is enacted by rules to be made by the President. He submits that as there is no such Act of Parliament no money can be released from the Consolidated Fund by the petitioner-Bank. He further submits that as there is no rule framed by the President a prescribed instrument for making such payment is required and as the petitioner had taken step to obtain such instrument from the judgment-debtor, the Subordinate Judge should not have issued the direction as contained in the impugned order and by passing the impugned order he committed error of law in rejecting the petition for recalling the notice issued under Or.21, rr. 52 and 56 CPC and thereby occasioned failure of justice, Secondly, he submits that the Court committed error of law in its decision in holding that the Chief Executive Officer of the Bangladesh Bank is a Public Officer for the purpose of Part-IV and r. 52 of Or. 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as defined under section 71 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 (President's Order No.127 of 1972). Thirdly, he contends that the Court below committed error of law in not holding that unless an Appropriation Act as contemplated under Article 90 of the Constitution is made, no money can be paid in satisfaction of the decree out of the Consolidated Fund. Lastly, he submits that if the ordinary Civil Court has power to attach the money kept in the Consolidated Fund and to order for payment out of such Fund as has been done by the impugned order, then the Constitution, the supreme order of the State, will be made nugatory.

5. Mr. M I Farooqi appearing for the opposite party 1, on the other hand, submits that the executing Court has ample authority under Or. 21, rr. 52 and 56 CPC to execute the decree against the Republic read with section 71 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 127 of 1972) as the Governor of the Bank, a Public Officer, is under legal duty to obey the direction of the executing Court for satisfaction of the decree. He further contends that no instrument as contended by Dr. Zahir is necessary to give effect to the order of the Court for payment of the decretal amount in as much as the Code of Civil Procedure and the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 127 of 1972) are Acts of Parliament and the mode of execution of the decree by attachment and by payment out of the Consolidated Fund as prescribed by the Code is in consonance with mandate of clause (e) of Article 88 of the Constitution.

6. Mr. Ariff also took the stand that for payment out of the Consolidated Fund the Annual Financial Statement must show the sum required to meet expenditure charged by and under the Constitution. This contention of Me. Ariff is founded on Articles 87 and 88 of the Constitution.

7. In order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates, let us first consider section 60(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 72 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. Section 60 deals with property liable to be attached and sold in execution of a decree. Section 60(1) reads:

"60(1). The following property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree namely, lands, houses or other buildings, goods, money, bank-notes, cheques, bills of exchange, hundis, promissory notes, Government securities bonds or other securities for money, debts, shares in a corporation and, save as hereinafter mentioned, all other saleable property, movable or immovable, belonging to the judgment-debtor or over which or the profits of which he has a disposing power which he may exercise for his own benefit whether the same be held in the name of the judgment-debtor or any another person in trust for him or on his behalf.

Proviso to section 60(1) of the Code provides for exemption of properties of certain classes from attachment and sale which does not exempt "money" as finds place in section 60(1) of the Code. Thus, from sub-section (1) of section 60 CPC it is seen that "money" is liable to be attached in execution of a decree made in a law suit by a Civil Court. Now the question is whether "debt" is "money". It has been held in a number of decisions of this sub-continent that money is debt.

<u>8. Section 72 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 also grants certain exemptions. The exemption also does not cover. the present decretal amount. According to section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure the word "property" also includes every type of interest that can be owned by the judgment-debtor over which he possesses power of disposal. Thus, it is seen that "money" is liable to be attached and in the present case money of the judgment-debtor in custody of the Bangladesh Bank kept in the Consolidated Fund is liable to be attached and paid as the same belongs to the Republic of which the judgment-debtor is a department. The decisions cited by Mr. Farooqi in the cases of Muktilal Agarwala Vs. Trustees of the Provident Fund of the Tin Plate Co. of India Ltd and others. AIR 1956 (SC) 336, the case of Smt. Radharani Dass W/o Narayan Chandra Ghose Vs. Smt. Binodamoyee Dassi W/o Abinash Chandra Ghose & others AIR 1942 (Cal) 92 and the case of Shulen Singh and others Vs. Ganendra Kumea Roy Chowdhury, AIR 1950 (Cal) 74 support this view.</u>

<u>In the instant case as these provisions are not directly on the point we refrain from discussing these.</u>

<u>9. Let us now find out the power of the Civil Court to pass an order of attachment of property in custody of Court or Public Officer. Order 21, rule 52 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:</u>

<u>"52. Attachment of property in custody of Court or public officer. Where the property to be attached is in the custody of any court or public officer, the attachment shall be made by a notice to such Court or officer, requesting that such property, and any interest or dividend becoming payable thereon, may be held subject to the further orders of the Court from which the notice is issued:</u>

<u>Provided that, where such property is in the custody of a Court, any question of title or priority arising between the decree-holder and any other person, not being the judgment-debtor, claiming to be interested in such property by virtue of any assignment, attachment or otherwise, shall be determined by such Court".</u>

<u>Thus it appears that there is a prescribed form of notice for attachment as mentioned in (Appendix-E) of First Schedule, (Form No. 21). Rule 52 prescribes a form of attachment for property which is in the custody of a Court or any public officer and the attachment is to be held subject to further order of the attaching Court. We have already found that the attached property is money and the executing Court has authority to direct the public officer to satisfy the decree. In this connection reference may be made in the case of EM Visvanadhan Chelly and two others Vs. Arunachelam Chetty ILR 44 (Mad. 100, in the case of Khaum Chand Vs. Moti Singh and another, AIR 1935 (Lahore) 914. Further it may be found that where property belonging to the judgment-debtor is in the custody of a Court or a public officer attachment shall be effected in accordance with r. 52 of the Code of Civil Procedure by a notice to the Court or the public officer to hold the property subject to further orders of the Court ordering attachment. It is held so in the case of Kanhaiyala Vs. Dr. DR Banaji and others, AIR 1958 (SC) 725, in the case of Khazan Chand Vs. Moti Singh and another AIR 1935 (Lahore) 914, and in the case of Surjamull Agarwala Vs. Ram Chandra Mistry and others AIR 1916 (CaJ) 570.</u>

<u>Thus, in view of the aforesaid provisions of law and the judicial pronouncement there is no doubt that the court has power for ordering attachment of the money in the hands of the Governor of Bangladesh Bank who is public officer as defined in section 72 of Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 and he is liable to pay the decretal amount.</u>

10. Now it is to be seen as to whether the money in question can be attached and be paid to the decree-holder out of the Consolidated Fund as directed by the Court without a separate instrument authorising to make such payment. This requres us to examine certain Articles of our Constitution.

Article 84(1) speaks about the Consolidated Fund while

Article 84(2) speaks about Public Account of the Republic.

Article 84(1) and (2) are:

"84.(1) All revenues received by the Government, all loans raised by the Government, and all moneys received by it in repayment of any loan, shall form part of one fund to be known as the Consolidated Fund.

(2) All other public moneys received by or on behalf of the Government shall be credited to the Public Account of the Republic."

Article 85 speaks about payment and withdrawal of the public moneys. Article 85 runs:

"85. The custody of public moneys, their payment into and the withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund or, as the case may be, the Public Account of the Republic and the matters connected with or ancillary to the matters aforesaid, shall be regulated by Act of Parliament, and until provision in that behalf is so made, by rules made by the President."

From Article 85 it is seen that payment into and withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund is to be regulated by Act of Parliament and until provision in that behalf is so made by rules made by the President. Article 88(d)(e) and (f) of the Constitution are relevant for our present purpose which reads as follows:

"88. The following expenditure shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund-

(a)	***			***				***

(b)	 ***			 ***				 ***

(c)	***			  ***				  ***

(d) all debt charges for which the Government is liable, including interest, sinking fund charges, the repayment or amortisation of capital, and other expenditure in connection with the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt;

(e) any sums required to satisfy a judgment, decree or award against the Republic by any court or tribunal; and

(f) any other expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund by this Constitution or by Act of Parliament."

11. Article 89 of the Constitution deals with Annual Financial Statement and under this Article such statement is laid before the Parliament. It consists of (i) Annual Financial Statement relating to expenditure charged upon to Consolidated Fund which may be discussed by the Parliament but shall not be voted and (ii) in the form of demand for grants in respects of which the Parliament have power to assent to any grant or to refuse. Clause (f) of Article 88 of the Constitution relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund by the Constitution or by an Act of Parliament. The Annual Financial Statement relating to other expenditure upon the Consolidated Fund is submitted in the Parliament in the form of demands for grants on the recommendation of the President. The Parliament have power to assent to or to refuse to assent to any demand or to assent to it subject to a reduction of the amount specified therein. It further appears that after the grants under Article 89 is made by the Parliament, an Appropriation Bill is to be moved under Article 90 of the Constitution to provide for appropriation out of Consolidated Fund all money required to meet (a) the grants so made by the Parliament and (b) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund but not exceeding in any case the amount shown in the Annual Financial Statement laid before the Parliament

A close reading of Articles 89, 90, 91 and 92 shows that there must be demand for grants for other expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund. And under Article 90(1) an Appropriation Act has to be enacted by the Parliament "to provide for appropriation out of the "Consolidated Fund" and Article 90(3) provides that" subject to the provision of this Constitution no money shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except under appropriation made by law passed in accordance with the provisions of this Article". Thus, Article 90(3) has to be read with Article 88 only to ascertain whether for payment out of the Consolidated Fund an Appropriation Act is necessary.

12. A close reading of these two Articles leads us to hold that only in respect of withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund relating to grants, an Act in the name of Appropriation Act is necessary and no instrument as contended by the petitioner is necessary for payment out of the Consolidated Fund as Article 90(3) is to be read "subject to the provisions of this Constitution" and Article 88(f) being a provision of the Constitution Article 90(3) is controlled by that and no other instrument is necessary for payment of the money out of Consolidated Fund. An Appropriation Act is temporary and is meant only for one financial year and relates to grant for expenditure in exclusion to the payment of debt as contemplated under Article 88(f) of the Constitution. But under Article 85, the Act of Parliament is permanent and constant. Article 90 is subject to Articles 85, 91 and 92. In this regard we may also refer profitably to a passage read out to us by Mr. Farooqi from Sir Thomas Erskine May's Treatise on "The Law, Privileges, Proceedings and Usages of Parliament Act (page 666)." The passage which we quote speaks about the importance of principle of appropriation in relation to ordinary expenditure voted upon estimate and traces also the early history of the practice of the parliament and its development the learned author says:

"The Appropriation of Expenditure-By constitutional practice which has been perfected in the course of two and a half centuries, the application of the grants of supply of the House of Commons to the services for which they are voted is secured annually by legislation, and is enforced outside Parliament by permanent machinery for administering and accounting for the sums issued to departments in accordance with the parliamentary grants. A brief mention has already been made of this external machinery in the preceding chapter (see pp. 654-60), but it is necessary here to recaptitulate the steps in the development of the practice in Parliament itself.

Although some attempts were made by the medieval parliaments to supervise the expenditure of the money they had voted, the practice of appropriation can only be said to have begun in 1668 and did not become regular until after the Revolution. It began as the appropriation of a tax or (later) or a specified sum out of the proceeds of a specially imposed tax. This was effected by a clause in the bill which granted the money or imposed the tax, or, as was usual in the eighteenth century, which both granted the money and imposed a tax to make good the grant Later, it became usual to introduce a bill at the end of the session which recapitulated and appropriated the several grants made by previous Acts of the same session. It was in this practice that the modern Appropriation Act originated. Payments, especially for new purposes outside the ordinary purposes of government, were sometimes charged on the proceeds of an existing tax; and specified taxes were earmarked to provide continuing funds for specified services. When the Consolidated Fund was instituted these separate funds were gradually discontinued, and the services previously provided by these funds were appropriated by being charged directly or indirectly upon the Consolidated Fund.

The importance of the principle of appropriation lies in its relation to ordinary expenditure voted upon estimates, which vary from year to year and reflect every change of policy, rather than in relation to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund, which is payable under continuing statutory authority and is relatively constant. Every step in the development of the appropriation of supply has tended to increase the effectiveness and extent of the control of the House of Commons over the Administration. Among these steps may be noted the establishment of a distinction of procedure between the voting of expenditure and the voting of taxation, the establishment of the Consolidated Fund, the transference of the expenses of civil government from the Civil List to the estimates, and the sub-division and classification of the estimates themselves into distinct votes to be separately appropriated. By these means the principle of appropriation has been made more precise and effective and extended to include the whole range of expenditure of the executive government."

<u>13. Apart from the above quoted passage it seems to us on a close reading of Articles 89, 90, 91 and 92 of the Constitution that there must be a demand for grants for other expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund. Article 92(1) prescribes that Parliament shall have power to authorise by law the withdrawal of money from Consolidated Fund for the purpose of which such grants are made. Under Article 92 Parliament may make law for withdrawal of moneys from the Consolidated Fund, "for the purpose for which such grants are made." Thus, it is seen again that Article 92 also speaks about Consolidated Fund relating to grant. Article 88(e) of the Constitution speaks about Constitution or the Act of Parliament. The Code of Civil Procedure and Bangladesh Bank Order 1972 (president's Order No. 127 of 1972) are Acts of Parliament. In view of what has been discussed above we find no difficulty to hold that the executing Court has acted on the strength of Or. 21, rr. 52 and 56 CPC read with section 71 of the Bangladesh Bank Order 1972 (president's Order No. 127 of 1972) to enforce decree legally, and keeping in view of the aforesaid constitutional provisions and specially Clause (e) of Article 88 of the Constitution we hold that the Governor of Bangladesh Bank is a Public Officer and as an authorised person is legally obliged to obey the direction of the Court for payment of the decretal amount out of the Consolidated Fund for the satisfaction of the decree and for such act no further instrument from the unwilling judgment-debtor, the Ministry of Works of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is required as Mr. Zahir could not place any authority before us to show that the decree is not executable against the Consolidated Fund lying with the Bangladesh Bank. It is worthwhile to state the statement made in paragraph 10 of the Affidavit-in-opposition by the Opposite party 1. Paragraph 10 reads:</u>

<u>"That as stated by the petitioner-bank, this opposite party got an ex parte money decree for a sum of Taka 2,07,520.00 with cost on 7.3.78 in Money Suit No. 8 of 1977 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the opposite parties 2 and 3; that the opposite parties Nos. 2 and 3 as judgment-debtors filed an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that the application under section 47 was allowed in Miscellaneous Case No.121 of 1979 on contest by Order dated 30.1.80, and that against the said order, this opposite party preferred an Appeal from Original Order No. 257 of 1980 in this Hon'ble Court; that a Division Bench comprising Mr. Justice Ranadhir Sen and Mr. Justice Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury allowed the appeal on contest on 14.12.l981 reported in 35 DLR 18; that thereafter this opposite party proceeded with the Execution Case, warsed to attach a vested property, (abandoned under President's Order No. 16 of 1972), but could not, as the law of abandoned property did not sanction of such attachment; that this was held by a Division Bench of this Hon'ble Court comprising Mr. Justice Syed Misbahuddin Hossain and Mr. Justice Bimalendau Bikash Roy Chowdhury in Civil Revision No. 1069 of 1987 filed by this opposite party; that while discharging the Rule, their Lordships, however, observed" .... It is, however, unfortunate that the Government being the judgment debtor failed to clear up the decretal dues in eleven years"; that on the prayer of this opposite party, the Executing Court attached the consolidated fund' of the Republic of Bangladesh under the law, and directed the officials of Bangladesh Bank to remit the decretal sum, which the officials of the bank are bound to comply with under the law." The petitioner Bank simply denied such statement in the affidavit-in-reply which does not afford any assistance to us.</u>

14. From the discussion of the various provisions of the statutory laws and Articles of our Constitution particularly clause (e) of Article 88 of the Constitution we are of the opinion that no error of law or illegality has been committed by the court below resulting in an error in passing the impugned order occasioning failure of justice.

15. Before we part with this judgment we must record deep appreciation for the assistance we received from the learned Advocates at the Bar.

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
This application is directed against an order passed by the Subordinate Judge, Noakhali allowing an application for addition of the heirs of deceased defendant No.1 (cha) under Order 1 rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession pending before her.

2. One Abdul Latif Chowdhury, paternal grandfather of opposite party Nos. 1 to 8 and father of opposite party Nos. 9 and 10 as plaintiffs brought the suit. The original defendant No. 1, predecessor of the petitioners and defendant No. 15 opposed the claim of the plaintiffs by filing 2 separate written statements. The original defendant No. 1 having died leaving behind 3 sons and 3 daughters petitioners 1-5 and one Amena Khatun as his heirs, they were substituted in his place as defendant Nos. 1 (ka) to 1(cha). Defendant No. 1 (cha) namely, Amena Khatun, died on 2nd February, 1990 leaving behind her legal heirs husband, Mohammadullah and 4 sons namely, Tazal Islam, Jafar Ahmed, Bachu Mia and Hasan Ahmed and 2 daughters Sufia Khatun and Zaheda Khatun but the said heirs were not brought on record within the time prescribed under the law.

3. On 26th June, 1990 the petitioners filed an application praying for recording an order of abatement of the suit for the failure of the plaintiffs to bring the heirs of the deceased on record within the period of limitation. On behalf of the plaintiffs an application was thereafter made on 12th July, 1990 for addition of the heirs as defendants under Order 1 rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating, inter alia, that he had no knowledge about the death until the receipt of the application for recording abatement. Both the applications were set down for hearing on 1st September, 1990. On that date the learned Subordinate Judge, after hearing the parties, allowed the application of the plaintiffs but refused the prayer of the petitioners for recording an order of abatement of the suit.

4. Being aggrieved the petitioners have preferred this revisional application.

<u>5. It is submitted on behalf of the petitioners that in view of abatement of the suit taking place owing to non-substitution of the heirs of the deceased defendant, the trial Court has committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order inasmuch as the fact of abatement could not be overcome taking resort to the provision of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate for the petitioners placed reliance on the decision in the case of Bhupati Biswas & others Vs. Niranjan Biswas & others reported in 40 DLR 517 which is distinguishable on facts from the present case.</u>

6. The law on the point is fairly settled. In the case of Rahim Baksha Gazi & others Vs. Enbar Gazi & others 22 DLR (Dhaka) a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court pointed out the legal position in the following words:-

"It is true that in ordinary circumstances the effect of abatement should not be allowed to be got over by securing an addition of the parties.

If the same would be freely permissible then the provisions of Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be rendered nugatory. This, however, did not mean that when there has been an abatement the Court is totally powerless to order addition of parties in respect of the heirs of the deceased on whose account the abatement took place. There are authorities to support the proposition that addition of parties is permissible in respect of the representatives and heirs of the persons relating to whom the suit had abated provided there are sufficient reasons to order that, in the interest of justice".

We find that this view is clearly supported by the observation of their Lordships of the Privy Council in the case of Mohomedally Tyebally and others Vs. Safiabai and others, AIR 1940 PC 215. Rankin, J while expressing the opinion of the Judicial Committee observed as follows:

"It is open to the Judge in his discretion under Order 1, rule 10 to add as a party to the suit the representative of a person against whom the suit has abated for the purpose of giving effect to the rights of the parties".

It is obvious, therefore, that in an appropriate case in the interest of justice, the heirs of a deceased in respect of whom, the suit has abated, can be permitted to be added as parties in the suit."

<u>7. To the same effect is the decision in Ujjal Hossain and others Vs. Firoja Khatun & others 41 DLR (HD) 481.</u>

8. Judging the facts of the case in the light of the principle enunciated in the above-mentioned cases I am of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed no error of law which calls for an interference from this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The application thus merits no consideration and the same is accordingly summarily rejected.

End.
