full_judgment:
A.R.M. Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.: This revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the decree holder Sonali Bank is directed against the order dated 22.4.89 passed by Mr. Tapan Kumar Rudra, Subordinate Judge & Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 23 of 1987.

2. It apears that decree-holder petitioner Sonali Bank obtained a decree in the High Court of  justice Queen's Bench Division, London (England), United Kingdom against the judgment-debtor opposite party Abidur Rahman for a sum of £4,31,845.70 with interest and costs. Thereafter decree-holder-petitioner Sonali Bank under section 44A(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (herein after referred to as the Code) filed the certified copy of the said decree in the Court of the Subordinate Judge & Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka for execution in Bangladesh and Money Execution Case No. 23 of 1987 was started. After entering appearance in Money Execution Case No. 23 of 1987 judgment-debtor opposite party Abidur Rahman filed an application contending, inter alia that the certified copy of the decree under section 44A(1) is to be filed in the District Court, Dhaka (i.e. Court of the District Judge, Dhaka) and that the Subordinate Judge & Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka had no jurisdiction to entertain the certified copy of the decree in question under section 44A(1) of the Code for execution. Upon hearing the parties the learned Subordinate Judge & Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka passed the impugned order dated 22.4.89 holding that he had no jurisdiction to execute the decree in question. Being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 22.4.89 the decree-holder-petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

Section 44A(1) of the Code reads as follows:-

"Where a certified copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in (Bangladesh) as if it had been passed by the District Court."

3. The question before us is whether the certified copy of the decree in question under section 44A(1) of the Code is to be filed in the Court of the District Judge or in the Court of the Subordinate Judge or in either of the Courts. In other words what does the word 'District Court' in section 44A(1) of the Code imply.

4. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the District Court includes not only the Court of the District Judge, but also the Court of the Subordinate Judge as the jurisdiction of each of them extends subject to the provision of section 15 of the Code to all original suits cognizable by civil courts. In this connection Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate referred to Section 15 of the Code and Sections 18 and 19 of the Civil Courts Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act). Relying on section 18 of the Act Mr. Ashratul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the jurisdiction of the District Judge and the Subordinate Judge extends to all original suits cognizable by Civil Courts subject to the pro-vision of section 15 of the Code. Both the Courts have unlimited concurrent pecuniary jurisdiction to try all original suits cognizable by Civil Courts. Both the Courts have been put at par under section 18 though under section 13 of the Act the teritorial jurisdiction of a Subordinate Judge may be limited to a part of the local limits of the jurisdiction of a District Court.

5. Mr. Asrarul Hossain referred to a notification dated 20.10.84 by which the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka has been given teritorial jurisdiction over the whole District of Dhaka (i.e. District Court of Dhaka) in respect of suits relating to Bank loans and other Banking matters. In other words, by this notification the Court of the District Judge of Dhaka and the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1 had been put at par with regard to the territorial jurisdiction of the District of Dhaka (i.e. the District Court of Dhaka). Further, the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka has been given exclusive jurisdiction to try all suits in respect of the matters covered by the above notification. In view of the above notification, he submits that the jurisdiction of the Court of the District Judge has been ousted in respect of the suits covered by the above notification. The Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka has exclusive jurisdiction to take cognizance of the suits covered by the above notification and no other Court including the Court of the District Judge has the jurisdiction to take cognizance of such suits. Mr. Asrarul Hossain also submits that in respect of the suits covered by the above notification the limitation as to pecuniary jurisdiction of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1 under section 19 of the Act will not be applicable inasmuch as the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1 can take cognizance of a suit of any value for recovery of Bank loan. In other words, the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in respect of suits covered by the above notification is not controlled by section 19 of the Act. Both the Courts, the court of District Judge and the Court of the Subordinate Judge, have unlimited concurrent pecuniary jurisdiction to try all original suits cognizable by Civil Courts of which the value exceeds Taka 50,000/-(Section 18 read with section 19 of the Act) Mr. Asrarul Hossain further submits that the decree in question has been passed in respect of a loan advanced by the decree holders petitioner, Sonali Bank, as such the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka had exclusive jurisdiction to entertain the certified copy of the decree in question under Section 44A(1) of the Code. He also referred to section 15 of the Code in support of his contention that the certified copy of the decree in question under section 44A(1) of the Code had rightly been filed in the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka. Under section 15 of the Code every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it and the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka is the Court of the lowest grade competent to try such suit out of which the present decree had been passed.

6. Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite-party, submits that the "District Courts in section 44A(1) of the Code means the Court of the District Judge and no other Court and as such the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka had no jurisdiction to entertain the certified copy of the decree in question. So the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka committed no error of law in passing the impugned order. In this connection Mr. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite-party, referred to section 2(4) of the Code. He submits that the "District Court" means the principal. Civil Court of original jurisdiction of a District. The principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction of a District is the Court of the District Judge and cannot include the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka. The Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka cannot be the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction of the District of Dhaka under section 2(4) of the Code though both the District Judge and the Subordinate Judge have been given concurrent jurisdiction under section 18 of the Act. He submits that only the Court of the District Judge which is the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction of the District has the jurisdiction to entertain the certified copy of the decree in question under section 44A(1) of the Code.

7. To find out the meaning of "District Court" as used in section 44A(1) of the Code, we are to take the aid of Sections 2(4), 3, 15 and 24 of the Code, sections3, 10, 18, 20 and 21 of the Act and section 3(15) of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

8. Sections 3 and 10 of the Act read as under:-

"3. There shall be the following classes of Civil Courts under this Act, namely:-

(1) the Court of the District Judge;

(2) the Court of the Additional Judge;

(3) the Court of the Subordinate Judge and

(4) the Court of the Munsif."

"10. -(1) In the event of the death, resignation or removal of the District Ridge, or of his being incapacitated by illness or otherwise for the performance of his duties, or of his absence from the place at which his Court is held, the Additional Judge or, if an Additional Judge is not present at that place, the Senior Subordinate Judge present thereat shall, Without relinquishing his ordinary duties, assume charge of the office of the District Judge, and shall continue in charge thereof until the, office is resumed by the District Judge or assumed by an officer appointed thereto.

(2) While in charge of the office of the District Judge, the Additional Judge Subordinate Judge, as the case may be; may, subject to any rules which the (High Court Division) may make in this behalf, exercise any of the powers of the District Judge."

9. From a reading of sections 3 and 10 of the Act there is no doubt that the Court of the Subordinate Judge and. Commercial Court No.1 is a Court lower in grade in relation to the Court of the District Judge and the Court of the Additional Judge.

10. Sections 18, 20 and 21 of the Act read as under:-

"18. Save as otherwise provided by any enactment for the time being in force the jurisdiction   of a District Judge or Subordinate judge extends, subject to the provisions of section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to all original suits for the time being cognizable by Civil Courts."

"20. -(1) Save as otherwise provided by any enactment for the time being in force an appeal from a decree or order of a District Judge or Additional Judge shall lie to the (High Court Division).

(2) An appeal shall not lie to the (High Court Division) from a decree or order of an Additional Judge in any case in which, if the decree or order had been made by the District Judge, an appeal would not lie to that Court."

"21. -(1) Save as aforesaid, an 'appeal from a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge shall lie-

(a) to the District Judge where the value of" the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed (seventy thousand taka) and

(b) to the (High Court Division) in any other case.

(2) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a Munsif shall lie to the District Judge.

(3) Where the function of receiving any appeals which lie to the District Judge under sub- section (1) or sub-section (2) has been assigned to an Additional Judge, the appeals may be preferred to the Additional Judge.

(4) The (High Court Division) may, with the previous sanction of the (Government), direct, by notification in the Official Gazelle, that appeals lying to the District Judge under sub-section (2) from all or any of the decrees or orders of any Munsif shall be preferred to the Court of such Subordinate Judge as may be mentioned in the notification, and the appeals shall thereupon be preferred accordingly."

<u>11. Under section 18 of the Act the jurisdiction of a District Judge or a Subordinate Judge extends (subject to provision of section 15 of the Code) to all original suits (for the time being cognizable by civil courts. Both the Courts have concurrent jurisdiction to take cognizance and try all original suits cognizable by Civil Courts. Under section 20 of the Act from a decree or an order of a District Judge or Additional Judge an appeal shall lie to the High Court Division. Under section 21(1)(a) of the Act-from a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge an appeal shall lie to the District Judge where the value of the original suit: in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed Tk. 70,000/-. On a reading of sections 20 and 21 of the Act it is apparent that the Court of the Subordinate Judge is lower in grade in relation to the Court or the District Judge though concurrent jurisdiction has been given to both the Courts under section 18 of the Act.</u>

<u>Section 3 of the Code reads as follows:-</u>

<u>"3. For the purposes of this Code, the District Court is subordinate to the (High Court Division): and every Civil Court of a grade inferior to that of a District Court and every Court of Small Causes is 'Subordinate to the High Court Division and District Court."</u>

12. Under section 3 of the Code every Civil Court of a grade inferior to that of a District Court is subordinate to the District Court. From section 3 of the Act, it is clear that the Court of the Subordinate Judge is of a grade inferior to the Court of the District Judge. Therefore, the Court of the District Judge is superior in grade to that of the Subordinate Judge and the Court of the Subordinate Judge is subordinate to the Court of the District Judge.

13.	Section 24 of the Code reads as follows:-

"24(1) On the application of any of the parties and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, or of its own motion without such notice, the High Court Division or the District Court may at any stage,

(a) transfer any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same, or

(b) withdraw any suit, appeal or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to it, and

(i) try or dispose of the same; or

(ii) transfer the same for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same;  or

(iii) retransfer the case for trial or disposal to the Court from which it was withdrawn.

(2) Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section(1), the Court which thereafter tries such suit may, subject to any special directions in the case of any order of transfer, either try it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

(3) For the purposes of this section, Courts of Additional and Assistant Judges shall be deemed to be subordinate to the District Court.

(4) The Court trying any suit transferred or withdrawn under this section from a Court of Small Causes shall, for the purposes of such suit, be deemed to be a Court of Small Causes."

14. Under section 24(3) of the Code the Courts of Additional and Assistant Judges shall be deemed to be Subordinate to the District Court. In other words, the District Court for the purpose of exercising the power under section 24 of the Code means the Court of the District Judge under section 3(1) of the Act.

Section 2(4) of the Code reads as follows:-

"2(4) "district" means the local limits of the jurisdiction of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction (hereinafter called a "District Court"), and includes the local limits of the ordinary original civil jurisdiction of the High Court Division."

<u>15. Under section 2(4) of the Code a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction of a District is called "District Court." Under section 44A(l) of the Code the certified copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of United Kingdom is to be filed in a District Court for the purpose of executing the same. Therefore we are to find out the meaning of "District Court" as used in section 44A(1) of the Code. In other words, could we regard the Court of the Subordinate Judge having concurrent jurisdiction with the District Judge under section 18 of the Act as the "District Court" under section 44A(1) of the Code. We have considered sections 3 and 24 of the Code and sections 3, 10 and 21 of the Act and come to the conclusion that the Court of the Subordinate Judge is inferior in grade in relation to the Court of the District Judge. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, frankly conceded that in view of section 13 of the Code the decree-holder-petitioner has filed the decree in question for execution in the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1. In other words, the decree had been filed in the Court of the lowest grade for execution. So he frankly concedes that the Court of the District Judge is superior in relation to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Therefore the court of the Subordinate Judge cannot be the principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction of a District called the "District Court" in section 2(4) of the Code.</u>

16. The plain meaning of the word principal as given in the Oxford Dictionary is-first in rank or importance, chief, main, leading, etc. The meaning of principal as given in Chambers dictionary is taking, the first place; highest in rank, character, or importance; chief; etc. The meaning of principal as given in Samsad dictionary is taking the first place, প্রথম স্থানীয়, highest in rank, character, or importance, পদমর্যাদায় গুণে বা গুরুত্বে সর্বোচ্চ; chief, প্রধান, মূখ্য etc. From the ordinary plain meaning of the word principal it is apparent that the Court of the Subordinate Judge can not be regarded as the principal court of original jurisdiction of a district.

17. Section 3(15) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 reads as follows:—

"3(15) "District Judge" shall mean the Judge of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction, but shall not include the High Court Division in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction".

<u>18. The word "District Court" as used in section 44A(1) is primarily to be interpreted with reference to the definition of the "District Court" as given in section 2(4) of the Code. On consideration of the plain meaning of "Principal" as given in the Oxford Dictionary read with section 24 of the Code; and section 3(15) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 we are of the opinion that the "District Court" referred to in section 44A(1) of the Code means the Court of the District Judge under section 3(1) of the Act and no other Court though under section 18 of the Act concurrent jurisdiction had been given to the District Judge and the Subordinate Judge in respect of all original suits cognizable by Civil Courts. Therefore, under section 44A(1) of the Code certified copy of the decree in question is to be filed only in the Court of the District Judge and in no other Court.</u>

19. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has referred to sections 38 and 39 of the Code.

Sections 38 and 39 read as under:—

"38. - A decree may be executed either by the Court which passed it or by the Court to which it is sent for execution.

39.-(1) The Court which passed a decree may, on the application of the decree-holder, send it for execution to another Court—

(a) if the person against whom the decree is passed actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business, or personally works for gain, with-in the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or

(b) if such person has no property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree sufficient to satisfy such decree and has property within the local limits of the jurisdiction of such other Court, or

(c) if the decree directs the sale or delivery of immovable property situate outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court which passed it, or

(d) if the Court which passed the decree considers for any other reason, which it shall record in writing, that the decree should be executed by such other Court.

(2) The Court which passed a decree may of its own motion send it for execution to any subordinate Court of competent jurisdiction."

<u>20. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has referred to the case of Indian General-Investment Trust LTD Vs. Sri Ramchandra 'Mardardja Doo, Raja' of Khalikote, reported in AIR 1952 (Cal) 508. In the instant case, we are not concerned with the transfer of the decree from one Court to another Court for execution of the same. In the is not case we are concerned with the function of receiving or entertaining the decree under section 44A (1,) of the Code. In other words, we are to determine of as to which Court is the proper Court for entertaining or receiving the certified copy of a degree passed by a Superior Court of United Kingdom for executing (he same in Bangladesh. Therefore, sections 38 and 39 of the Code have no manner of application in the instant case. The case reported in AIR 1952 (Cal) 508 does not also help us in any way to determine the question before us.</u>

21.On a query by us, Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, informed us that after the impugned order was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1, Dhaka the plaintiff decree-holder-petitioner Sonali Bank had filed the certified copy of the decree in question in the Court of the District Judge', Dhaka where it is still lying (pending) for disposal.

<u>22. Considering the, contentions of both the parties and the laws discussed above we are of the opinion that the "District Court" mentioned in section 44A(1) of the Code means only the Court of the District Judge. In other words, the certified copy of the decree under section 44A(1) of the Code must be filed in the Court of a "District Judge."</u>

23. For the reasons stated above, we do not find any reason to interfere with the impugned order be the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka.

The rule is accordingly, discharged without any order as to costs. Communicate this order to the District Judge, Dhaka, at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Haque J: Since two appeals, namely, FA No. 47 of 1990 and FMA No. 124 of 1990 have arisen out of one judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, they are heard together and disposed of by the one judgment.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of this case are, that for conduction of bridges and culverts in Comilla-Chandina by-pass project, Government received funds from the International Development Association (IDA), and the Roads and Highways Department of the Government invited tenders on 16.4.80. Titas Prokaushali Limited (TPL), namely, the present appellant submitted tenders along with others for the aforesaid works and being lowest, the appellant got the said works under two contracts known as BC-1(for construction of bridges) and BC-2 (for construction of culverts.) During the construction works on the aforesaid two contracts, several disputes were raised and TPL, namely, the appellant, suffered losses and for that reason they lodged claims during the execution of the works. As par terms of the contracts the disputes, which are 20 in number, were referred by the appellant to the Engineer, a Foreign Consultant, engaged by the Government for supervision of the works, as per conditions of the contract, for decision of the engineer under relevant heads. The Consultant Engineer gave his decisions on the 20 claims lodged by the appellant and being dissatisfied with the decisions of the Consultant Engineer, the appellant wanted to refer the matter for arbitration as per terms of the contract. Ultimately, both the parties agreed to refer the disputes to arbitration and as a result the arbitration entered into a reference on 2.8.84.

3. On 25.8.84 the appellant filed the aforesaid 20 disputes before the Arbitrators with amendment of the claimed-amount in claim No. 1 only of Be-1, and BC-2, Before the Arbitrators the Government filed the written statement on 4.9.84. On 5.9.84 the Arbitrators framed the issues. Thereafter the Arbitrators took evidence of both the parties, heard the arguments and on perusal of the papers and documents on records unanimously gave an award on 10.11.84. It appears that in total the appellant submitted a claim to the Arbitrators for a sum of Taka 1,62,56,189.00. Ultimately, after hearing the parties and perusing the materials on record the Arbitrators gave an award for a sum of Taka 90,52,986.00 in addition to Taka 1,58,097.00 as given by the Consultant Engineer. After passing the aforesaid award the appellant submitted the award before the learned Subordinate Judge for making it a Rule of Court as required under section 14 of the Arbitration Act. As against the award the Roads and Highways Department, the respondent, also filed a case, namely, Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of the learned Subordinate Judge Dhaka, dated 29.11.80 under section 38 of the Arbitration Act. The presentation of the award before the learned Subordinate Judge was registered as Title Suit No. 8 of 1985. Since this Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and the Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 had arisen out of the same award, the learned Subordinate Judge heard both the-cases together and disposed of them by giving one judgment which is before us under challenge. The learned Subordinate Judge, after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record, passed his judgment on 29.11.89 by which the Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 was dismissed and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 was allowed and as a result the award of the Arbitrators dated 18.11.84 was set aside. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in the aforesaid two cases the above appeals have been preferred, one with regard to Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and the other with regard to Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984.

4. From the judgment it appears that the award was set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge on two counts. Firstly, the claims within the contracts must have to be lodged within 30 days from the date of cause of action before the Consultant Engineer as per terms 67(1) of the Contract Since the claims lodged to the Consultant Engineer were beyond the period of 30 days, the terms of the contract have been violated and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge held that the Arbitrators misconducted themselves in giving the award. Secondly, the amounts claimed in 20 disputes before the Consultant Engineer were raised before the Arbitrators. Since the claims made before the Arbitrators were higher than the claims made before the Consultant Engineer, the award has been vitiated and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the award. The respondent-Government raised some other points before the learned Subordinate Judge, but the same were not accepted. Mainly on two counts as stated above the award was set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge. From the judgment it appears that learned Subordinate Judge held that the Arbitrators have misconducted themselves in passing the award and this misconduct was a legal misconduct. There was no finding as to the personal misconduct of the Arbitrators.

5. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in his judgment inasmuch as though the Arbitrators had acted within the bounds of the two contracts and not outside the contracts, the learned Judge illegally set aside the award by the impugned judgment and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. He further submits that all the disputes arose within the limit of the two contracts. Since the Arbitrators had not crossed the limit of the bounds of the contracts and since the Arbitrators had not done or decided or held anything in the award which is totally contrary to any existing provisions of law, the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be sustained in law. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the Court has no authority to set aside the award of the Arbitrators on merit however erroneous or irregular it may be. Only the Court is entitled to set aside an award on the ground of legal misconduct or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators. The provisions for setting aside an award have been incorporated in section 30 of the Arbitration Act which runs as follows:

"Grounds for setting aside award; An award shall not be set aside except on one or more 'of the following grounds, namely:

(a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings;

(b) that an award has been made after the issue of an order by the Court superseding the arbitration or after arbitration proceedings have be come invalid under section 35;

(c) that an award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid."

In interpreting the section it comes to us that an award can be set aside by a court of law only on the ground of legal misconduct or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators or the umpire as the case may be.

6. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that it is alleged in the impugned Judgment that the terms as contained in condition No. 67(1) of the contract had been violated allegedly on the ground that within 30 days from the date of cause of action the disputes were not lodged to the Consultant Engineer. Since terms of contract were violated, the award was set aside. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that this is absolutely a misconception of law, in view of the fact that the Arbitrators had not gone beyond the limit of the contract. During the contract works several exigencies took place as a result of which the appellant lodged claims to the Consultant Engineer. In total 20 claims were lodged to the consultant, but the same were not rejected on the ground that those were not placed before him beyond time; rather some of them were accepted in part and some others were rejected on their own merit, according to the Consultant Engineer. But no ground has been shown that those were placed before him after due time. There might be some irregularities or laches or lapses in performance of the terms and conditions of the contract in between the parties during the contract works, but that is within the periphery and ambit of the contract. Since those disputes had been raised within the bounds of the contract and not beyond the contract, we are of the view that on such ground a Court cannot set aside an award inasmuch as in order to resolve such disputes the parties jointly-referred the matters to arbitration. If such ground is allowed, it will amount to interference into the merit of the award which the Court is not competent to do. It appears from the judgment as well as from the award submitted before us that the 20 disputes arose within the periphery of the two contracts and in order to resolve above claims and disputes both the parties jointly referred those disputes to the Arbitrators. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, was the Arbitrator for the Government and Md. Jamiruddin Sirkar, Bar-at-Law, an Advocate of the Supreme Court, was the Arbitrator for the appellant.

7. Mr. Bhuiyan has drawn our attention to the references to the arbitration which were formed as issues in the arbitration. The issues for the arbitration were as follows:

"I. Whether there was any delay in issuing the letter of Intent, in supplying the construction materials, design, equipment on the part of the Second Party in respect of construction of bridges under Contract No. BC-1 and culverts under Contract No. BC-2, and, if so, whether the First Party is entitled to claim any damage, increase of rates, costs, etc, on this score and to what extent?

2. Whether the First Party is entitled to any damage and compensation, as claimed, during the course of contracts and, if so, to what extent ?"

8. From the issues framed by the Arbitrators it appears to us that disputes within the aforesaid two contracts were referred to the Arbitrators. Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent, submits that since the terms of the contract were violated i.e. the disputes were not lodged before the Consultant Engineer within 30 days from the date of their occurrence, this was clear violation of the terms of the contract and, as such, the Arbitrators had gone beyond the contract and as a result the award has been rightly set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge. It is difficult to accept the contentions of the learned Assistant Attorney-General. The issues as framed for the Arbitration above clearly show that the disputes relating to the aforesaid two contracts were referred before the Arbitrators and it cannot be shown that any of the 20 claims and disputes was outside the bounds of the aforesaid two contracts. Any disputes relating to the aforesaid two contracts can be referred to the Arbitrators and both the parties agreed to refer all the 20 disputes to the Arbitrators. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that this objection was never raised before the Arbitrators as to the time limit of lodging the disputes to the Consultant Engineer. Neither in the written statements nor during argument the respondent raised such objection before the Arbitrators. For the first time the respondent raised it before the learned Subordinate Judge and on such ground learned Subordinate Judge set aside the award. From the 20 claims and disputes as referred to in the award it appears to us that all the disputes were within the ambit and bounds of the two contracts, namely, contract No. BC-1 and contract No.BC-2. In that view of the matter we hold that the finding as regards time limit of lodging the dispute before the Consultant Engineer cannot be accepted and on that ground the learned Subordinate Judge is not empowered to set aside the award in question.

9. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that first the claims were lodged before the Consultant Engineer showing claims of specified amounts in different disputes. When the claims were placed before the Arbitrators, only there were some variations as to the amounts of the claims. The claims were alright, but some enhancement was made in respect of the amount after assessment and verification of the works done during contract. He submits that such enhancement of amount of claim here and there will not vitiate in any manner the award of the Arbitrators in view of the fact that all the disputes were referred to the Arbitrators after the same were previously considered by the Consultant Engineer. Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, on the other hand, submits that since their claims were different to the Arbitrators than the claims made before the Consultant Engineer, the same cannot be accepted and, as such, the award itself is vitiated. It is difficult to accept the above contention of the learned Assistant Attorney-General in view of the fact that the disputes as a whole within the bounds of the contracts were referred to the Arbitrators jointly by both the parties. The amount of claim is not a material factor. The amount may be higher or may be lower after total verification, assessment and checking up the whole works. Since the disputes with regard to the claims were referred to the Arbitrators which were within the bounds of the contract as stated above, we are of the view that the setting aside of the award on that ground of claiming some higher amount before the Arbitrators will not vitate the award itself and as a result the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge on that ground cannot be sustained in law.

<u>10. As regards the sanctity and propriety of an award passed under the Arbitration Act, particularly with regard to an "unanimous award", Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has referred to several decisions of the Higher Courts of this Sub-Continent. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that section 30 of the Arbitration Act starts with a negative compulsion clause, namely, "an award shall not be set aside excepting on one or more of the following grounds," that means a compulsion in negative terms has been added which means that beside in exceptional cases an award of the Arbitrators should not be touched. He has referred to the case of Smt. Santa Shaila Devi. Vs. Dhirendra Nath Sen, AIR 1963 (SC), 1677. In the aforesaid judgment it was described as to what would be the attitude of the Court towards an award. It was held there that the Court attitude must always be to support it and not to destroy it. Two other decisions reported in AIR 1924 (All.) 800 and AIR (Bom) 296 show that court of law should not touch the award on merit. The Court can only touch the award if it can be shown that there was legal or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators, because in an arbitration the parties must choose their own judges at their own choice and they must be bound by the decision of their own judges. It means, neither of the parties can retract from its own judgment. Court cannot substitute the reasonings of the Arbitrators. Nowhere in the whole judgment the learned. Subordinate Judge has found anything to the effect that the Arbitrators went beyond the reference or contract or the issues which relate to the two contracts made between the parties. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that mere criticism of the award, however strong it may be, will not vitiate the award and in support of this contention be has referred to the case of Kripa Sindhu Biswas Vs. Sudha Biswas, AIR 1973 (Cal) 496. In the judgment of the case of Fazal and others Vs. State 43 DLR 41, a single Bench of this Court held that the Court which is required to make the award a Rule of the Court and before whom the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act is filed is not a Court of appeal. Having participated in the arbitration of their own accord the parties cannot raise any dispute as to the issues before the Arbitrators which are decided unanimously. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the main two objections as were not in fact raised and agitated before the Arbitrators and for the first time they were agitated before the learned Subordinate Judge and, as such, no issue was framed by the Arbitrators on such points. Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to the case of Ghulam Abbas Vs. Trustees of the Port of Karachi PLD 1987 (SC) 393 wherein it was held by their Lordships that even if the award is wrong, even then it cannot be the subject of review by the Court. Arbitrators are the judges in all questions of facts as well as law and, as such, the decision of the Arbitrators should not be interfered with by the Court. In the decision reported in AIR 1963 (SC) it is held by their Lordships that in a proceeding of setting aside an award it is not open to the Court to reappreciate the evidence and to sit in appeal over the conclusion the Arbitrators arrived at. In the case of the President of Union of India Vs. Kalinga Construction Ltd, AIR 1971 (SC) 1946, it is held that objection against an award is not to be heard as if it were an appeal against the decision of the Arbitrators.</u>

<u>11. Upshot of all the above decisions appears to us that when an award is unanimously passed by the Arbitrators the court of law shall not interfere in it except in a very rare case where the Arbitrators have misconducted themselves on any legal point or in the personal dealings. As regards legal misconduct we are of the view that if the Arbitrators have done anything in deciding the matter or in passing the award contrary to any specific provision of law, that can be treated as legal misconduct. Further, this legal misconduct can be extended to the extent that if the Arbitrators have done anything beyond the contract or beyond the reference or beyond the issues, in that case also it can be termed as legal misconduct. As to personal misconduct we are of the view that it relates to the personal dealings of the Arbitrators in conducting the proceeding of an award in a case. In the present case there is no finding as to personal misconduct; rather there is finding of legal misconduct. So, considering the materials on record and the judicial pronouncements on arbitration award as referred to above, we hold that there having been no legal misconduct of the arbitrators the learned Subordinate Judge illegally set aside the award in question and, as such, his judgment cannot be sustained.</u>

12. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that at the time of filing objection against the award under section 30 of the Arbitration Act the aggrieved party must file an application with security of at least 50% of the awarded amount, but in the present case when the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act was filed before the learned Subordinate Judge no such security was given rather, the Superintending Engineer on behalf of the Government had given an undertaking with the application. Subsequently, the Government ratified the undertaking of the Superintending Engineer beyond the period of 30 days. He submits that such undertaking docs not fulfil the requirements of the provisions of section 30 as amended. It appears that on 9.2.84 the Superintending Engineer had submitted an undertaking on behalf of the present respondent which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry of Communication, Government of Bangladesh on 24.11.88 by a Memorandum. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that such an undertaking is not a legal security as contemplated under the law. So-called ratification by the Government came long after the period of limitation and, as such, this undertaking cannot be accepted. A similar argument was advanced before the learned Subordinate Judge. It is true that the Superintending Engineer had given an undertaking at the time of filing of the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. Security means that it must be something positive to be placed before the Court on which the party can easily realise the amount through Court if it is decided in its favour. In the present case the undertaking was given by the Superintending Engineer on behalf of the Government which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry. Since Government is that party here which filed the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act and since such a responsible officer of the Government had given an undertaking on behalf of the Government which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry of the Government, in the peculiar circumstances of this particular case, we hold, it can be treated as a sufficient security and compliance of the provisions of law. In that regard the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge do not require any interference by us; rather we find that the findings are very much cogent, reasonable and legal. So this objection of Mr. Bhuiyan has no substance.

13. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that when the disputes were lodged before the Consultant Engineer of the Government, in some of the disputes the claim was straightaway rejected and in some of the disputes claims were partially accepted, but the learned Subordinate Judge has set aside the award as a whole ignoring even the admitted amount. Such an award cannot be sustained in law.

14. Arbitrator is not a court and arbitration proceeding is not a court proceeding. Bangali meaning of the word arbitration is “সালিশ”. In our view, such Salish is some sort of endeavour for amicable settlement of the disputes in between the parties through the arbitrators (Salishdars) without going to' the Court. It is not required to follow all the procedures of a legal proceeding like a Court of law. It is same thing like voluntary give and take in between the parties without entering into legal proceeding in a Court of law for speedy benefit or relief to the parties who mutually agree upon to do it. So, the Court must not touch the award except on the ground of misconduct of the Arbitrators or umpire.

15. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in setting aside the unanimous award in question in view of the fact that he failed to show any legal misconduct on the part of the Arbitrators. If on such flimsy grounds, which were not even agitated before the Arbitrators, an award is allowed to be set aside, then we are afraid, the sanctity of the award given under law cannot be safeguarded. We disapprove of such attitude of the Court in view of the fact that the Court does not sit as a Court of appeal over the award and it cannot touch the award on merit. But in the present case we find the learned Subordinate Judge has touched the award on merit by usurping the functions of the arbitrators. Such an action without jurisdiction is totally disapproved by us.

In the result, both the appeals are allowed and the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 along with Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 are hereby set aside. In respect of Title Suit No. 8 of 1985, left the award be made Rule of the Court and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 is dismissed. The trial Court is directed to draw up the decree in accordance with law.

Send down the LC records immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J.: These two appeals are directed against the judgment and decree dated 27.06.74 passed in Probate Case No. 6 of 1973 (20 of 1972) and Letters of Administration Case No. 7 of 1973 (22 of 1972) and Miscellaneous Case No. 469 of 1972 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka.

2. The respondents here were the petitioners before the learned District Judge and the objector-opposite party No. 1 before the learned District Judge is the appellant before this court. There are two cases, one for probate and another for Letters of Administrate in respect of the suit property. The case of the petitioner-respondents is that one Protab Chandra Das was the land holder and resident of 48, North Brook Hall Road. He possessed considerable movable and immovable properties. At the time of his death he left behind his widow Preomoyee Das and son Shirish Chandra Das. Wife of Shirish Chandra Das was Rajjaswari Chowdhurain. Shirish Chandra Das had four daughters, namely, Sharojini, Promila Sundari, Sukumari and Indomati. This Sharojini had five sons, namely, Nirmal, Bimal, Amal, Sudhangshu and (Monmoth, predeceased). As Shirish Chandra Das had no sons, he adopted Nirmal, son of Sharojini and after adoption this Nirmal was mimed as Sudhir Chandra Das. This Sudhir Chandra Das died on 7th June, 1970. Sudhir Chandra Das was childless and his wife was Trinayani. On 20th May, 1969 this Sudhir Chandra Das made a testamentary disposition of his property vide a will, Ext 7, which was registered on 22nd May, 1969. As Sudhir Chandra Das had no child, all his properties were given in absolute right to his wife Trinayani. By the aforesaid will Trinayani was appointed as sole executrix and the sole legatee under the will. After the death of Sudhir Chandra Das, his widow Trinayani had been enjoying and administering the entire property left by Sudhir Chandra Das.

3. On 22nd September, 1971 Trinayani presented an application for probate of the Will in the court of the District Delegate at Dhaka and this application was registered as Probate Case No. 10 of 1971. But, unfortunately, this Trinayani died on 29th July, 1972, before she could obtain the probate. Trinayani during her life time made a will (Ext. 15) duly executed and registered on 4th March, 1972 bequeathing all her properties in favour of her four brothers' sons who are the petitioners in Letters of Administration Case No. 22 of 1972. These four applicants filed an application before the District Delegate praying for permission to continue the proceeding as substituted heirs in place of Trinayani in Probate Case No. 10 of 1971. But at the death of the sole executrix who was made the sole legatee under the will of Sudhir Chandra Das died during pendency of the probate case, the right to sue did not survive and the proceeding in Probate Case No. 10 of 1971 abated. The present petitioners made fresh applications for grant of Letters of Administration with a copy of the will annexed in their own right under section 233 of the Succession Act and this application was registered as Letters of Administration Suit No. 22 of 1972 which was renumbered as Letters of Administration Case No.7 of 1973 and in respect of the will of the Trinayani they had applied for grant of probate and this probate case was registered as Probate Suit No. 20 of 1972, renumbered as Probate Suit No. 6 of 1973.

4. The objectors in this Letters of Administration Suit and Probate Suit are three natural brothers of Nirmal Kumar Chowdhury, who was subsequently adopted under the name of Sudhir Chandra Das by Shirish Chandra Das. The objectors filed written objection assailing the genuineness of both the wills and maintained that the petitioners are not entitled to get Letters of Administration in respect of the alleged wills of Sudhir Chandra Das and Trinayani Das. In respect of the will of Trinayani Das claimed the suit property as reversionary heirs of Sudhir Chandra Das and they have pleaded in defence that this Trinayani died as Muslim woman, the passing of the properties to the hands of the petitioners is illegal, inasmuch as they arc trespassers therein and they instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 469 of 1972 for appointment of receiver. Both the parties filed several affidavits and counter-affidavits in the aforesaid proceedings. The petitioner-respondents, examined as many as 9 witnesses in these cases whereas the objector appellant examined 5 witnesses in their favour. Petitioner respondents filed several papers and documents which have been marked as Exts. 1 to 20 (a). The documents and papers filed by the objector-appellant were marked as Exts. A to Ext. O. After considering the material evidence on record and hearing the parties the learned District Judge passed the judgment on 27th June, 1974 decreeing the aforesaid Letters of Administration Suit and Probate Suit in favour of the petitioner respondents and rejecting the Miscellaneous Case for appointment of receiver. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the objector opposite party No. 1 preferred this appeal before this court. Out of the three objector-opposite parties only Bimal Chandra Chowdhury preferred this appeal and other two objectors were shown as proforma respondent Nos. 5 and 6, but both are dead.

5. We will consider the relevant exhibits at the time of discussion of the points raised by the learned Advocates. As regards oral evidence it may be mentioned that PW 1 stated that he came to know that Sudhir made a will, Ext. 7, in favour of his Pishi Trinayani. Further, he proved the will Ext.15 executed by Trinayani in his favour and his other brothers. He also stated that in sound health and free mind she executed the will Ext. 15 in presence of witnesses. PW 2 is the attested witness in Ext. 15. He stated that Trinayani signed in his presence and others and she was in sound mind and good health PW 3 is an attesting witness in the will Ext. 7. He proved execution of Ext. 7 stating that Sudhir signed the will in presence of witnesses and he was in good health and sound and free mind. PW4 is also an attesting witnesses of Ext. 7 who proved the execution of the will by Sudhir. Both PWs 3 and 4 stated that though they were not present at the time of execution of will Ext. 15, yet Trinayani told them that she executed the will Ext. 15 in favour of her brothers sons. PW 6 was the scribe of Ext. 7. He proved the execution of the will Ext 7. He made a detailed statement in favour of the petitioner respondents. He further stated that though he was not present at the time of execution of Ext. 15, Trinayani told him that she executed this will Ext.15 in favour of her brothers sons. PW 7 is the scribe of the will Ext. 15 and PWs 8 and 9 are the attesting witnesses of the will Ext. 15. They all proved the execution of Ext.15 by Trinayani stating that the testator Trinayani executed it out of her free will and mind and in sound health. Amongst the PWs. PW 4 was the relation of Sudhir, even then he deposed in favour of the petitioner-respondents. PWs also stated that Trinayani did not embrace Islam as she performed all the religious rites of the Hindus till her death.

6. DW No. 1 is the objector Bimal Chandra Chowdhury himself. He stated that Ext. 7, the will, is not a genuine document. He further stated that in 1928 Sudhir made another will Ext N. But the copy of the will in original was with Sudhir. Trinayani had life-interest after the death of Sudhir and after the death of Trinayani, the properties of Sudhir would revert back to the objectors as they were the brothers of Sudhir (Nirmal). DW 2 stated that by affidavit dated 15.5.71 one Trinayani became Muslim. During that period many people became Muslim by swearing affidavit. DW 3 is an employee of former Habib Bank Ltd. Sadarghat Branch Dhaka. On 5.8.71 Trinayani opened Bank account No. 3931 there and she was identified by one Munira Begum whose CD account number was 3924. DW 4 is the clerk of Advocate Md. Ali Karim Siddiqui. He stated that one Trinayani had sworn the affidavit on 15.5.71 embracing Islam and he identified Trinayani in the affidavit.

7. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the Exts 7 and 15, namely, the two impugned wills, one by Sudhir Chandra Das and another by Trinayani Das, were not the legal documents in view of the fact that those were not executed in accordance with law. Since these two exhibits cannot be accepted in the eye of law as valid documents, the property of Sudhir Chandra Das who is the natural brother of the objectors will revert to the reversionaries, namely, the objectors. We have perused these Exts. 7 and 15. It appears that Ext. 7 was registered in 1969 and Ext. 15 was registered in the year 1972. From the evidence of PWs 1-9 it is apparent that both the exhibits were proved by the attesting witnesses which we have discussed above. On this point the learned District Judge made elaborate discussion and gave his detailed findings. We fully affirm the findings of the learned District Judge and hold these two documents were registered in accordance with law and the petitioner respondents have been able to prove these two documents to be genuine and valid executed and registered in accordance with law. So, the submission of Mr. SC Das has got no substance.

<u>8. Mr. SC Das then submits that the adoption of Sudhir Chandra Das, who was previously named as Nirmal Chowdhury and who was full brother of the three objectors was not done in accordance with section 480(3) of the Hindu Law. Since this adoption was made contrary to the provision of Hindu Law, the adoption itself was illegal and void and as such this Sudhir Chandra Das had no legal authority over the properties of Shirish Chandra Das and to transfer the suit properties by way of will in favour of his wife Trinayani. Mr. Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner respondents, submits that the adoption was taken in the year 1906 while Sudhir (Nirmal) was aged about 5/6 years and upto the death of Sudhir Chandra Das in 1970 no objection was taken by anybody. Mr. Zakir Hossain has drawn our attention to sections 513, 513A and 514 of the Hindu Law. From the provisions of the aforesaid sections of Hindu Law it appears that if anybody wants to challenge any adoption in court, the limitation is six years from the date of taking adoption. Mr.Zakir Hossain further submits that this type of objection was neither taken in the written objection nor in the oral depositions of the DWs, nor it was made an issue in the suits, nor it was argued during hearing of the aforesaid suits before the learned District Judge. For the first time they are raising this objection before this Appellate Court in 1993 after 87 years from the date of adoption of Sudhir Chandra Das. He further submits that being the natural brothers they cannot raise this type of objection before this court inasmuch as their full brother was taken in adoption by late Shirish Chandra Das. It is difficult for us to entertain such a preposterous argument at this stage by one of the objectors before this court at the time of hearing of the appeal. The adoption was taken in the year 1906 and till the death of Sudhir Chandra Das in 1970 his brothers did not raise any objection whatsoever. They slept over the matter for a period of 87 years and after such long time they woke up from slumber and on one fine morning suddenly discovered an absurd story to the effect that the adoption of Sudhir Chandra Das made in the year 1906 is illegal and void. We with much patience, allowed Mr. Das to waste Court's valuable time to make such absurd submissions.</u>

9. It is their case that since the adoption was void ab initio the objector can raise objection at any stage of the proceeding and in support of their contentions the appellant has referred to section 480(3) of the Hindu law. Section 480(3) runs as follows:

"Who may be adopted-subject to the following rules any person who is a Hindu, may be taken or given in adoption.

(1) the person to be adopted must be a male;

(2) he must belong to the same caste as his adopting father; thus a Brahman cannot adopt a Kshatriya, a Vashya or a Shudra; it is not necessary that he should belong to the same sub-division of the caste;

(3) he must not be a boy whose mother the adopting father could not have legally married; but this rule has been restricted in many recent cases to the daughter's son, sister's son and mother's sister's son.

This prohibition, however, does not apply to Shudras, Even as to the three upper classes, it has been held' that an adoption though prohibited under this rule, may be valid, if sanctioned by custom".

<u>10. From the aforesaid provisions it appears to us that there was prohibition no doubt, but at the same time there was relaxation in that law. So, in this matter this Sudhir Chandra Das was the daughter's son of Shirish and as such we find that this type of adoption cannot be void ab initio under the Hindu law. Considering the above, we are of the view that such an objection as regards adoption of Sudhir Chandra Das which took place in the year 1906 cannot be entertained by us.</u>

11. Mr. Das further submits that Exts. 7 and 15, the two wills, had not given to the executrix the full right over the property. In Ext. 7, if any right is given, it is at best a life interest of Trinayani and after the death of Trinayani the present objector appellant and his brothers will inherit the property of Sudhir. Since no absolute right was given to Trinayani, Trinayani had no right to alienate the property by will or otherwise. We have gone through the language of the two wills. Mr. Zakir Hossain, on the other hand, submits that the contents of the two wills must be read and construed as a whole and if the contents are read as a whole, it will appear that the absolute right was given to the respective executrix in these two wills. Mr. Zakir Hossain in this connection has referred to Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th Edition, Vol. 50, page 213, para 370. This paragraph 370 of Halsbury's Laws of England runs as follows:

"Functions of the court of construction. The cardinal rule of English law as to the effect of a will is that the testator's intention, as declared by him and apparent in the words of his will, has effect given to it, so far and as nearly as may be consistent with law. The application of the rule requires a court of construction to consider two matters (1) the intention of the testator disclosed by the will and (2) the manner in which effect can be given to that intention. In ascertaining the testator's intention, it is a settled principle that his intention is to be sought in the words that he has used in his will given, normally, their natural and grammatical meaning, but that meaning can admit of modification to accord with a real intention shown by the will as a whole".

12. We have considered the very language of the two wills, Exts. 7 and 15 The fundamental principle in granting a will is this that an intention of the testator must be expressed in clear language and the testator must be in sound mind and health. From the language of the Exts. 7 and 15 and also from the evidence of PWs 1-9 it appears to us that the two wills were executed by the testators in accordance with law and by those two wills absolute right to own and possess the suit properties was given to the legatees and as such we do not find any illegality in the aforesaid two documents, namely, Exts. 7 and 15 The learned District Judge has also made elaborate discussions on this point and found that the two wills were executed in accordance with law. We have no reason to interfere with the findings of the learned District Judge.

13. Mr. Das further submits that Trinayani instituted Probate Case No. 10 of 1971 for getting the probate from the learned District Judge in pursuance of the will given to her by her husband and during the pendency of that probate case and before getting the probate Trinayani died in the year 1972. So, whatever right Trinayani had over this matter ceased to exist with her death and the probate case abated as a whole and as a result the reversionaries of Sudhir Chandra Das will get the properties of Sudhir Chandra Das. In support of this point Mr. SC Das has failed to point out any provision in Hindu Law or in the Succession Act or in any judicial pronouncement. It is simply his argument. Mr. Zakir Hossain, on the other hand, has drawn our attention to sections 232, 233 and 234 of the Succession Act. Sections 232, 233 and 234 run as follows:

232When-

(a) the deceased has made a will, but has not appointed an executor, or

(b) the deceased has appointed an executor who is legally incapable or refuses to act, or who has died before the testator or before he has proved the will, or,

(c) the executor dies after having probate of the will, but before he has administered all the estate of the deceased.

an universal or a residuary legatee may be admitted to prove the will, and letters of administration with the will annexed may be granted to him of the whole estate, or of so much thereof as may be unadministered.

233. When a residuary legatee who has a beneficial interest survives the testator, but dies before the estate has been fully administered, his representative has the same right to administer with the will annexed as such residuary legatee.

234. When there is no executor and no residuary legatee or representative of a residuary legatee, or he declines or is incapable to act, or cannot be found, the person or persons who would be entitled to the administration of the estate of the deceased if he had died intestate, or any other legatee having a beneficial interest, or a creditor, may be admitted to prove the will, and letters of administration may be granted to him or them accordingly.

14. In the present case it appears that Trinayani got the will in the year 1969 and filed this Probate Case No. 10 of 1971 in the court of the learned District Judge for obtaining probate. But during continuance of the proceeding she died in the year 1972 and she could not obtain any probate. In pursuance of the provisions of the above quoted sections we hold that though Trinayani could not get the probate, but she being the universal legatee was entitled to the whole of the property as covered by the will and before obtaining the probate she executed a will in favour of the present petitioner respondents. Since she had the legal right over the estate by virtue of the will, she had every legal right to alienates the property during her life time. As such the second will will be valid in the eye of law and as a result the petitioner-respondents are entitled to the property of the will as given by Trinayani in the year 1972. Considering the above, we are of the view that in pursuance of the provisions of section 233 and the application for Letters of Administration and the application for probate filed in the Court of the learned District Judge are maintainable and the petitioner-respondents have got the legal right to proceed with these two suits in the court below.

15. Lastly Mr. SC Das submits that in the year 1971 this Trinayani embraced Islam and after embracing Islam she had no authority under the Hindu Law to execute and register a Will in favour of the petitioner-respondents. In support of his contention he has referred to a copy of affidavit, Ext T, by which the learned Advocate tried to show that Trinayani by swearing affidavit on 15th May, 1971 embraced Islam. In this connection Mr. SC Das has referred to section 7(3) of the Hindu Law. DW 2 stated in his deposition that many people embraced Islam in 1971 and one Trinayani had solemnly affirmed an affidavit and she was identified by his learned Advocate. Mr. Zakir Hossain, on the other hand, submits that this piece of paper, namely, typed copy of such affidavit is not admissible in evidence. Further, he submits that the two witnesses of the defendants did not say anywhere that they knew Trinayani, wife of Sudhir Chandra Das and that Trinayani had sworn the affidavit. In view of the above it is difficult for us to accept the Ext. T as exhibit and valid evidence in the eye of law.

16. Further, Mr. Zakir Hossain submits that Trinayani executed her Will, Ext 15 in 1972. She was admitted in a clinic at Dhaka and when she was burnt in Shashan Ghat the certificate from the Shashan Ghat will show that she was Hindu by religion and everything was done according to Hindu rites and also all ceremonies were performed according to the system of Hindus. Deposition of DW 3, application for probate dated 22.9.71, registered deed of Will Ext. 15 dated 4.3.72, Shashanghat receipt Ext. 4 dated 29.7.72 and Medical Officer's receipt Ext. 3 dated 29.7.72 clearly proved that Trinayani was a Hindu lady till her death. On this point the learned District Judge had discussed in his judgment in details. The learned District Judge has considered this rnauer even to that effect that in the year 1971, that is, during liberation period even a man in order to save his life embraced Islam that will not be a legal embracement. But after the danger is over, if any man performs his religious rites according to Hindu law, then this mere show of acceptance of different religion will not disentitle him from his own religion and property. This is an unfortunate argument advanced by Mr. SC Das taking an advantage of an event of the year 1971 when many people did many things in order to save their lives in this country. In this case, in view of so many evidence that Trinayaniup to her death was a Hindu and she performed all religious rites and ceremonies according to Hindu law, the above argument of Mr. Das vanished in the air. We strongly disapprove such type of argument with regard to a person who even out of fear might have done something in the year 1971. It may be mentioned that before 1971 this Trinayani had got absolute right and interest in the suit property by virtue of Ext. 7. On this point the lengthy discussion of the learned District Judge has got full substance and we have nothing to interfere with the findings of the learned District Judge. In this case section 7(3) of the Hindu Law has no manner of application.

17. About the Ext. N the alleged Will dated 1.10.28 we fully accept the findings of the learned District Judge inasmuch, as learned Advocate has failed to satisfy us that it was the last Will of Sudhir Chandra Das. Considering the evidence on record we hold that the above alleged Will cannot be accepted as valid piece of evidence in the eye of law.

18. Mr. JK Paul, who appeared on behalf of the proforma-respondents, in fact submitted that the adoption of Sudhir Chandra Das was void ab initio and it will continue as void and it cannot be rectified and the provision of limitation will not be applicable in this case. We have answered to the submissions above when we discussed the arguments on this point advanced by Mr. SC Das.

19. An application dated 01.09.93 was filed by the learned Advocate Mr. Mir Mokhlesure Rahman allegedly on behalf of Hitendra Kumar Chowdhury who is respondent No. 4 in this appeal before us. In the application it is stated that this respondent No. 4 never executed any vokalatnama nor power of attorney in favour of Mr. Zakir Hossain, Advocate, nor he did appoint Mr. Zakir Hossain as an Advocate and constituted attorney nor an Advocate on his behalf. It is further stated that his signature in the vokalatnama is forged. This man Hitendra Kumar Chowdhury lived in Murshidabad, West Bengal, India. Affidavit was sworn by one Srimati Shantimovee Dey, wife of late Monshacharan Dey.

20. Mr. Zakir Hossain submits that this is absolutely a false and frivolous application in view of the fact that this four brothers petitioners, who are respondents here had given him power and authority to conduct the aforesaid cases in the Lower Court and they also had given power to conduct the appeal before this court. The power given by Hitendra Kumar Chowdhury appears to be a frivolous and concocted one in view of the fact that how this vokalatnama came from India had not been described in the application. Since this alleged Hitendra Kumar Chowdhury lives in India and allegedly sent this power from India, it ought to have been authenticated or endorsed by the Notary Public or by any other relevant authority so that the court may take cognizance of a foreign document. There is no folding mark of this vokalatnama allegedly signed by Hitendra Kumar Chowdhury from India. It is a plain vokalatnama having no folding mark. If it came from India, its appearance would have been otherwise. From the appearance of this vokalatnama it appears that it was concocted and manufactured in the very chamber of the learned Advocate Mr. Mir Mokhlesur Rahman. This sort of frivolous application and concocted power cannot be entertained at this stage of the appeal and as such we disapprove such conduct of the learned Advocate and accordingly we are rejecting this frivolous application.

21. We have gone through the judgment of the trial Court and we are of the view that the learned District Judge has considered each and every point in details relying on the material evidence on record and as such we find no reason to interfere with any of the findings of the learned District Judge. In this view of the matter we find that there is no substance in these appeals and accordingly they are liable to be dismissed.

22. In the result, both the appeals are dismissed with costs and the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge are by affirmed.

Send down the LC records immediately to the trial Court.

End.
