full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury, J.: This Rule was issued calling upon opposite parties 1-4 to show cause why the order dated 23.11.92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 19 of 1989 shall not be set aside.

2. The petitioner's case, in short, is that they as plaintiff instituted Money Suit No. 19 of 1989 before he aforesaid Court against opposite parties 1-5 and also proforma defendant No. 6 for realisation of Taka 1,40,53,942.00, but during the pendency of the suit the plaintiff-petitioner dropped their claim against opposite party No. 5 as he has not purchased the shares of opposite party No. 1, though opposite party No. 6 has been impleaded but no relief was claimed against him. The case of the petitioner also is that it is an international lease finance Company comprising of five international organisations and two local ones and they carryon business of lease finance of machineries rented by industrial concerns under standard lease agreements. That opposite parties 1-4 leased out machineries mentioned in 'Ka' Schedule of the plaint and according to the lease agreement, the opposite party was to select the machineries and arrange for import and setting up of the same within four weeks of their arrival. Their further case is that the machineries were imported from India and carried to the factory site of the opposite parties 1-4 at the cost of the plaintiff but those machineries were not installed and when after repeated reminders the opposite parties failed to execute the lease by giving a certificate, that the same were installed, the plaintiff had to file the Money suit for realisation of Taka 1,40,52,942.00 for damages as rent, cost of the machineries, etc. It is also the case of the plaintiff-petitioner that the defendants mortgaged 'Kha' Schedule property as security for carrying out obligations under the lease.

3. Before the trial Court opposite-parties 1-4 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing written statement and their case is that they failed to install the machineries in time due to the fault of the erectors and gas supply. The Money Suit was ultimately decreed on contest by the trial Court by judgment dated 16.1.92 and the decree was drawn up on 16.2.92. Thereafter the decree was put into execution but at that time it came to the notice of the petitioner that instead of directing sale of the mortgaged 'Kha' schedule property by foreclosure the trial Court directed foreclosure of plaint Schedule 'Ka' property. The petitioner then by a petition moved the trial Court for amendment of the judgment and decree by incorporating 'Kha' schedule property in place of 'Ka' schedule property. The learned Subordinate Judge, thereafter, by order dated 23.11.1992 rejected the petition filed under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff-petitioner then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

4. Dr. M Zahir, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the trial Court while passing the judgment wrongly mentioned 'Ka' schedule property in the ordering portion instead of 'Kha' schedule property. He argued that this 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged with the plaintiff by opposite party Nos. 1-4 and 'Ka' schedule properties were handed over to the defendants on a rental basis meaning thereby that the 'Ka' schedule property belong to the plaintiff and by selling the property of the plaintiffs' their claims against the defendants cannot be satisfied. He further submits that for security of the loan advanced 'Kha' schedule property was earlier mortgaged with the plaintiff. So, the inclusion of 'Ka' schedule property instead of 'Kha' schedule property is a mistake or omission which may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and for finding out the mistake the Court 'can' look into not only the judgment but other materials, i.e. the pleadings of the parties. Dr. Zahir contends that the trial Court wrongly found that there was no clerical or arithmetical mistake or omission by mistake so that the provision of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure may be invoked. According to Dr. Zahir the trial Court ought to have looked into the pleadings of the parties and find out the mistake which is apparent on the face of the record or the cases of the respective parties.

5. As against this Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not contemplate such correction. The decree may be corrected if it is not in conformity with the judgment. Here, in this case the decree is in full conformity with the judgment If anything is to be done for variance of the judgment as submitted by Dr. Zahir, his remedy lies either in a petition for review of the judgment or in appeal. The trial Court cannot correct the judgment under the provision of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure as it is not a clerical or arithmetical mistake or mistake on omission. He argued that the trial Court consciously by its own hand incorporated the last portion of the sentence, that is, the foreclosure of the plaint 'Ka' schedule property. So, it cannot be found that this is a typing mistake. This portion of the ordering portion of the judgment was written by the Judge himself. So the correction of this, if any, must be by an appeal or a review petition but not under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If any error in the judgment is to be corrected it must be corrected either by an appeal or by review but not in the manner as prayed for by the plaintiff.

6. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties lastly contends that the petition filed by the plaintiff for correction is barred by limitation as he had notice of the decree at least when he got the certified copy of the decree and put it into execution. Such petition for correction is not contemplated under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Before proceeding further let us see what section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides. It runs as follows:

"152. Clerical or arithmetical mistake in judgments, decrees or orders or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected by the Court either of its own motion or on the application of any of the parties".

8. So, from a perusal of this provision of section 152 of the Code it appears that any clerical or arithmetical mistake in judgment, decrees, or orders or errors arising therein, that is, in the judgments and decrees or orders or errors from any accidental slip or omission may be corrected by the Court at any time either of its own motion or on the application filed by an aggrieved party.

9. Dr. M. Zahir while arguing the case submits that the language of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure is wide enough to include any accidential slip or omission of which the source may be somewhere other than the judgment and decree. He submits that the machineries imported were leased out to the defendants on rental basis. That is the clear plaint case which has not been denied by the defendants. He also submits that 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged with the plaintiff by the defendants as a security for their advance which also has not been denied. When 'Ka' schedule property admittedly belonged to the plaintiff and leased out to the defendant on rental basis the decree cannot be satisfied by selling their own properties which very well indicate that the insertion of word 'Ka' in the ordering portion of the judgment is a mistake committed by the trial Court. He further submits that the question of foreclosure comes when a property is mortgaged and in this case 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged by the defendants. At our instance the parties placed the plaint and the written statement for our perusal. In Para 6 of the plaint it has been specifically stated as follows:

“ইহা ছাড়া ইজারা চুক্তি মোতাবেক ১নং বিবাদীর সমস্ত দায়দেনা পরিশোধের সিকিউরিটি হিসাব এই মানের ‘খ’তপছিলে বর্ণিত ৩নং বিবাদীর সমস্ত সম্পত্তি বাদীর অনুকুলে ইকুইটেবল মর্টগেজ সৃষ্টি করা হয় এবং ৩নং বিবাদী ১৪ই সেপ্টেম্বর ১৯৮৬ ইং তে বাদীর অনুকুলে মেমোরেন্ডাম বা দলিল দ্বারা উল্লেখিত বন্দক স্বীকার করেন”

We have also gone through the written statement and from paragraph No. 13 it appears that the defendants admitted that 'Kha' schedule property has been mortgaged with the plaintiff. The plaintiff`s further case in the plaint is that the machineries were leased out to the defendants for installation on rental basis which has also not been denied by the defendants in their written statement. The defendants, it appears adduced oral evidence before the trial Court and there is no denial of the fact on the mortgage of 'Kha' schedule property with the plaintiff and the leasing out of the machineries to them on rental basis.

10. Now with this back drop of the facts let us find out whether the trial Court has committed any error or there is any accidental slip or omission in incorporating 'Ka' schedule property in place of 'Kha' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment.

11. While arguing their cases the learned Advocates placed several decisions of the higher courts of the sub-continent in support of their respective cases. One such case which is very relevant in the matter was placed by Dr. Zahir which is reported in 22 DLR 130 (Province of East Pakistan Vs. His Highness Maharaja Kirit Bikram Kishore Deve Barman Manikya Bahadur), where a Division Bench of this Court has held that the language of section 152 is wide enough to include any accidential slip or omission of which the source may be somewhere other than the judgment and the decree.

12. Dr. M Zahir placing reliance on this decision contends that the respective cases of the parties in the present case clearly indicate that in the ordering portion the trial judge accidentally wrote 'Ka' in place of 'Kha', as this 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged with the plaintiff.

13. Dr. Zahir also placed another decision though of the Single Bench of this Court reported in 29 DLR 81 (Ibrahim Sk. and others Vs. Janab Sk. alias Janab Ali Sk. & others), where it has been held that where a mistake has crept into the description of an item of property in the plaint schedule and the mistake has been carried over in the decree, the Court certainly has power to correct the error in the decree. It has also been held that if the court is satisfied that the mistake made by the parties in the pleadings is an accidental slip or omission or is due to inadvertence and it is so palpable that nobody can possibly have any doubt as to what the parties meant, the Court can set it right. The decision it appears has been based on the cases reported in 19 CWN 1021 (Mohabir Prosod Vs. Chandra Sekhar) and AIR 1952 Cal. 86 (Bela Deb; Vs. Bam Behari Roy). Dr. Zahir placing reliance on this decision contends that when there was a scope for making correction after passing the decree the mistake as noticed in the decree may very well be corrected by the trial Court.

14. Dr. Zahir also placed reliance in another decision reported in AIR (PC) 136 (MRKRM Somasudram Chetty Vs. MRMVL Subramanian Chetty), where it has been held that accidental slip or misstatement of the Judge's intention in the judgment can also be corrected. Dr. Zahir submits that the learned Judge ordered that the defendants should satisfy the decree within 60 days but in case of their failure the plaintiff company may get back their money through the process of the court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property. But the question of foreclosing of 'Ka' schedule property does not arise when 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged. So this is an accidental slip or misstatement of trial Judge's intention which is liable to correction.

15. Dr. Zahir also placed reliance in another decision reported in AIR 1967 (SC) 1440 (Samarendra Nath Singha and another Vs. Krishna Kumar Nag), where it has been held that errors arising from accidental slip can be corrected subsequently not only in the decree drawn up by ministerial officer but even in the judgment pronounced and signed by the Court. From this also Dr. Zahir submits that mistake committed by the trial Court is very much apparent as for realisation of the decretal dues the trial Court cannot order for foreclosure of 'Ka' schedule property which admittedly belongs to the plaintiff decree-holder.

16. Dr. Zahir also placed reliance on another decision of our Appellate Division, reported in 1982 BCR (AD) 166 (Golam Nabi Vs. Mohammad Hoque Chowdhury, being dead his heirs: Mohammad Ali and others). In para 5 of this decision it has been observed as follows:

"As to the observation of the High Court Division that the disputed figures in the judgment were put deliberately by the trial Court, we do not find any basis for this observation in that it is the trial Court which replaced item No. 131 by item No. 132 and the figures 154 by the figures 134 without any basis whatever. This mistake or error is found to have been caused by accidential slip, and correction thereof is within the scope and ambit of section 152 of Civil Procedure Code. For correction of such mistake no separate suit is contemplated in the Civil Procedure Code".

17. Placing reliance on this decision Dr. Zahir submits that it is nobody's case that 'Ka' schedule property was mortgaged, rather it is the admitted case that 'Kha' schedule property has been mortgaged with the plaintiff. So, for foreclosure there cannot be any order for 'Ka' schedule property. So, this inclusion of 'Ka' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment is an accidental slip and this may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dr. Zahir placing the judgment of the trial Court submits that the trial Court came to the finding that the plaintiff company has succeeded in proving their case and as such the company is entitled to get the relief prayed for and thereafter the court ordered that the decree be passed accordingly. For proper appreciation let us quote here the ordering portion of the judgment and it runs as follows:

Ordered

"that the suit be decreed on contest against the defendant Nos. 1-4 with costs. The defendant Nos. 1-4 are hereby jointly and severally directed to pay a sum of Taka 1,40,52,942.00 only + costs of the suit to the plaintiff company within 60 (sixty) days from this day, failing which, the plaintiff company will be entitled to realise the said amount along with the costs of the suit through the process of the court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property".

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioner contends that if the plaint, written statement, and the judgment are gone into, it would clearly reveal that instead of mentioning 'Kha' schedule property the learned Judge through mistake mentioned 'Ka' schedule property which is an accidental slip or omission.

19. As against this Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 submits that such a mistake, if any, may be corrected only by an appeal preferred against the judgment and decree or by a petition for review of the judgment. The provision of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application. He submits that if the decree drawn up is not in conformity with the judgment this may be corrected under section 152 of the' Code of Civil Procedure, but if the judgment is to be corrected it is by way of review or appeal. Placing a Single Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in AIR 1953 (Cal) 257 (Nirmal Chakrabarti and others Vs. Land Acquisition Collector, Alipur and others) Mr. Huq contends that the mistake as submitted by the petitioner is not a clerical or arithmetical mistake or accidental slip or omission. Considering the facts and circumstances of that case it was held that amendments sought for does not come within the ambit of mistake or accidental slip referred to in section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that decision it has been held that section 152 of the Code deals only with correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes, or accidental slips or omissions. The nature of the amendment concerned cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to fall within the mistakes or slips as referred to in section 152 of the Code. Mr. Huq contends that in the present case the trial Judge deliberately wrote 'Ka' schedule property instead of 'Kha’ schedule property and that was done consciously which was incorporated by his own hand and there is no scope for correction. This inclusion of 'Ka" schedule property is deliberate. So, no relief is available to the plaintiff-petitioner under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

20. Mr. Moinul Huq also placed reliance in the case of Nandlal Tanti and others Vs. Jagdeo Singh and others, reported in AIR 1962(Pat.) 36, which is also a single bench decision and submits that only clerical mistake may be corrected.

21. Mr. Huq also placed a decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 42 Bazlur Rahman Bhuiyan Vs. Bangladesh Shipping Corporation) .Placing reliance on this decision Mr. Huq submits that the only remedy available for the petitioner is by way of review. For appreciation of the whole matter, we like to quote the relevant portion of the decision which runs as follows:

"10. In the facts of the case the plaintiff pointed out the error which needed rectification and that could be done only by way of review. The error crept in the ordering portion while prescribing the mode of payment without assigning any reason thereof in the body of the judgment. Where nothing was said in the judgment about it, the Court, however, in the decree laid down a mode of payment which was not the bargain of the parties. Thus clearly a case of review was made out and it was incumbent upon the Courts below to allow the review because its variation was neither set up by the parties nor the variation in mode of payment flowed from the judgment, so as to reflect in the decree which is mode of formal expression of the adjudication made by the Court. The Privy Council says, it is imperative that it should conform to the judgment. (Ord. 20, rule 6). Every Court has power to amend its decree so as to carry out its own meaning (section 152). For the purpose of interpreting a decree no other document is so directly in point as the judgment or can in the nature of things, have comparable force "Manakchand Vs. Monoarlal, AIR 1944 PC 46".

22. The learned Advocate contends that the alleged mistake pointed out by the petitioner can only be rectified or corrected by review of the judgment or in an appeal and section 152 of the Code is not applicable for such correction or rectification.

23. Mr. Huq also placed reliance in another decision reported in 23 DLR, 45 (Tejendra Chandra Dhar and others Vs. Rohini Ranjan Saha and another), where it has been held that a decree may be corrected only under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure if it is not in conformity with the judgment.

24. Mr. Huq lastly placed reliance in the decision reported in 4 DLR (PC) 1 (Piyaratana Unnase Vs. Wahareka Sounuttara Unnase), where it has been held that the Court may at any time either of its own motion or on the application filed by any or the aggrieved parties correct any clerical or arithmetical mistake of the judgment or order arising therein from any accidental slip or omission which is necessary to bring the decree into conformity with the judgment. It has been held that the general rule is clear that once an order is passed and entered or otherwise perfected, in accordance with the practice of the Court, the court which passed the order is "funcus officio" and cannot set aside or alter the order however wrong it may appear to be. That can only be done on appeal. The learned Advocate contends that the trial Court in the present case intentionally included 'Ka' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment which finds place in the decree itself. There is no clerical or arithmetical mistake or omission or slip as emphasised under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. So, the trial court rightly rejected the plaintiff's prayer for amendment of the judgment.

25. We have carefully heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and also gone through the decisions cited by them in support of their respective contentious. The consistent view of the higher courts of this sub-continent including the Privy Council is that the decree may be amended if it is not in conformity with the judgment. This is the consistent view and there is no doubt about it. The decree should reflect what has been stated in the judgment and if the decree does not reflect that, it may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But here in the present case before us the petitioner's contention is not on wrong drawing up of the decree but their case is that the trial Court committed an accidental slip or omission in incorporating 'Ka' schedule property instead of 'Kha' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment. We have carefully gone through the plaint, written statement and judgment and it appears that the definite case of the plaintiff is that 'Ka' schedule property was leased out on rental basis to the defendant and 'Kha' schedule property was duly mortgaged by the defendants in favour of the plaintiff which was necessary for security of their loan or advance.

26. The trial Court after examination of the evidence adduced from the side of the parties came to the clear finding that the plaintiff is entitled to the decree prayed for and passed the necessary order but while writing the ordering portion the trial Court directed that in case of failure of the defendants to pay the decretal amount to the plaintiff company within 60 days from the date of the judgment, the plaintiff company will be at liberty to realise the decretal amount along with the costs of the suit through process of the Court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property.

27. Admittedly, schedule 'Ka' property are the machineries which were leased out to the defendants on rental basis. So, for realisation of their own money, their own property cannot be sold by the plaintiff. For the security of the loan certain properties have been mortgaged and the question of foreclosure arises only when there is a mortgage and in the present case the defendants mortgaged certain properties. So, the question of realisation of the decretal amount with costs by foreclosing 'Ka' schedule property does not arise. It ought to be 'Kha' schedule property. Though this foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property has been written by the trial Court judge himself but the materials on record and the facts and circumstances of the case indicate that this insertion of 'Ka' is an accidental slip or omission. The case reported in 1982 BCR (AD) 166, 29 DLR 81, 22 DLR 130, AIR 1926 (AD) 166, AIR 1967 (SC) 1440 comes in aid of the petitioner and all these decisions consistently propounded that such a mistake in the judgment may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

28. Mr. Moinul Huq cited certain decisions which we have incorporated above, where it has been decided that a decree may be corrected if it is not in conformity with the judgment. There is no dispute on the proposition of law but it is not the case before us. The case before us is that the ordering portion of the judgment was not drawn up in accordance with the contents of the judgment. The petitioner's prayer is for the correction of the ordering portion of the judgment which is not in accordance with the pleadings of the parties as well as of the contents of the body of judgment. The mistake is only in the ordering portion. So the decisions cited by Mr Huq has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case before us. So we are of the view that for this small omission or accidental slip the plaintiff cannot be forced to prefer an appeal or file a review petition.

29. Mr. Huq also raised a plea of limitation and he submits that the decree was, drawn up in accordance with the terms of the judgment with notice to the plaintiff and the plaintiff took the certified copy of the decree and put it into execution and when they were proceeding with the execution the so-called defect came to their notice and thereafter they filed a petition for correction of the judgment. But by this time a long period has elapsed. He argued that such a petition under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure ought to have been filed within the shortest possible time and on the obtaining of the certified copy of the judgment with the so-called wrong contents. But it has been held in the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 125 (Ismail ullah being dead his heirs Baizid Vila and others Vs. Sukumar Chandra Das and others that the decree may be amended at any time, of course if it is not in conformity with the judgment. Quoting from the decision of the case of MRKRM Somasundram Chetty Vs. MRMVL Subramaniah Chetty reported in AIR 1926 (PC) 136 the Appellate Division opined that the decree may be amended. In that decision of the Privy Council it has been decided as follows:

"The only cases in which the Court can interfere after the passing and entering of the judgment are (1) Where there has been an accident or slip in the judgment as drawn up, in which case the court has power to rectify it; and (2) Where the Court itself finds the judgment as drawn up does not carry state what the court actually decided and intended."

So, from this decision of the Privy Council as well as of our Appellate Division it is apparent that if there is any mistake or omission or any accidental slip this may be corrected at any time. Here in the present case before us on perusal of the pleadings of the parties and the judgment we held that instead of incorporating the plaint schedule 'Kha' property in the last sentence of the ordering portion the trial Court by an accidental slip incorporated 'Ka' which requires rectification and this may be done under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. There is therefore no force in the argument advanced by Mr. Huq that the matter lapsed due to limitation. In this respect we may very well look into the decision, reported in 28 CWN 873 (Chandra Kumar Mukhopadhya Vs. Sudhansu Badani Deb and others), where Suhrawardy, J. observed as follows:

"It is, however, urged that section 152 gives the Court a discretion to allow or not an application for amendment of a decree. In my opinion, this is not the correct reading of the section. It no doubt says that when a clerical or arithmetical mistake is discovered in the decree, the Court may at any time correct it. The word 'may' in the section does not make it discretionary with the Court to order the correction but merely enlarges the power of the Court by providing that such correction can be done "at any time" or in other words, the section simply emphasises that no lapse of time would disentitle the court to make the correction. As has been observed, the intention of the law is to make it obligatory upon the Court whenever any such mistake is discovered to correct it and section 152 merely emphasises that duty of the Court by saying that it may be done at any time without limitation."

30. This also lends support to the contention of Dr. Zahir that there is no limitation to correct the mistake as pointed out in the present case.

31. We have considered these decisions and also the facts and circumstances of the case and we are in full agreement with the submission made by Dr. Zahir.

<u>32. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides and on consideration of the aforesaid decisions we hold that the trial Court committed illegality and wrong in not exercising the jurisdiction vested in it under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and correct the mistake which occurred due to accidental slip or omission and we are inclined to make the Rule absolute.</u>

33. The Rule, is accordingly made absolute without any order as to costs. The last sentence of the ordering portion of the judgment dated 23.11.93 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in the aforesaid suit is hereby interfered with and the ordering portion of the judgment delivered in that suit be corrected by incorporating 'Kha' in place of 'Ka' schedule property.

34. The decree should also be corrected accordingly.

35. The connected Civil Revision No. 3412 of 1992 is also disposed of without any order as to costs.

The execution case shall proceed after making necessary correction in the judgment and decree. The petitioner should produce a fresh certified copy of the decree before the executing court after its correction.

End.

full_judgment:
This rule at the instance of the defendants namely the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh and its Secretary is directed against the judgment and decree dated 18.5.87 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1987 affirming the judgment and decree dated 11.11.86 passed by the learned Munsif 4th court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 1021 of 1985. 

2. The plaintiff-opposite party brought the suit for declaration that the order of dismissal dated 7.8.83 issued by defendant No.2 at the instance of the defendant No.1 was illegal, inoperative, without jurisdiction, of no value in the eye of law and not binding upon the plaintiff and for a further declaration that the plaintiff is in service of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh as executive officer. 

3. The plaintiffs case was that he was an Assistant Executive and was posted to Com ilia to start his office-cum-sale center there. On 15.2.80 he was appointed as junior executive and was transferred to Dhaka. After he joined at Dhaka the plaintiff received on 27.11.80. an order of suspension and after four- teen and a half months a charge bearing some false allegations were served on him on 11.2.82. The allegations were on three counts namely that (1) He was irregular in attending office and in opening the sale center; (2) that he purchased cycle parts and did not record the expenditure in the relevant register and lastly (3) that he spent over Taka 10,000/- on account of purchase of stationary without recording them in the register. The plaintiff submitted reply denying the allegations and claiming them to be false. The defendants appointed Mr. Moazzem Hossain, Deputy Secretary, Establishment Division who after inquiry laid a report on 10.4.82 that the charges on the count Nos. 2 and 3 were not proved but that the charge under count No.1 that is his being irregular in attending office and in opening sale centre was proved and recommended for giving him a warning. The plaintiff objected to the report pleading that the report was based on a photo copy of the attendance register which was a fabricated document whereupon the defendants after considering his representation appointed another inquiry officer namely Mr. A.K.M. Shamsuzzaman and he submitted report saying that even the charge under count No. 1 was not proved. Thus in-spite of the said report of the inquiry officer to the effect that none of the charges was proved the defendants by the impugned order illegally dismissed him from service. This violated the Government Servant's (Discipline and Appeal) Rules as also the principles of natural justice and the plaintiffs representation to the higher authorities having not been considered the plaintiff brought the suit. 

4. The defendants contested the suit pleading that the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and was liable to be dismissed and that the suit has no merit because the plaintiff was dismissed from service after following the procedures prescribed by the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules. 

5. The learned Munsif after considering the evidence found that the dismissal order passed by the defendants was not legal and was against the principles of natural justice and also that the suit was not barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff had prayed for consequential relief. Accordingly he decreed the suit making the declaration as was prayed adding that the plaintiff holds his service with all rights and privileges attached to his office though there was no such prayer in the suit by way of prayer for consequential relief with advalorem court fees under section 7(4)(c) of the Court Fee's Act. 

6. On appeal the learned District Judge reassessed the evidence and concurred with the finding of the learned Munsif and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court. 

7. Present Civil Revision is directed against the said decree. 

Mr. Kazi A.T. ManwarUddin, the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners submitted that the learned courts below failed to notice that the required procedures as per Government Servant (Disciplineand Appeal) Rules were duly followed in asmuch as specific charges were served on the plaintiff opposite party and upon his reply to the charges inquiries were got hold by two inquiry officers and upon consideration of the inquiry reports the plaintiff was found guilty of the charges of misconduct and was dismissed accordingly. He also submitted that the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh has no disciplinary rules of its own but it adopted and used the Government Servant (Discipline and Appeal) Rules as far as was practicable and there was no violation of the said rules nor there was any violation of the principles of natural justice in passing the order of dismissal. 

8. The learned Advocate also pointed out that the learned Munsif wrongly held that the non- reference of the matter before the Public Service Commission in terms of Rule 7(f) was an illegality without noticing the fact that the said rule could be applied only in respect of persons in the service of the State and not in respect of the plaintiff who was an employee of the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh and was not a person in the service of the State. 

9. It was next submitted that in this suit the plaintiff did not pray for any consequential relief and framed the suit as a simple declaratory suit only to seek declaration that the dismissal order was illegal and another declaration that the plaintiff is in service. So he submitted that the suit was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In support of his contention he cited the decisions reported in 3S DLR High Court Division at page 224 and B.C.R. 1988 High Court Division at page 44 besides an unreported decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 229 of 1983. 

10. In this connection the learned Advocate also submitted that the District Judge while passing the impugned order wrongly held that the second declaration sought in the plaint namely that the plaintiff is in service amounts to consequential relief ignoring the decision of the Appellate Division which was referred to him wherein it was clearly held that a second declaration namely that the plaintiff is in service does not amount to consequential relief. 

11. On behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate submitted at so far as the factual merit of the suit is consrned there was no scope for controversy namely .at the principles of natural justice were violated because the inquiry officer who was appointed by the defendant petitioner subsequently himself gave finding that none of the charges was proved and in such report the defendant had no legal scope to pass the order of dismissal against the plaintiff who as found innocent of the charges upon inquiry held y the defendant's officer. So to sustain such illegal order of dismissal against the employee namely the lain tiff who was innocent of the charges would amount to serious injustice and, therefore, the courts in concurrently deciding to decree the suit knitted no illegality. 

12. On the point of maintainability of the suit Mr. Fazlul Karim submitted that from the facts indenture of the case the suit seeking declaration that the dismissal order was illegal and seeking a further declaration that the plaintiff is still in service constituted the suit as one for both declaration and for conquential relief. Mr. Fazlul Karim elaborated his arguments by further submitting that according to the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act only much relief which are necessary for the plaintiff to take and such reliefs without which the object of the suit and the purpose of the declaration is not proved are required to be sought. According to him in e present case if the plaintiffs prayers as contained I the plaint namely declaration of the dismissal order as illegal with further declaration that the plaintiff is in service will serve the whole object of the lit and, therefore, no further relief was required to sought within the meaning of the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Advocate supported the reasons given by the learned District Judge namely that a further declaration that was night for declaration that the plaintiff is in service 'as in essence a consequential relief within the leaning of the proviso. 

13. Mr. Fazlul Karim referred to several decagons in support of his contention such as those rerated in P.L.D. 1949 (P.C) 1, P.L.D. 1954 (Sind) 19. 37 D.L.R. (H.C) 20, 13 D.L.R. (H.C.) 341and A.I.R. 1954 Bombay 217. 

14. Before going into the cited decisions I first of all refer to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The said section and its proviso are as follows: 

"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief; 

Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so." 

15. According to the said section it is a discretion of the Court to make a declaration of any status or right upon a suit being instituted by a person who is entitled to such status or right. But the section at the same time provides a positive bar that no court shall make such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so. It is to be seen what is meant by the words 'being able to seek further relief. This further relief must flow necessarily from the relief of declaration and the reliefs must be one which would complete the claim of the plaintiff and not lead to multiplicity of suits. If the relief is remote and is not connected with the cause of action then the plaintiff need not claim such relief. The further relief must be a relief which is absolutely necessary for serving the object of the suit and the purpose of the declaration. If, however, the declaration sought by it- self is sufficient to serve the object of the suit and serves fully the relief for which the cause of action for the suit arose then no further relief need be sought. But contrarily if the declaration sought by the suit itself does not serve the object of the suit and meet the purpose of the declaration then of course such further relief which willfulfill the object of the suit and declaration must be sought. For example if a plaintiff is in possession of a land he can maintain a simple suit for declaration of title without seeking any further relief like confirmation of possession as mere declaration of title serves fully the object of the suit when his title is disputed while the plaintiff is fully in possession of the land. But if a plaintiff is out of possession then his suit. for mere declaration of title without any prayer for recovery of possession is hit by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act because without having possession of the land the object of the suit will be frustrated and the declaration of title will be of no consequence. 

16. In this connection Mr. Fazlul Karim referred to the decision of the Privy Council wherein it was held that a further proceeding may be instituted for such relief in future. The learned Advocate wanted to suggest that if after the declaration as was prayed by the plaintiff if the defendants do not reinstate him in service or give him any posting or salary, he may bring fresh suit for such relief. Mr. Fazlul Karim also argued that there was no reason for the plaintiff to presume or to apprehend that the Corporation namely the defendants will not reinstate him in service and will not pay him his wages even after such declaration is made and confirmed by the highest Court. 

17. So far as the Privy Council decision re-ported in P.L.D. 1949 (P.C.) at page 1 is concerned it may be noted that in that case the law provided in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was not considered. But section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and its proviso clearly bars a suit in which relief which is consequential to the declaration and without which the declaration becomes meaningless and frustrates the object of the suit must be claimed in the suit and, therefore, there is no scope that such suit will be maintained leaving an opportunity to the plaintiff to bring fresh suit for the further relief which was consequential to the declaration. 

18. Now the real test as to which relief falls within the words being able to seek further relief has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. 

19. So far as the present suit is concerened the plaintiff brought the suit seeking two declarations-(1) that the dismissal order passed against the plaintiff was illegal and (2) that the plaintiff is in service. Both are the reliefs of declaration as was worded in the plaint itself as also in the impugned order and decree. It was, however, sought to be interpreted by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the second declaration namely that the plaintiff is in service of Trading Corporation of Bangladesh as executive officer is a consequential relief. This contention is to be rejected outright and as a matter of fact this contention was inconsistent with the other submission of Mr. Fazlul Karim himself namely that the declaration sought was them-selves sufficient to serve fully the object of the suit and that further consequential relief by way of rein-statement in service giving posting and pay were unnecessary. In other words Mr. Fazlul Karim submitted that if the declaration sought as prayed for was made the plaintiff will automatically get his rein-statement in service, his posting and his pay and all benefits. This contention does not appear to be acceptable. No doubt according to the plaintiffs prayers in the suit both the declarations have been made by the court namely that the dismissal order is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service. But the fact remains that the plaintiff upon the dismissal has been thrown out of his office and has for all intents and purposes out of his office posting and pay. If inspite of this decree the defendants do not reinstate him in service and do not give him any posting or pay or office what benefit he will derive simply by holding a decree with a declaration that his dismissal order is illegal and he is still in service. The suit was brought with the allegation that he was illegally and vindictively dismissed from service and that inspite of his representation up to the highest authority he could not get any redress whereupon he was obliged to seek relief in the court. Now after getting a decree for declaration that the dismissal order is illegal and that he is in service this decree will not give him any benefit for which he brought the suit because by remaining out of office and out of posting his remaining at home with the declaratory decree in his pocket will serve no useful purpose of the suit and of the declaration. 

20. The position of the plaintiff will be that he will have the declaration by the decree without any legal scope to implement it. On the other hand if along with the declaration he would have asked for a mandatory direction on the defendants to reinstate him in service with effect from the date of dismissal and to give him immediate posting and also salary then only he could get the practical benefit of the suit and the decree. So within the meaning of proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act by way of mandatory direction on the defendants to reinstate him in service with effect from the date of dismissal and posting, office and pay were the reliefs consequential to the declaration that fall within the meaning of the word 'being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title. 

21. It is true that the decisions reported in 13 D.L.R. (H.C.) 341, 37 D.L.R. (H.C.) 7, P.L.D. 1954 (Sind) 199 and A.I.R. 1954(Bombay) 217 decided that a suit for declaration that the dismissal is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service is maintainable without any prayer for consequential relief. But the other decisions referred to from the side of the petitioner namely the decisions reported in 35 D.L.R. (H.C.) 224, B.C.R. 1988 (H.C.) 44 and an unreported decisions of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 229 of 1983 which is a judgment of affirmance of the decisions reported in 35 D.L.R.(H.C.) 224 has clearly decided that a suit for declaration that the dismissal order is illegal and that the plaintiff is in service is not maintainable and is hit by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

22. The judgment of the Appellate Division was passed in respect of O.C. Suit No. 15 of 1982 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur for declaration that the order of dismissal passed by defendant-respondent No. 1 is illegal, ultravires, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the plaintiff is still in service. The present suit is exact- y similar as it is also a suit for self same declaration. So there is no distinguishing point. 

23. Mr. Fazlul Karim tried to draw a distinction by submitting that in the suit before the Appellate Division it was held by the courts that the dismissal order was legal while in the present suit the dismissal order was held to be illegal. The findings n the suit though different does not make any distinction regarding the framing of the suit which was exactly same. So there is no scope to give a different finding on the point of law namely about the bar of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act after the decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court which is dated 7th September, 1983. 

24. So upon a consideration of the point of maintainability of the suit I find that the present suit was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in as much as no consequential relief was sought in the suit for declaration and that in the absence of any relief being sought for consequential relief by way of mandatory direction for reinstatement in service from the date of dismissal and for giving the plaintiff posting and salary the decree of declaration would be not only ineffective but also infructuous and of no benefit to serve the object of the suit. 

25. Mr. Fazlul Karim lastly contended that even if it is found that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from error of law still the said impugned judgment and decree can not be revised as it did not occasion any failure of justice. 

26. Mr. Fazlul Karim, in this connection, submitted that there were three charges brought against the plaintiff-opposite party by the defendants of whom the charge No. 1 namely his irregularity in attending office and opening sale centre was only found to be proved by the first inquiry officer namely Mr. Moazzem Hossain who in the concluding part of his report stated that only the charge No. 1 i.e. irregularity in attending office has been duly established'. Thus he found the other two charge about corruption and financial irregualrity not proved. After this report the plaintiff opposite party made a representation to the defendants that this finding was wrong as the inquiry was made with reference to a photo copy of the attendance register which was a fabricated document. This representation was accepted in as much as the defendants appointed another inquiry officer namely Mr. Shamsuzzaman to hold further inquiry with reference to the original attendance register that lay with the anti-corruption department and according to the plaintiff the said inquiry officer after making the inquiry with reference to the original attendance register gave his finding that this charge No. 1 i.e. irregularity in attending office and in opening sale centre was also not proved. But in- spite of that the defendants passed the impugned order upon perusal of the inquiry report and upon finding that the charges of neglect of duty, misconduct and corruption were proved and with such finding the dismissal was ordered. Mr. Fazlul Karim, therefore, submitted that the order of dismissal was passed without any actual consideration of the inquiry report and rather ignoring the inquiry report and this was done without any kind of inquiry or any basis and this was not only in violation of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules but also against the principles of natural justice. This fact was borne out by the document proved and both the courts below concurrently found it to be so. I have perused all the documents in this connection. and the contention is found to be correct. In other words while the first inquiry officer upon inquiry gave his finding that only the charge No. 1 i.e. irregularity in attending in the office was established but other charges were not established and the second inquiry officer after inquiry with reference to the original attendance register found that even charge No. 1 namely irregularity in attending office was not established the impugned order showed that the defendants without holding any other inquiry in presence of the plaintiff found the plaintiff guilty of neglect of duty, misconduct and corruption for which no basis or material was even referred to and upon such arbitrary finding the dismissal was ordered which has certainly violated the principles of natural justice as also the spirit of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules which was admittedly adopted by the defendants Corporation. 

27. The impugned order of the District Judge affirmed the decree of the Munsif declaring the said dismissal order as illegal on a proper and correct finding both on point of fact and law. So Mr. Fazlul Karim submitted that though the said decrees could not be passed because of the bar of the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and for that even if those decrees' suffered from error of law that alone could not give a cause for revision of the said orders because the defendant petitioner did not suffer any in- justice thereby.  

28. Mr. Fazlul Karim referred to the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submitted that in view of the said provision as it exists now the revisional power of the High Court Division has been restricted by providing that even if any order is found to suffer from error of law that alone can not be a ground for revision unless it has occasioned a failure of justice. 

29. Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is in the following language: 

"The High Court Division may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to the High Court Division and in which no appeal lies thereto and if such subordinate Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division may make such order in the case as it thinks fit." 

According to the said provision of law the error of law in the impugned order is not by itself a ground for revision unless the said error of law has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

30. From my foregoing findings it appears that by the impugned decree an illegal order of dismissal that was passed by the defendants was declared as being not binding on the plaintiff and though this impugned order and decree suffer from error of law only on the legal ground namely that consequential relies was not sought in the suit and the declaratory decree was barred by the proviso of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but the fact remains that the said de Cree can not be held to have occasioned any failure 0 justice. If the impugned decree which suffers from error of law stands the defendants will not suffer any thing .beyond that they will not be able to reap the benefit of an illegal order passed by them and deprivation of such illegal benefit can not be said to having  occasioned failure of justice to them. In this view the matter it is held that though the impugned order suffers from error of law but they having not occasioned any failure of justice they do not call for an revision within the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

The rule is, accordingly, discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J:- This Civil Rule arises out of an application filed by the petitioner under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure for withdrawal of the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 317 of 1987 from the Court of the District Judge, Chittagong to this Court for analogous hearing with First Appeal No. 26 of 1987 pending in this Court. 

2. The petitioner instituted Other Suit No. 75 of 1980 for specific performance or contract on the basis of a compromise decree made in a suit. The petitioner also filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 467 of 1981 under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for preempting certain land against the opposite parties. The suit and the Miscellaneous Case were heard analogously and dismissed by the Subordinate Judge by one judgment on 26.9.87. That the petitioner preferred First Appeal No. 26 of 1987 in this Court from the decree made in the Other Suit No. 75 of 1980. He also filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 317 of 1987 from the order made in Miscellaneous Case No. 467 of 1981 dismissing the pre-emption case filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the Court of District Judge. 

3. The petitioner submits that as both the Misc. Appeal pending in the Court of District Judge and the First Appeal No. 26 of 1987 of this Court arise out of similar circumstances and the facts and the questions of law involved in both the appeals are similar, the appeal pending before the court of the learned District Judge is required to be withdrawn to this Court and should be heard analogously for the sake of convenience and to meet the ends of justice as in both the First Appeal pending in this Court and the Miscellaneous Appeal pending in the Court of District Judge evidence and documents are common and points involved to be decided are also common. 

4. Mr. Syed Moazzem Hossain, the learned Advocate in support of the Rule, submitted that in view of the facts stated above the appeal pending in the Court of the District Judge should be withdrawn and heard analogously with the First appeal pending in this Court by High Court Division and for such withdrawal there is no bar under clause (b) sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submission he placed two decisions in the case of Messrs Muhammad Umar Muhammad Aslam Vs. Messrs Muslim Oil Mills, P.L.D. 1962 Lah. 680 and in the case of Sanganbhat Vs. Vasudev and others, 1976 Kamataka 229. 

5. The learned Advocate for the opposite-parties on the other hand contends that in case the appeal is withdrawn to this Court and heard the opposite parties will lose a valuable right of revision to this Court and as such the petition should not be allowed. 

6. Let us now consider the arguments of the learned Advocates. In Messrs Muhammad Umar-Muhammad Aslam the appeal was tried by a Bench of the High Court of Lahore but the judgment was kept reserved. In the meanwhile there was an amendment of the West Pakistan Civil Courts Ordinance, 1962. Section 28(3) of the said Ordinance provided that on the commencement of the Ordinance, if any, suit or appeal was pending in the High Court or any other Civil Court which under this Ordinance is to be tried or heard by some other Court, such suit or appeal shall stand transferred to the Court competent under this Ordinance to try or hear the same. The objection taken in that case was that as the appeal stood transferred from the High Court to the Court of Civil Judge the judgment was not in accordance with law. But the High Court repelled the contention on the ground that the High Court was empowered to order for transfer such appeal to it under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In Sanganbhat the learned Chief Justice who delivered the judgment of the report held that the High Court had got power to transfer an appeal pending in the lower Court to it for hearing and disposal. We have also found a decision exactly on the point in the case of Mst. Aysha Bai and others Vs. Daleep Singh, A.I.R. 1961 Raj. 186. In that case a precise question as to loss of valuable right of appeal and revision was raised in the event an appeal pending in the lower appellate Court be transferred under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the High Court. In dealing with the said contention the learned Chief Justice observed: 

"The petitioners contend that they have been deprived of a right of second appeal to this Court, which would have been available to them if the appeal had been decided by the District Judge. This contention is illusory. A right of second appeal to this Court is limited merely to errors of law. Here, they have had the advantage of the entire evidence being reviewed by two Judges of a Superior Court who after a careful examination of the matter pronounced their judgment in the appeal." 

The aforesaid observation was made in connection with a review petition which arose out of a judgment and decree passed by the High Court in First Appeal No. 68 of 1954, D/-4-5-1960. The said judgment out of which the review petition arose was from a decree passed by the trial court in a money suit. An appeal from such decree lay to the District Court under section 21 of the Rajasthan Civil Courts Ordinance, 1950. The aforesaid observation is an answer to the contention and lays down the principle of law with regard to the power of the High Court under section 24 of the Code so far as it relates to withdrawal and transfer of an appeal or other proceeding to any Court subordinate to it or to itself. We do not also find in the language of Section 24(1) (b) of the Code that the power of withdrawal of any suit, appeal and other proceeding pending in any court subordinate to the High Court Division to itself is so circumscribed by the right of appeal or revision to the Court subordinate to the High Court Division. The power conferred under section 24(J)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure is an unfettered one as and loss of a valuable right of revision or appeal as contended by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties is no bar to the exercise of such power by the High Court Division. 

7. For the above reasons, we direct the withdrawal of the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 317 of 1987 pending in the Court of the District Judge, Chittagong to this Court to be heard analogously with the First Appeal No. 26 of 1987 pending in this Court. We make the Rule absolute. No order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This appeal is directed against the order dated 31.8.77 passed by Additional District Judge, Rangpur in Misc. Appeal No. 25 of 1976, affirming the judgment and order dated 8.7.75 passed by Mr. SB Haque, Sub-Judge, Rangpur in Misc. Case No. 1 of 1975.

2. The relevant facts of the case in short are that, Abdul Aziz and Naziruddin Ahmed obtained a decree for declaration of title and recovery of khash possession in Title Suit No. 96 of 1959 of the Sub-Judge's Court Rangpur and put the decree in Execution in Title Execution Case No. 34 of 1969. The judgment debtor-opposite party filed objection against the execution of the decree under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the execution case, inter alia, on the ground that the decree is not executable. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the petition holding that one of the decree holders namely, Abdul Aziz was an Indian national and his interest in the suit, property became enemy property according to the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and subsequently vested property and vested in the Govt. of Bangladesh, in view of the provisions made in The Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act 1974 (Act LV of 1974).

3. On appeal, the learned Additional District Judge has confirmed the order of learned Subordinate Judge, holding that as one of the decree holders was an enemy and his property became enemy property and subsequently vested property, the decree cannot be executed in view of section 83 CPC.

4. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has taken me through the impugned orders of courts below and other relevant papers. He firstly submits that there is no evidence to show that Abdul Aziz, one of the decree-holders, was an Indian national and his property became enemy property or vested property and as such, the decision of courts below are erroneous, as based on no evidence, The contention of the learned Advocate seems to be correct. From the petition under section 47 CPC filed by the judgment debtor-respondent, It appears that they also did not allege that Abdul Aziz was an Indian national or enemy national, It may be pointed out that in an earlier petition under section 47, the judgment debtors alleged that Abdul Aziz is an Indian national and as such, he is an enemy national. There is however no evidence to establish the finding that Abdul Aziz was an Indian national and his property was declared as enemy property.

5. It appears from the petition for execution of the decree that Abdul Aziz's address is given at Patgram within district Rangpur and in the Memo of present appeal, the same address of Abdul Aziz is given. After his death, his heirs were substituted. Now even assuming that Abdul Aziz was an Indian national and as such an enemy, the learned Advocate submits that after the emergence of Bangladesh, Abdul Aziz ceased to be an enemy national, and as such, the Courts below were not justified in allowing the Misc. Case and dismissing the execution petition. In support of his contention, he referred to the Bangladesh (SC) Digest Vol-II at page 27 where it was held as follows:

"Section 83: Applicability of the section After proclamation of Independence and Emergence of Bangladesh.

The plaintiff-decree holder-petitioners instituted an execution case which was contested by Respondent No. 1 u/s 47 CPC. The only question was that two of the decree holders were residing in India and since 1965 they become alien residents.

Observed: The High Court Division had rightly noticed that section 83 of the Code is no longer operative in the present case and the execution case as a whole in its entirety may proceed at the instance of the decree holders irrespective of their residence. The point is correct.

Held: Since independence of Bangladesh, whatever the state of affairs that existed between India and Pakistan since 1965 had finally terminated by the proclamation of Independence on 10th April, 1971 and as such there was no such continuance of state of affairs between India and the territory which has emerged as Bangladesh."

<u>6. In view of the above position of law it seems that the contention of the learned Advocate is correct. But the fact remains that if Abdul Aziz was really an Indian national prior to emergence of Bangladesh in 1971 and his property vested in the Govt. after the emergence of Bangladesh, in view of the provisions of the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act 1974 (Act LV of 1974), it is to be investigated whether the decree is executable as both the courts found concurrently though without evidence and thus erroneously that Abdul Aziz was an Indian national at the relevant time, and that finding of fact is binding one. Even assuming that decree holder Abdul Aziz was an Indian national and his interest in the decretal properties became enemy and/or vested property and as such the decree to the extent of his share or interest cannot be executed, there is no reason why the decree to the extent of the share or interest of the other decree holders is concerned cannot be executed.</u>

7. In view of the above facts and circumstances and the legal position discussed, the appeal is allowed. The impugned orders of the courts below are hereby set aside and the case is sent back on remand to the executing court for making fresh decision, according to law and in the light of the observations made above. There will be no cost of this appeal.

End.

This Rule under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil of Civil Procedure, arising out a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession, is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Patiya passed in other appeal No. 293 of 1983 dismissing the appeal and allowing the cross-objection of respondent No. 8 and affirming the judgment, and decree of the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania, passed in title suit No. 248 of 1969 with modification.

2. The opposite-parties Nos. 6-15 as plaintiffs instituted the suit stating, inter-alia, that the suit land belonged to Askar Ali in Whose name CS Khatain was recorded. Askar Ali died leaving son Hossain Ali who transferred 5 kanis of land to Akmal Ali by kabala dated 23rd Kartick 1264 ME and Akmal Ali transferred the same to Maniruzzaman and Safar Ali by kabala dated 15th Sraban 1293 ME Maniruzzaman and Safar Ali died leaving the plaintiffs as heirs who have been possessing the suit land on payment of rent. CS and RS plots in respect of the suit land are identical and RS khatain in the name of Reazuddin is wrong. The defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. Their documents are false and fraudulent.

3. The defendant No. 1 Sultan Ahmed (predecessor of petitioners Nos. 1-5) and defendant No. 4 Yakub Ali Petitioner No. 6) contested the suit by filing written statements. The case of defendant No. 1 in short is that the suit land appertaining to Nayabad Taluk belonged to Promode Ranjan Das Gupta. Previously the suit land Was Nonamara land near the Bay of Bengal and the korfa tenant Askar Ali surrendered the suit land to the landlord who inducted Reazuddin, father of defendant No. 1 Sultan Ahmed, predecessor of petitioners Nos. 1-5 as tenants. Reazuddin used to cultivate the suit land and created a house on it and the R.S. khatian was prepared in his name. Ahmed Kabir Chowdhury landlord of the suit land, brought a rent suit against Reazuddin in 1949 and got a decree, In Rent Execution case No. 305 of 1948, the suit land was put to auction and defendant No. 4 Yakub Ali auctioned purchased the same, got sale certificate and delivery of possession of the suit land. PS khatain stand recorded in the name of Yakub Ali who transferred 2 kan is 7 gondas of land to defendant No. 1 predecessors of petitioner Nos. 1-5, by a kabala dated 24-11-57. Defendant No. 3 (petitioner No. 2) wife of defendant No. 1, also purchased 8 gandas land from Yakub Ali and his son defendant No. 2 (petitioner No. 1 since deceased) purchased 7 gandas of land from Yakub Ali and the remaining land was in possession of defendant No. 4. The house of the defendant No. 1 stands on R.5 plot No. 71 and he extended his houses upto RS plot No. 70. The defendant No. 1 paid rent and got dakhilas. BS khatian stands in the name of defendant No. 1 RS PS and BS khatians are correct.

4. The case of defendant No. 4 in short is that the suit land was correctly recorded in his name and in the name of Reazuddin. For arrears of rent the interest of Reazuddin was put to auction and defendant No. 4 purchased the land in auction and got sale certificate and delivery of possession. Defendant No. 4 transferred 3-2 gandas of land to defendant No. 1 and his wife and son by different kabalas and since then they have been possessing the land and the balance of 15 gandas of land is in possession of defendant No. 4. The plaintiffs have got no title and possession in the suit land.

5. Before the trial court opposite-parties Nos. 1-5 got them impleaded in the suit by way of an application under Order 1, Rule 10.

6. After hearing both the parties the learned Munsif dismissed the suit. Against the decision of the learned Munsif the plaintiffs filed the appeal and the defendant No. 9 (opposite party No. 1) filed a cross-objection in respect of certain observation made in the judgment of the learned Munsif. At the hearing of the appeal it was pointed out on behalf of the contesting defendants respondent that the appeal abated as the heirs of deceased defendant No. 1 Sultan Ahmed, respondent No. 1 in the appeal, were not brought on record by way of substitution, The learned Subordinate Judge held that for non-substitution of the heirs of deceased respondent No. 1 the appeal was liable to be abated. The learned Subordinate Judge heard the appeal and dismissed it, allowed the cross-objection and affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif with the modification that "the finding of the learned Munsif as regards correctness of RS PS and BS khatians, the title of the suit land remaining with the principal defendants and their possession over the land of RS plot 71 be expunged therefrom" and against the decision of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge the petitioners, the heirs of deceased defendants No. 1, have obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr M Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that in view of the provisions of Order XLI, rule 22(4) of the Civil Procedure Code, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in law in proceeding with the cross-objection when the appeal abated. In support of his submission he has referred to two cases namely, the case of Abdullah Miya vs Mohamed Miya Gula Husain and others, AIR 1949 (Born) 27 and the case of Lt. Col. PH Chowdhury vs Altaf Ahmed and another, AIR 1963 (Andh) 382. In the said two Division Bench cases it has been held that when appeal abates for non-substitution of legal heirs and representatives of deceased party in the appeal the cross-objection cannot be heard and determined. In the case reported in AIR 1949 (Bomb) 276 Chagla, CJ observed, "Under sub-rule (4) of rule 22 of Order 41 of the Civil Procedure Code when an appeal is withdrawn or is dismissed, the cross-objection may nevertheless be heard. Therefore, the original rigour of the law has been released but it has been relaxed only to this extent, viz. in the two cases laid down in sub rule (4), (1) where the appeal is withdrawn, and (2) where the appeal is dismissed. It is significant to note that sub-rule (4) does not provide for a case of abatement of an appeal. Therefore, it is clear that the Legislature did not intend that cross- objection should be heard when the appeal had abated. Under the circumstances, as this case is not a case of withdrawal of an appeal or dismissal of an appeal, but it is a case of abatement of an appeal, Mr. Shah's clients have no right to have their cross-objection heard." In the case reported in AIR 1963 (Andhra Pradesh) 382 it was observed:-"Memorandum of cross-objection not falling within the purview of sub-rule i.e. sub-rule (4) of rule 22 of Order XLI of the Cl'C) such as when the appeal has abated, cannot be heard and determined. If that were so, the memorandum of cross-objection should be dismissed in limine without further consideration." The facts of the present case are similar to those of the said two cases. Therefore, the principle laid down in the said two cases is applicable in the present case. A sound and well-considered proposition of law is propounded in the said two cases and in agreement with the principle laid down in the said cases, I hold the view that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record occasioning failure of justice in hearing and determining the cross-objection after lie appeal abated and as such his decision is not sustainable.

Mr Rabisankar Chakraborty, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties Nos. 1-5 has not been able to lay his hands to any decision as against the view taken in the said two cases.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge are set-aside and those of the learned Munsif restored.

End.
