full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Chowdhury, J.: This Rule arises out of an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay in filing the appeal being FAT No. 567 of 1989.

2. Facts leading to this in short are, that the Agrani Bank, Motijheel Commercial Area Branch, Dhaka as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 381/86 in the court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1 Dhaka against Rupali Jute Baling Limited, a private Limited Company having its registered office at 67, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka and six others for foreclosure of the suit property alleging that the petitioner defendant No.1 namely, Rupali Jute Baling Ltd. had an account with the plaintiff Bank since pre-liberation days. In August 1982 the defendants approached the Bank to allow cash credit facilities. This plaintiff, as per banking practice, allowed the cash credit facilites of Taka 175 lacs by creating mortgage of the properties mentioned in the schedule to the plaint and also signing personal guarantee of all the Directors namely, defendant Nos. 2 to 7. The plaintiff Bank also advanced a sum of Taka 2.37 crores to defendant No.1 by way of preshipment credit to procure jute goods for export against foreign letter of credit but defendant No. 1 failed to export the jute. As on 22.9.86 the defendant No.1 had a debit balance of Taka 7,05,81,038/88 paisa with interest thereof. As the loan is secured by the mortgage of properties mentioned in the schedule and as the defendant failed to pay even on repeated demand, the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit for closure.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 by filing a written statement. It is the case of the defendant No. 1 that the alleged liability is not correct and it is highly inflated and that the plaintiff Bank without following the Government's direction as per Shahadutullah's Commission report, which recommended various reliefs to the Jute traders as to interest, multiplied the interest till the filing of the suit. The defendant also stated that the alleged agreement dated 13.6.85 between the plaintiff Bank and the defendant being violative of the Government Regulations was invalid. On this pleadings the court below took up the hearing of the suit during which the plaintiff examined PW 1 and was cross examined by the defendant's lawyer on 22.12.88 and the suit was fixed for further hearing on 13.2.89. On that day the defendant prayed for time on the ground that the learned Advocate conducting the suit for the defendant is engaged in a part-heard matter before the High Court Division and hence not in a position to appear but the court rejected the petition and closed the evidence and passed the judgment on 14.2.89 which is on the next day and decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree the defendants filed a review petition under Order 47 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 14.3.89 which is 30 days after the judgment and decree and Miscellaneous Case No. 49 of 1981 was started.

4. The plaintiff opposite party filed written objection in the said Miscellaneous case on 21.5.89. The said review petition was heard on contest on 16.11.89 and after hearing of the matter the court dismissed the said petition filed on review holding, inter alia, that admittedly the appeal is pending and when an appeal is pending, the review application is not maintainable, further holding that this review application does not speak anything about the impugned judgment and the application for review had prayed for re-opening the whole judgment and decree by rehearing of the whole matter which is not possible by the court in review and the review petition was dismissed.

5. The defendants in the suit, who are the petitioner in the review petition then preferaed an appeal before this court against the original judgment and decree and it was reported by the Stamp Reporter that the appeal has been filed on 14.12.89 with proper court fees but the appeal is filed long after the period of limitation. Application under section 5 of the Limitation Act thereafter is filed for condonation of the delay. This court on hearing of that application for condonation of delay of 288 days, issued the instant rule to show cause as to why the delay should not be condoned. The Rule is contested by the Bank by filing a written objection and is disposed of after hearing by this judgment

6. Mr. HR Sharif, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner-appellant along with Mrs. Seema Zahur, submitted that in the instant case the office did not calculate the days of delay properly. According to the learned Advocate, the days by which appeal is out of time should be 198 days. He has submitted that the period of 247 days which were occupied in the review petition, having been pursued bonafide and in good faith by the defendant No. I, ought to have been excluded in computing the limitation and, according to the learned Advocate such period is always excluded in computing the limitation during which the parties conducted the case in a wrong forum in good faith. This is the law and in support of this contention he has also referred to a decision reported in 36 DLR page 136. He has further submitted that in the instant case the impugned judgment and' decree of the trial Court, having not been passed after full hearing of the suit but in the absence of the learned Advocate for the defendant it was considered to be in the nature of an ex parte judgment and decree and hence a review petition was filed under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure with a bonafide belief that the said would be a proper step taken and if there is any mistaken view of the law, which might have been committed by the learned Advocate for the defendant, the appellant ought not to be penalised for no fault of his own and this according to the learned Advocate is the consistent view taken by the court in this regard and, therefore, this case could not be an exception to the general rule envisaged in those decisions referred to. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate Mr. HR Sharif, that the appellant in the instant case in the facts and circumstances is entitled to the benefit of the days spent wrongly in a wrong forum caused by a genuine mistake on the part of the lawyer which may be caused due to the mistaken view of the law and, therefore, the delay be condoned for ends of justice and the appeal be ordered to be registered.

7. This rule is contested by opposite party Agrani Bank by filing an affidavit-in-opposition through their lawyer Mr. SA Rahim, Mr. SA Rahim, by reference to the averments made in the affidavit-in-opposition, submitted that the defendant No.1 did not pursue the review petition either bona fide or in good faith before the court below which decreed the suit because the grounds made out in the review petition are no grounds for review under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, it could not be said that the review petition was presented and pursued in good faith and bonafide. He has further submitted that the court below gave several adjournments to the defendant No, 1 and defendant No. 1 had been given full opportunity to contest the case but the defendant No, I contesting the case half way through remained absent on unwarranted grounds on subsequent dates and the decree was passed by the court after considering the elaborate written statement filed by the defendant No.1 in the suit. It is not an ex parte judgment and decree and it has never been stated to be so in the judgment itself. The appellant in the instant case did not pursue the review petition in good faith and bonafide, as the grounds mentioned in the review petition are never a ground for any petition for review under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

8. In the instant Rule the point to be decided is whether in the facts and circumstances of the case it could be said that the defendant appellant had pursued the review petition before the court, which issued the judgment and decree, bonafide and in good faith for the matter to come under section 14 or the Limitation Act. Section 14 of the Limitation Act provides that in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any suit, the time during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding whether in a court of first instance or in a court of appeal, against the same party for the same relief shall be excluded, where such proceeding is prosecuted in good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction, or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it.

9. The limitation and condition as provided in section 14 of the Limitation Act would cover the grounds as in section 5 of the Limitation Act which section 5 provides that any appeal or application for any other application to which this law would apply' may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed therein when the appellant or the applicant satisfied the court that he had "sufficient cause" for not preferring the appeal or making the application within such period and this sufficient cause which prevented him from preferring the appeal within the time would be referable to the period or days during which he had been prosecuting the matter with due diligence in a wrong forum also but in good faith. Section 5 refers to sufficient cause for delay. Section 14 of the said Act provides that should it be delayed for prosecuting in a wrong forum diligently and in good faith those days would be excluded. The expression "good faith" has been defined both in the General Clauses Act and in the Penal Code. Section 52 of the Penal Code provides that nothing is said to be done or believed in good faith which is done or believed without due care and attention. Sub-section 20 of section 3 of the General Clauses Act defines that a thing shall be done in "good faith" where it is in fact done honestly. whether it is done negligently or not.

<u>10. Therefore. mere presentation of a review application in a wrong forum would not exclude the period spent there unless it could be shown that the grounds of the said review application have been grounds for review as under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said has been prosecuted with due diligence. honestly and with due care and attention initially in filing the application. though on a mistaken view of the law or on being wrongly advised. keeping in mind that the said belief that the review application is proper and bonafide should continue during the whole period of such prosecution and unless it could be shown that the said mistake was pointed out to the petitioner in the pleading of other party or otherwise and hence if the petitioner in review "persisted" in spite of the mistake shown to him in the pleading of the other party the continuation of the plea that the matter is being done in good faith and honestly before a wrong forum would not be available and it would not also be available if the review petition itself does not contain the grounds on which a review is competent.</u>

<u>This is the legal position in this regard and in support of this a number of decisions both of the Indian Jurisdiction and of the Privy Council has been referred to us to which we shall advert presently and we wish to do that after narrating certain other circumstances which are material in the instant case.</u>

11. In the instant case the bank filed the suit for realisation of money on account of cash credit given against mortgage of the schedule properties. In that suit the plaintiff Bank asked for realisation of an amount of Taka 7.05.81.038.88 by sale of the properties mortgaged against the loan. It is seen from the judgment that the defendant contested the suit by filing written statement. In the written statement it is the case of the defendant that the loan taken by the defendant in 1979-80 from the Bank could not be paid as during that time there was depression in the jute market. The jute traders during those days suffered a loss and to give relief to the jute traders the Government framed a commission to examine the laws and it made certain recommendation by way of giving relief in terms of recurring interest and penal interest yet in the instant case the bank has calculated the amount due by adding inflated interest in violation of the recommendation of that commission and. therefore the claim was not fully accepted and it was pleaded that the suit be dismissed.

12. The Court found that the defendant did not produce any document in support of their claim though they have filed written statement and cross examined the witnesses. The court also observed that the trial started on 20.12.88 and thereafter the defendant took many adjournments and even on 13.2.89 in part hearing of the matter they prayed for time which was rejected and judgment delivered and it is seen from the judgment that the court has also considered the agreement entered into between the Bank and the defendant and found that in the agreement dated 10.6.85 the defendant promised that till 13.6.85 the amount due being 5.70.22.762.88 would be paid by them on and from July 1985 at the rate of Taka 55 lac per month therefore the court on the admission came to a finding that on the basis of the said agreement it is clear that the defendant acknowledged that till 10.6.85 they owe to the bank an amount of Taka 5.70.22.761.88 but yet for no reason the defendant did not pay even that admitted amount to the bank and further the court came to a finding that as the defendant has admitted the amount due to be Taka 5.70.22.761.88 the claim of the plaintiff Bank that till 22.9.88 which is 3 years thereafter from the agreement dated 10.6.85. the defendant owe to the bank in total with interest an amount of Taka 7.05.81.038.88 is correct The Bank is entitled to get a decree for the said amount against the defendant No.1 Rupali Jute Baling Ltd. and the suit was decreed accordingly. It was ordered that over the decretal amount the bank would be entitled to an interest at the rate of 18% from 23.9.86 and ordered the defendant to pay the same within three months from the date of judgment in default the schedule mortgaged properties would be sold for realisation of the said money. There was an execution proceeding thereafter for sale. At the time of issuance of this Rule after the appeal has been preferred no stay of any execution proceeding has been granted by this court nor it was prayed for. It is further seen from the judgment and decree against which this appeal has been preferred that it was a contested suit and the suit and the decree was passed in presence of the parties.

13. As narrated earlier, against that judgment and decree a review application has been preferred. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner appellant has produced before us a copy of the said review application and from a perusal of that application it is seen that there it has been stated that, on 20.11.88 PW 1 has been examined and cross examined partly by the lawyer of the defendant and it was part heard and the next day was fixed on 13.5.89. On that day Mr. HR Sharif, the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant petitioner being engaged before the Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 316 of 1986, could not be present before the court on that day and an application was moved for adjournment stating the grounds therein but the court did not allow time and proceeded with the suit and decreed the suit in the absence of the lawyer of the defendant and as the defendant for unavoidable circumstances and sufficient cause could not produce their learned Advocate before the court on that day for representing their case, the review petition is filed without going for an appeal and it prayed for rehearing of the matter. From a reading of the grounds of the review it thus appears that the prayer of the petitioner defendant was to set aside the judgment and decree after ordering rehearing of the matter as they were prevented from just cause from appearing. That being the position this review application does not appear to attract the grounds on the basis of which a review application can be allowed under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure because under Order 47 a review of the application can be made though an appeal is allowed but from which no appeal has been preferred on the ground that from the discovery of any new matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not to his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time of trial or when the decree was passed or order made and secondly, on account of some mistakes or error apparent on the face of the record or any other sufficient reasons.

14. Mr. SR Sharif, the learned Advocate, submits by reference to the decision of the case reported in 36 DLR 136 in which one of us had been a party, that for the mistake and bonafide mistake of the Advocate who may be even a senior Advocate, his client need not suffer and according to the learned Advocate in the instant case it was a mistake of the lawyer in presenting the review application before the Court and it was done on a mistaken assumption that it was an ex parte decree. This in our opinion also has no substance because if a decree is ex parte the provision of Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be attracted. Under the law in circumstances like this even if a decree has been passed ex parte against a defendant, the defendant could have two alternative remedies to him either to file an appeal or to file application under Order 9, rule 13 and also a review but on the grounds as under 47 rule (1) of the Code. This, in our opinion, is not a mistaken view of the law but rather an ignorance of the law which is not a defence. We do not find the said review application is done bonafide on good faith with reasonable care and diligence and due attention in proceeding with the matter for the simple reason that even in the review application, the grounds stated for the review is not within the provision of review as under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, the period spent in prosecuting the review application would not be prosecution in a wrong forum in good faith and with due diligence to come within the provision of section 14 of the Limitation Act or section 5 of the said Act explaining a reasonable cause for delay in filing the appeal.

15. In the case of Brij Indar Singh Vs. Kansni Ram and others reported in 44 Indian Appeals (Privy Council) at page 218 the judicial committee of the Privy Council at the beginning of this century, had occasions to examine a similar matter and the observation of the said judicial committee has thereafter being quoted with approval in subsequent decisions throughout the whole sub-continent including our court in the decision reported in 8 DLR at page 662 and in the decision reported in 36 DLR at page 136. It was also subsequently quoted in the case of Chhazzu Ram Vs. Neki, reported in AIR 1922 PC 112 and in other decisions of the Bombay High Court and of the Calcutta High Court to which we shall also refer.

In that case before the judicial committee of the Privy Council short facts need be narrated in order to appreciate the facts and circumstances of that case. In that case Reza Balbir Singh of faridkot brought a suit against Kanshi Ram and Jotimal, decree-holders, Mr. GH Coates, Judgment debtor and two others for a declaration that certain property, attached under Kanshi Ram and Jotimal's decree, was plaintiff's property and not of the judgment debtors. The matter could not be heard easily so an application was filed by the plaintiff Reza Balbir Singh for transfer of the case to the Chief Court but the petition was rejected and the case was taken up for hearing. At the time of hearing an application was made to the Chief Court to revise that order of the District Judge. The said petition remained in the Chief Court for some time when in the meantime certain death occurred among the parties. Reza Balbir Singh died in the meantime and was succeeded by his heir. The latter applied to the Chief Court for substitution and he was ordered to be so substituted by the Chief Court. In the meantime defendant No. 2 also died and hence substitution is ordered for both. The papers went back from the Chief Court to the District Judge Court when an application was made to the District Judge by Kanshi Ram defendant No. 1 and Achhru Ram, one of the sons of Jatimal, praying for an order of abatement on the ground that none of the representatives of Reza Balbir Singh, Jotimal have been brought on record within time. The new District Judge, it appears without inquiry and without notice to the plaintiff and obviously without looking at the previous order of the Chief Court, summarily ordered abatement with costs. Thereafter, upon petition by the plaintiffs who have been previously substituted by the Chief Court, the succeeding District Judge reconsidered the ex parte order of abatement passed by his predecessor and set aside the order of abatement insofar the original plaintiff is concerned. The said District Judge thereafter took up the other two deaths, namely that of Jotimal and Kotesh, and set aside those abatement orders also in respect of them when on both occasions it was urged before the District Judge that the law does not authorise such review but it was rejected. Thereafter the matter was brought to the Chief Court and the Chief Court opined that the order in review subsequently by the succeeding District Judge was bad in law holding that against that order of abatement passed earlier, though ex parte, an appeal would lie and a review was not competent. After this order the plaintiff immediately filed an appeal which was opposed on the ground of limitation. The objection was upheld but the learned judge after careful consideration gave leave to appeal to his Majesty in Council. The Judicial Committee after careful examination of the provision of section 14 of the Limitation Act and also section 5 of the said Act, which incidentally is the same in our law, observed that section 5 of the Limitation Act is positively the same as in section 14 of the Limitation Act which provides that for prosecuting in a wrong forum the prosecution needs to be done in good faith in order to satisfy the court that he has been prevented from sufficient and just cause in not appealing within time. It was further held that the true guide for a court in matters like this where it is alleged that time was consumed in prosecuting in wrong forum, to see whether the appellant had acted with reasonable diligence in prosecuting his appeal, and he ought ordinarily be deemed to have acted with diligence when the whole period between the date of the decree appealed against and the date of presentation of the appeal does not, even after excluding the time spent in prosecuting with due diligence, a proper application for review of judgment, exceed the period prescribed by law for presenting the appeal and in holding so their Lordships reiterated the principle as laid down in Karam Bakhsh Vs. Daulat Ram case reported in 1818 PR No. 183. The judicial committee after holding that mistake in law may be a foundation for the relief held the standard applied to be whether the proceeding in the review was reasonably prosecuted and prosecuted in good faith. Considering the facts of that particular case where the plaintiff after the abatement order and the subsequent order setting aside the abatement order on review, were not themselves on the wrong side of law in not filing the appeal because the subsequent order setting aside abatement passed on review was good in law until set aside by the Chief Court when immediately after it was set aside they filed an appeal and in view of that circumstances their Lordship found that the appellant having never persisted in prosecuting before a wrong forum with knowledge and in fact the subsequent appeal having been presented with 15 days, the appeal be admitted.

16. In the case of Hazi Md. Yousuf Vs. M/s Ahmed Brothers and others reported in 8 DLR 662 a Division Bench of this Court had occasion to examine a simillar matter. That Division Bench after quoting with approval the principle as laid down in this regard in a number of cases of Indian Jurisdiction namely the case reported in AIR 1927 Bombay 226, AIR 1925 Calcutta 253, AIR 1922 PC 112, lLR 15 Cal. 242 held that time taken for prosecuting a review application on ground not covered by Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code and not in good faith, cannot be excluded in computing the period of limitation. In that 8 DLR case their Lordships observed thus:

In the present case the grounds taken for review are not covered by Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and should have been taken in an appeal. In spite of that fact the petitioner moved this court and it was probably trying to have a cheap remedy and postponed the filing of the appeal till the application for review was rejected. The proceeding in the review therefore were not reasonably prosecuted and were not in good faith and the application for review was certainly not a bonafide application diligently pursued. The petitioner only tried his luck in an economical summary procedure." Their Lordships in holding so discharged the Rule without any order as to cost.

17. In the case of Ashanullah Vs. The Collector of Dacca reported in ILR 1888 (Calcutta) at page 242 it was held thus :

"The mere presentation of an application for review, where it is not shown that the ground thereof are reasonable and proper, is not a sufficient reason for admitting an appeal after the period of limitation prescribed for such appeal has passed."

In the case of Kailash Chandra Nag and others Vs. Bejoy Chandra Nag and others, reported in AIR 1925, Calcutta at page 253 in a similar matter, where the grounds taken in review were not within the scope of Order 41 rule I of the CPC in the relevant portion of the judgment it was held thus:

"The application, therefore, was similar to the one mentioned in the case of Ashanullah Vs. The Collector of Dhaka in which it was held that the mere presentation of an application for review, where it is not shown that there was reasonable ground for making the review, is not a sufficient ground for not presenting an appeal within time. The decision in the case of Brijindar Singh Vs. Kanshi Ram recognises the same principle and their Lordships of the Privy Council endorsed the view that an appellant was entitled to exclude time spent in prosecuting with due diligence a proper application for review of judgment."

<u>18. From an examination of the review application as observed hereinbefore by us, it is seen that in the said review application the grounds that were taken are not the grounds for any review application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the judgment and decree we do not find it also to be an ex parte decree and hence an application under Order 9 rule 13 would not also be competent, an appeal therefore would have been the only proper remedy. The grounds in review in the instant case also clearly show that the review application was made to open up the whole matter on re-hearing without coming for an appeal. This was thus an attempt to get a cheap remedy without paying the proper court fees which ought to have been paid if an appeal would have been preferred because the suit was valued at Taka 7 crores and on appeal the court fees paid would be more than Taka 28,000.00.</u>

19. We find that this application for review had not been prosecuted in good faith, honestly and diligently. We would further add that the petitioner before this court in fact persisted to prosecute the wrong application even after it was taken to his notice in the written objection by the other side that he is fighting in a wrong forum, with wrong grounds and there was no error apparent on the face of the record for the court to review. Yet the petitioner appellant persisted to prosecute in the wrong forum and for his wrong action he cannot be allowed to be profited and may not be granted the privileges as under section 14 of the Limitation Act The decision reported in 36 DLR at page 136 is not applicable in the facts of this case.

In the result, this rule in discharged without any order as to cost. The appeal being FAT No. 567/1989 is dismissed being barred by limitation.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 21.9.92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Narayanganj, in Mortgage Suit No. 220 of 1991 rejecting an application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the order of dismissal for default of the suit.

2. The present-appellant as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit in the court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Narayanganj for realisation of Taka 2,61,266,29.00.

3. The suit was fixed for hearing on 16.3.92. But as the plaintiff Bank failed to take steps in the suit on that date, the suit was dismissed for default on 16.3.92. Thereafter the plaintiff filed an application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 19.3.92 which was registered as Miscellaneous case No. 15 of 1992. After hearing both the parties and perusing the materials on record the Artha Rin Adalat passed an order on 21.9.92 holding that under the Arthas Rin Adalat Act 1990 as amended such an application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC is not maintainable and on such finding the Artho Rin Adalat rejected the aforesaid application of plaintiff-appellant. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 21.9.92 the plaintiff appellant preferred this present Miscellaneous Appeal.

4. Mr. Ahsan Ullah Patwary, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the Artha Rin Adalat has committed an error of law in dismissing the application filed by the plaintiff-Bank under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He submits that if the provision of sections 5, 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act are read together, it appears that an application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC is very much applicable in the present case.

5. In order to consider the submission of Mr. Patwary let us consider the provisions of sections 5, 6, and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act. Section 5(4) of the said Act provides that Artha Rin Adalat shall be deemed to be a civil Court and subject to the provision of Artha Rin Adalat Act, the Artha Rin Adalat will have all the powers and jurisdiction as a civil Court has got under the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 5(5) provides that unless there is anything contrary to the provisions of this Act, the Artha Rin Adalat shall follow the same procedure in conducting the cases as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 6(1) of the said Act provides that, subject to section 7 of the Act, the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat shall not be questioned in any court or by any other authority. Sub-section 2 of section 6 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section 1 of section 6, if anybody, aggrieved by an ex parte decree of any Artha Rin Adalat, wants to file an application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC for setting aside the ex parte decree, the aggrieved person will have to deposit 50% of the decretal amount in the court and unless such amount is deposited his application will not be entertained by the court. Section 7 of the aforesaid Act provides that if anybody is aggrieved by any judgment or decree of the Artha Rin Adalat, he shall have to file an appeal before the High Court Division within 30 days from the date of judgement or decree. But no appeal shall lie against any inter-locutory order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat.

6. Admittedly, in the present case the suit was dismissed for default as the plaintiff failed to appear before the court on the date of hearing and the plaintiff filed an application within time under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit on setting aside the order of dismissal of the suit for default.

7. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, submits that the application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable in the present case in view of the fact that the provisions of section 5(4)(5) of the said Act are subject to the provisions of Artha Rin Adalat, Act 1990. Mr. Khandker submits that the application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC is not attracted under section 6(1) of the said Act inasmuch as the provision is laid down to the effect that all the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of Artha Rin Adalat cannot be challenged in any court or by any other authority. Mr. Khandker submits that any court included the trial Court itself and when the suit is dismissed for default, that court dismissing the suit is not entitled to entertain an application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC. It is difficult for us to accept such contention of Mr. Khandker in view of the fact that the law laid down in section 6 (1) of the said Act is very clear and from the provisions it appears to us, proceeding, order, judgment and decree of any Artha Rin Adalat cannot be challenged in any other court or by any other authority except as provided under section 7 of the Act. So section 6(1) of the said Act, in our opinion, does not preclude the aggrieved plaintiff from filing an application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the self-same Artha Rin Adalat which passed an order dismissing the suit for default

8. Mr. Khandker further submits that plaintiff ought to have filed appeal under section 7 of the said Act inasmuch as section 7 of the Act provides, if any person is aggrieved by any judgment or decree of Artha Rin Adalat, he must file appeal within 30 days from the date of judgment and decree in the High Court Division. Mr. Khandker submits that the order for dismissal for default of the suit amounts to judgement as contemplated under section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In order to consider the submission of Mr. Khandker let us look to the provisions of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In section 2(2) of the CPC. the definition of the 'decree' is given wherein it is specifically provided that any order of dismissal for default is not decree. So under the provision of section 2(2) (b) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the order of dismissal for default passed by the Artha Rin Adalat is not a decree.

<u>9. Section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure has given the definition of 'judgement'. It speaks that judgment means the statement given by the judge of the grounds of the decree or order. Section 2(14) provides that 'order' means the formal expression of any decision of the civil Court which is not a decree. Mr. Khandker submits that since section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure has given the definition of the judgment which speaks that the order is also a judgment, the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge dismissing the suit for default is a judgment and, as such, section 7 of Artha Rin Adalat is attracted and the appellant ought to have filed an appeal under section 7 of the Act before the High Court Division instead of filing application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court. It is difficult for us to accept the above contention of Mr. Khandker in view of the fact that the order of dismissal for default, in our view, cannot be called a judgment or order as contemplated under section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In a judgment a Judge is required to give the statements of the grounds of his decision. Finality of an issue in a case is called a judgment. As for example, in a Title suit when final decision is given it is called a judgment and a decree is framed over the statements and grounds given by the Judge in the judgment. In a pre-emption case the issues are framed and the finality of the matter is given in the form of an order and such an order is not called a decree but the statement of the Judge in the judgment. In a pre-emption case the issues are framed and the finality of the matter is given in the form of an order and such an order is not called a decree but the judge gives his reasonings and findings after framing issues in the disputed matter. In our opinion, the judgment as contemplated in section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure will mean an order where the issue will be framed and the matter will be decided finally by the court on giving the grounds and reasonings over the disputed issues. So, in our opinion, this order of dismissal for default of a suit saying that since the plaintiff fails to take any steps in the suit, the suit is dismissed for default, does not come within the definition of 'judgment' as contemplated in the definition of judgment given in section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>10. Considering the above provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure in juxtaposition with the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, we are of the view that the order passed by the learned Artha Rin Adalat dismissing the suit for default cannot be called a judgment as contemplated under section 7(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Act. It further appears that it is an order of dismissal for default. Section 6(1) provides that the proceeding, order, judgement and decree of Artha Rin Adalat cannot be questioned in any court or by any other authority subject to the provisions of section 7. Section 7(1) provides that only the judgment and decree can be challenged in the High Court Division and proceeding and order are omitted in section 7(1) of the Act. So, it appears that the legislature intentionally made this provision of appeal against the judgment and decree only and not against any order.</u>

11. Section 6(2) of the said Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) if anybody desires to file an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree he can file an application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC on depositing 50% of the decretal amount in court. From the provision of this sub-section it appears to us that this Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is ordinarily attracted but further provision is made for depositing 50% of the decretal amount. This sub-section (2) clearly shows that an application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC is maintainable and it is specifically mentioned in the Act only because in this sub-section (2) further condition of depositing 50% of the decretal amount and if this further condition is not required for filing application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC it is not required to add this sub-section 2 of section 6 of the aforesaid Act.

<u>12. Considering the above we are of the view that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable in this case before' the Artha Rin Adalat subject to any embargo or condition as laid down in the Artha Rin Adalat Act and unless and until any special provision is made in this Artha Rin Adalat Act in the matter of trying the suit; we hold, all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, in pursuance of section 5(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Act, will be applicable in trying and disposing of a suit by the Artha Rin Adalat.</u>

13. In this view of the matter, we find that the submission as made by Mr. Khandker has no substance and, as such, we hold that the Artha Rin Adalat committed an error of law in rejecting the application under Oder 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. Mr. Khandker further submits that the appellant ought to have filed a regular appeal under section 7 of the Act even against the impugned order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. He further submits that though the Miscellaneous Appeal was filed within time; the required ad-valorm court-fee was not given in this appeal and, as such, this appeal is not maintainable. We are unable to accept the above contention of Mr. Khandker in view of the fact that we have already held that application filed under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable and if such application is rejected, then a First Miscellaneous Appeal under Order 43 rule 1 (c) of the Code of Civil Procedure may be preferred before this court and, as such, we do not find any substance in the last contention of Mr. Khandker.

<u>15. Since the Artha Rin Adalat Act does not provide any provision, directly or indirectly, contrary to provision of Order 9 rule 9 CPC an application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC can be entertained by the Artha Rin Adalat.</u>

16. In the result, this appeal is allowed and the order of the Artha Rin Adalat dated 21.9.92 is hereby set aside. The Artha Rin Adalat is directed to hear and dispose of the application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the plaintiff in accordance with law.

There will be no order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J :—This appeal arises from First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 170 of 1982 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka which affirmed the judgment and order of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court. Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981.

2. Appellant No. 1, M/s. Gannysons Limited was incorporated under the Companies Act in East Pakistan, as it then was, on 19th September, 1962. Appellant No. 2 is a resident Director holding 19,000 shares of the company since 1962. Other Directors are (1) Ashraf A. Ganny, a British national holding 11, 500 shares, (2) Mohammad Ali Ganny, a British national holding 10,000 shares, (3) Arif Ahmed, a Bangladeshi national holding 3,500 shares and (4) Abdul Wahed Ibrahim, a Bangladeshi national holding 5000 shares. Appellant company being the owner and possessor of the building at 35-36, Bangabandhu Avenue mortgaged the said properties with the then National Bank of Pakistan, now Sonali Bank, through their Directors, Mr. Dada Abdul Gani and Md. Yunus Abdul Sattar (both now retired) and appellant N). 2 for cash credit limit of Rs. 4,50,000/-.

3. After the emergence of Bangladesh, the aforesaid property which under the trade mark name of "Gannys" were being controlled and managed by appellant No. 2 and the members of the staff were taken over by the Government as abandoned property. Properties were taken over including buildings, stock-in-trade and the running business. In spite of the repeated attempts of the Directors of the company the properties were not released by the Government. Representations were made by appellant No. 2 to Sub-Divisional Officer, Dhaka on 10th August, 1972 to the same effect and the other dates on which similar representations were made are mentioned to be 15.4.73, 3.2.74, 4.9.74, 5.12.74, 28.2.75, 13.12.75, and 14.5.76  Appellant No. 2 in reply to his letters received Memo. No. SP (Com) -91/76/266 dated 29th June, 1976 asking him to furnish copies of the aforesaid letters. On 5th July, 1976 appellant No. 2 complied with the request to furnish the copies of their previous letters. Subsequently, appellants wrote letters on 5.10.76, 16.11.76 and 21.12.76 to the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce. By their Memo. No. SP (Com)- 91/76/706 dated 11th January, 1977 the Ministry of Commerce directed the appellant to approach the prescribed Authority under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In reply, appellant No. 2 apprised the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce that they have already made representations to the prescribed Authority, namely, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Dhaka. On 15th March, 1977 another representation was made to the Ministry of Commerce for releasing the properties. Meanwhile, the matter was referred by that Ministry to the Ministry of Works. Hence, the appellant wrote a letter on 16th November, 1976 to the Ministry of Works which, by their Memo. No. SEC-XVI/IF-98/72/90 dated 19.1.77 requested the appellants to produce the original documents. This was duly complied with. By their Memo. No. SEC-XIV/2P-3-13/72/196. dated 26.2.77 the Ministry enquired as to why so long the application for realease was not made. In reply, the appellant stated that representations were being made to different authorities since 1972 when the properties were taken over by the Government, but with no effect.

4. On 25th April. 1977 the appellant served legal notice upon the Government for releasing the assets and properties of the company and having received no reply the appellant filed Writ Petition No. 300 of 1977 which was, however, subsequently withdrawn to make further efforts for the release and restoration of property.

The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, who is the prescribed Authority held thorough enquiry, inspected relevant documents, examined witnesses and thereafter submitted a report to the Government expressing the view that the property being a private limited company registered in the territory now comprising Bangladesh and the Directors of the share-holders of the company being citizens of Bangladesh and United Kingdom and that they are ready and capable to manage the affairs of the company and further stating that the property ought not to have been declared as abandoned property, he recommended for release of the properties.

While such diligent and persistent efforts were being made by the appellant company to have its properties and assets released by the Government, respondent No. 1, M/S. Sonali Bank, the successor of the former National Bank of Pakistan, instituted Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 for foreclosure and sale of the mortgaged properties in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the following :

(1) M/s. Gannysons Ltd., 35-36 Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka.

(2) The People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and Housing.

(3) The Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade, representing the Government of Bangladesh,

(4) Bangladesh Consumers Supplies Corporation, as Principal Defendants.

Abdul Rahman Abdul Majid, appellant No. 2, Dada Abdul Gani and Mohammad Yunus Abdus Sattar were made proforma defendants. M/s. Gannysons Ltd. having been in control management of the Government was made defendant No. 1 but no relief was sought for against the company managed by the original Directors. It may be mentioned that Dada Abdul Ganny and Mohammad Yunus Abdus Sattar ceased to be directors/share-holders of the appellant company prior to 1969.

5. The aforesaid suit for foreclosure and sale of the mortgaged properties was decreed ex parte. Decree-holder Sonali Bank put the decree in execution in Title Execution Case No. 46 of 1980. A notice was published in the Bangladesh Times on 21st July, 1981 for sale of the holding No. 36-36, Bangabandhu Avenue in pursuance of the execution case. On 5th August, 1981 the appellant requested the Ministry of Works to stop the sale of the properties as advertised. On their instruction the Court was moved which by its Order No. 13 dated 24th August, 1981 stayed the execution case till October 20, 1981. Appellant company filed Writ Petition No 720 of 1981 and a rule was issued, but the Writ Petition abated on March 24, 1982 in consequence of the Promulgation of Martial Law. The Government, however, did not take any steps to protect the properties. The appellant, therefore, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure claiming that the decree in question is incapable of execution in view of Article 14 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1072. The aforesaid Miscellaneous case was disallowed by the Court on the ground that the execution case could not be allowed to be frustrated at the instance of M/S. Gannysons Ltd. since the properties were abandoned and the Government did not come forward to save the properties in question from the sale by taking advantage of the provisions of Article 14(1) of P.O. No. 16 of 1972. The appellants who were shown as judgment-debtors in the decree preferred an appeal from Original Order No. 170 of 1982 before the High Court Division and obtained a Rule. After hearing the appeal and the connected Rule on 9th November, 1982 the High Court Division dismissed the appeal and the Rule was also discharged. The views of the Subordinate Judge were approved by the learned Judges.

6. On 6th March, 1982 appellants obtained special leave to appeal on the contentions that the properties through not abandoned properties and required to be released in their favour, the Government's stand by treating them as abandoned property could not be supported as it had been given protection under Article 14 read with Article 21 of P.O. No. 16 of 1972.

<u>7. Mr. T.H. Khan, Counsel for the appellant, contended that since the properties in question, though mortgaged with the appellants being abandoned property, the decree obtained by the respondent Bank is incapable of execution in view of the fact that the decretal abandoned properties have vested in the Government. There is also the express bar in the provisions of Article 14 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Management, Control and Disposal) Order, 1972, P.O. No. 16 of 1972. The trial court as well as the High Court Division ought to have taken judicial notice of such provisions in spite of the Government's failure to invoke them. Article 14 provides as follows;</u>

<u>14. (1) Any property vested in the Government under this Order shall be exempt from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority, and no injunction or other order of whatever kind in respect of such property shall be granted or made by any Court or any other authority, and the Government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property by operation of any law for the time being in force.</u>

<u>(2) Any such legal process as aforesaid subsisting immediately before the commencement of this Order shall cease to have effect on such commencement and all abandoned properties in custody of any Court, receiver, guardian or other person or persons appointed by it shall upon delivery of the same being called for by the Government, be delivered to the Government."</u>

<u>From these provisions it appears that once any property is declared or treated as abandoned property under the aforesaid Act it cannot be subjected to any legal process such as seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority and further, that the Government cannot be divested or dispossessed of such properties.</u>

8. According to the learned Counsel, even though the bar imposed by the provisions of Article 14 of the aforesaid Act was not expressly pleaded on behalf of the Government, it was the duty of the Courts to take judicial notice of the provisions as required by section 57 of the Evidence Act. Apart from the legal bar against execution of any decree obtained against such abandoned properties as provided in Article 14 of the aforesaid Act, the Court is seen to have failed in its duty imposed by the aforesaid section.

9. On these grounds which seem to be substantial, Mr. Khan, Counsel for the appellants, assailed the findings as well as the reasoning of the trial court. After observing that the properties were mortgaged to the then National Bank of Pakistan by M/S. Gannysons Ltd. long before President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force as security of loan advanced by the Bank to the company and that in Title Suit No. 249 of 1976, the Government of Bangladesh and the Secretary, of Commerce were also made parties besides M/S. Gannysons Ltd. and others, the Court arrived at the following findings:

"Moreover, the Government in the Ministry of Commerce have by an application dt. 6.8.81 expressed its willingness and readiness to pay of the decretal dues to the decree holder Bank. The Govt. in whom M/S. Ganny sons Ltd. and its properties have vested as abandoned properties have not come forward to save the properties in question from sale taking the advantage of the provisions of Article 14(1) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

In the circumstances, I am unable to accept that the execution case should be allowed to be frustrated at the instance of M/S. Ganny Sons Ltd. on the ground of the properties being abandoned."

10. Mr. Khan also contended vehemently that the trial court ought to have considered the objection filed by the Government to the effect that Article 14(1) of the aforesaid Act is a bar to the execution of decree as prayed for by the respondent Bank.

11. As to the failure of the appellants to take any steps either by way of appeal against the trial court's judgment or an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside the ex parte decree, the learned Counsel submitted that they were completely unaware of the suit as well as the ex parte decree in question. They came to know about the proceeding from the advertisement in the newspaper for sale of the properties in question. The appellants were diligently pursuing the remedy available under the provisions of the aforesaid Act and making regular correspondence with the Government for the release of the proper-ties as has been noted above.

<u>12. As against these circumstances which prevented the appellants from taking any steps earlier, the respondent Bank has not been able to prove that the appellants were aware of the institution of Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 or the ex parte decree passed by the Court or even the proceeding in execution in Title Execution No. 46 of 1980 until the advertisement appeared in the newspaper already referred to above. The respondent Bank has equally failed to show how the decree obtained in the aforesaid suit can be executed in respect of properties which had vested in the Government under the provisions of P.O. No. 16 of 1972. Further, though M/S. Gannysons Ltd. was made defendant No. 1 in the aforesaid title suit it was shown as having been in control and management of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and no relief was sought for against the company managed by the original directors. Only three Directors, namely, Dada Abdul Gani, Md. Yunus Abdus Sattar and Abdur Rahman Abdul Majid were made proforma-defendants in the suit showing them as Directors of M/S. Gannysons Ltd. of 35-36, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka. As a matter of fact, Dada Abdul Gani and Mr. Yunus Abdus Sattar ceased to be directors/share-holders prior to 1969. It is however, not understood why in the decree itself the proforma-defendants have been shown as "defendants".</u>

<u>13. It is also difficult to understand why, if the loan was obtained by M/S. Gannysons Ltd. before it was treated as abandoned properties, the Bank, instead of proceeding against the directors of the company who continued till it was declared as abandoned, it proceeded against it when it came to be treated as abandoned property by the Government. The Bank wanted to proceed against the properties which were offered as security against the loan obtained by the appellants before it was treated as abandoned property, but in all fairness the Bank should have made them parties as well as the Government and should have sought relief against them, particularly when the previous directors were persistently pursuing their remedies, for the release of the properties in question.</u>

14. For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed. Decree dated 27.3.1980 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 be stayed for six months and the Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 pending in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, be struck down. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause why the Order No. 37 dated 19.3.85 passed by Munsif, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 188 of 1982, should not be set aside.

2. The facts of the case are, that Abdul Huq, opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff, along with 3 others filed Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka for permanent injunction against this petitioner and 2 others as defendants.

3. The plaintiffs case is that the suit originally belonged to Sk. Munshi and Balla, Ali in 8 annas share each. After their death the land devolved upon their 3 sons and 2 daughters. The 3 sons are plaintiff Nos. 2 to 4 and two daughters are proforma defendant Nos. 2 to 3. The plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land but the defendant No. 1 Hajee Abdul Latif is telling the local people and threatening that he will enter into the suit land and cut away the paddy grown by the plaintiffs. Hence the plaintiffs filed the suit for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into the suit land.

4. The defendant appeared and filed written statement. His case is that jote recorded under CS Khatian No. 285 of Mouza Mirpur along with other lands under different Khatians belonged to one Sk. Munshi and Bahar Ali and their names were duly re-corded in the CS Khatian. On amicable partition Sk. Bahar got the suit land along with other lands. There-after Bahar Ali died leaving only son Manik Chand. Manik Chand continued to possess the suit land. The plaintiff Abdul Huq is the son of late Sk. Munsih. While Manik Chand was the owner in possession of the suit plot he sold the suit land along with other lands to one Zainul Abedin Master under registered Kabala dated 6.3.42 corresponding to 22nd Falgun, 1348 BS and made over possession to the purchasers. While said Zainul Abdin Master was possessing the suit land he permanently settled the suit land with the defendant under a registered kabuliyat dated 24.10.1951 corresponding to 6th Kartick, 1358 BS and made over possession of the suit land to this defendant and realised rent from him till the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government. The defendant got his name recorded in all stages of SA and RS operation, mutated his name in the Government Sherista and has been regularly paying rent. The suit plot was once acquired by the Government in LA case No. 15/1955-56 and all notices relating to owner-ship and possession of the suit land were issued to the defendant. The scheme for which this land was acquired was ultimately abandoned by the Government and the suit plot was released in favour of the defendant. The defendant is in possession of the suit land althrough.

5. In the said Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 the plaintiffs also filed an application for temporary in-junction but the prayer for temporary injunction was rejected by the Munsif, First Court, Dhaka on 2.5.1981. Thereafter on 9.9.84 the Munsif dismissed the said Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 for default of the plaintiff. The said Abdul Huq again filed the present Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka with the same prayer for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from entering into the suit property on the same cause of action. The suit property, cause of action and the parties are all same in the present suit as were in the earlier suit No. 210 of 1981.

6. In the Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 the defendant appeared and filed written statement and he took the same plea as in the earlier Title Suit No. 210 of 1981. The defendant filed an application on 13.3.1985 under Order 7 rule 11 CPC for dismissing the Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 in view of the dismissal of the earlier Title Suit No. 210 of 1981. The learned Munsif by his Order No. 37 dated 19.3.85 rejected the defendants petition on the ground that the dismissal of the previous Suit No. 210 of 1981 for default will not create any bar to file this present Suit No. 188 of 1982. The Munsif also found that in the present suit there is a new cause of action and the suit is not barred by any law. Rule 11 of Order 7 provides as follows:

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases—

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action :

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so :

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so :

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."

The defendant (present petitioner) could not show that if the suit is dismissed for default another suit cannot be brought if a new cause of action arises or that the present suit is barred by any law. The Munsif, First Court Dhaka dismissed Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 by his Order No. 31 dated 9.9.84 which is as follows:

"Defendant files hazira plaintiff file no hazira and take no steps CF paid is correct. Hence,

'A'

Ordered

That the suit be dismissed for default:

7. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, raises a small but important point of law and submits that this order dated 9.9.84 was an order under Order 9 rule 8 for dismissing a suit where the plaintiff does not appear and as such the present Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 is barred under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that under Order 9 rule 9 a plaintiff, whose suit has been dismissed for default, may apply for an order to set aside the dismissal and if he can satisfy the Court that there is sufficient cause for his non-appearance when the suit was called for hearing, the Court may make an order setting aside the dismissal upon such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit. True, the plaintiff did not make such application. But there is no provision that unless a suit has been decided on merit, a fresh suit cannot be brought if the same cause of action continues or a new cause of action arises.

<u>8. From the perusal of the record of this case it appears that Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 was filed on 2l.4.81 vide Annexure 'A' of the petition. Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 was filed on 17.4.82 vide Annexure 'C' of the petition. It thus appears that both the title suits (which were for the same cause of action in all respects) were pending at a time. According to section 10 of the CPC, no Court shall proceed with the trial of a suit if the subject matter is directly in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties. Since these two suits were filed one after another and were pending for trial during the same time, the later suit, namely, Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 ought to have been stayed by the trial Court under section 10 of the CPC till disposal of the first suit i.e. Title Suit No. 210 of 1981. Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 having been dismissed for default on 9.9.84, the Court was justified in proceeding with the later suit No. 188 of 1982. The petitioner filed application under Order 7 rule 11 for rejection of the plaint on 13.3.85 when out of the two suits only Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 was pending. Therefore, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under Order 9 rule 9 the plaintiff is precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action or that he may apply to set aside the dismissal order of the previous suit is not sustainable in law. Under Order 9 rule 9 a plaintiff is precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action only when a suit is wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8 of Order 9. In the present case it is found that although Title Suit No. 210 of 1981 was dismissed for default on 9.9.84. Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 was validly pending at that time Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 has not been brought afresh after the dismissal of the Title Suit No. 210 of 1981. Therefore rule 9 of Order 9 of the CPC has no manner of application in the present case.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Gafur has further submitted that the cause of action for both the cases are directly and substantially the same. In this connection he has referred to a decision in the case of Haji Nurul Islam Vs. Ashraf Ali and others, reported in 30 DLR at page 215 wherein the cause of action has been explained. Relying on this decision it is submitted that the present suit appears to be an unnecessary harassment to the defendant and, therefore, it should not be allowed. It has been found already that since the present Title Suit No. 188 of 1982 was already pending and has not been filed after the dismissal of the previous suit it cannot be said that the later suit No. 188 of 1982 is a prolongation of litigation for the purpose of unnecessary harassment and expenses to the defendant.</u>

For the reasons stated above this Rule is discharged without any order for costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C. J.-This appeal is against the judgment and order of the High Court Division passed in Second Appeal No. 177 of 1978 on April 6, 1982.

2. Plaintiff-respondent filed S.C.C. Suit No. 5 of 1970 in the 4th Court of Munsif, Narayanganj for ejectment of the defendant appellant from the suit premises and obtained an ex-parte decree on May 19, 1972. Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1972 filed by the defendant-appellant under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was allowed on contest on December 13, 1972 restoring the S.C.C. suit to its file. Plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No. 182 of 1974 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Narayanganj on the allegation that the aforesaid order dated 13.12.72 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1972 was illegal, null and void. It was contended that since the defendant-appellant did not comply with the provisions of section 17(1) of the Small Causes Court Act, the miscellaneous case was not maintainable and the court which allowed it had assumed jurisdiction not vested in it by law. Its order was therefore, a nullity.

3. Defendant-appellant who contested the suit stated that the plaintiff-respondent must be estopped from raising any objection after the miscellaneous case was allowed on contest. Since the defendant-appellant did neither raise any such objection before the court allowing the miscellaneous case nor moved the higher court in revision against the order passed in the miscellaneous case, a regular suit for a declaration that the restoration of the S.C.C. suit was illegal was not maintainable as being barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Moreover, the plaintiff-appellant suffered no injury by the order of restoration of the S.C.C. suit.

4. On the ground that the requirement of section 17(1) of the S.C.C. Act which is mandatory having not been fulfilled by the defendant-appellant, the order passed in the Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1972 was a nullity.

5. Defendant-appellant filed Title Appeal No. 39 of 1977 against the judgment and Order of the trial court and being unsuccessful filed Second Appeal No. 177 of 1978 before the High Court Division which was dismissed by the learned Single Judge.

6. Defendant-appellant obtained leave from this Court to consider whether the High Court Division was wrong in not allowing the defendant-appellant to furnish security bond or to deposit the decretal amount after drawing up the decree as decided by this Court in the case of Binode Behari Shaha vs. Nitya Gopal Shaha (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 130. It has been contended before us by Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Counsel for the defendant-appellant, that the decision of the learned Single Judge as to the mandatory nature of the provisions of section 17(1) is not based on the correct interpretation of the principle underlying this decision. According to him the provisions of this section were merely directory and not mandatory and therefore, non-compliance with them did not make the order of restoration of the S.C.C. suit a nullity. Section 17(1) runs as follows:

“The procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of 1908) shall save in so far as is otherwise provided by that Code or by this Act be the procedure followed in a court of small causes in all suits cognizable by it and in all proceedings arising out of such suits.

Provided that an applicant for an order to set aside decree as passed ex-parte or for a review of judgment shall at the time of presenting of the application, either deposit in the court the amount due from him under the decree or in pursuance of the judgment or give such security for the performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment as the court may, on a previous application made by him in this behalf, have directed."

7. In interpreting the proviso to section 17(1) of the Act, the learned Judge observed as follows:

‘'In case of furnishing security the applicant must obtain a prior order from the court granting him permission to give security. This is a condition precedent to the granting of a fresh trial to any applicant and the said condition being mandatory in nature an application filed without following the provision and the condition as laid down in the proviso would not be entertainable by a court as in that case there would exist no application in the eye of law and if there would be no application in the eye of law there could be no order granting fresh trial and any order passed for such a fresh trial without an application validly made an order passed would be an order passed without jurisdiction and thus nullity."

8. Further, it was observed by the learned Judge that an order passed by the court without jurisdiction being a nullity, submissions to the court made by a party in such a case would not confer "jurisdiction upon it "when it bad none to exercise on the basis of an application which was not competent". Dismissing the view that an illegal order passed by the court does not establish that the court exercised power without jurisdiction, the learned. Judge observed that the present case was one where the court was seen to assume jurisdiction which it did not have in view of the incompetency of the application. The word "shall" used in the proviso was, therefore, construed as "must", In so interpreting the proviso to section 17(1) of the Act, the learned Judge is seen to have relied upon a decision of this Court reported in (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 130.

In appears from the decision that the proviso to section 17(1) was required to be strictly complied with as it was not mere directory in nature. Further, it would be wrong to give the proviso a literal interpretation.

<u>9. Insofar as the wording of the proviso to section 17(1) goes, it is seen that the requirements are that prior to filing an application for setting aside an ex-parte decree, the amount due under to decree or judgment must be deposited in court, in the alternative such security as may be directed" to the court for the due performance of the decree or compliance with the judgment must be deposited in the court. Normally and without exception these conditions must be fulfilled at the time of filing such application. It may, however, be mentioned that no consequences for not fulfilling the conditions are laid down in the proviso or else-where in the Act. Obviously enough, not merely the defendant-appellant failed to fulfill these conditions, the non-fulfillment was neither detected by the court nor pointed out by the plaintiff-respondents at the time of hearing of the Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1972 or before the order allowing the same was made by the court. The omission of the defendant-appellant to make any such deposit as mentioned in the proviso has equally been matched by the omission of the plaintiff' respondents to take objection to it during the hearing of the case. As a consequence, no notice of the same was taken by the court.</u>

<u>10. Apart from this omission to object at the earliest opportunity, the plaintiff-respondent did not move the higher court in revision. On the contrary he sat on the order of the court made in the miscellaneous case for nearly a period of two years and then filed Title Suit No. 182 of 1974 for the declaration that the order made in the miscellaneous case was illegal, null and void on the grounds already mentioned above. It appears that the plaintiff-respondent wants to take advantage of the wrong committed by the defendant appellant. Conceding that it was so, the plaintiff-respondent has, by keeping silent over such omission at the relevant time, done some wrong. If he took the objection he is taking now at the time of hearing the Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1971, the court would not have entertained the case or passed an order allowing it. This would not have also afforded an opportunity to the defendant-appellant to cover up his omission by taking appropriate steps. In the circumstances, therefore, the plaintiff-respondent cannot be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong. Law and justice do not function in the vacuum. It is true that the requirements to fulfill one of the two conditions laid down in the proviso to section 17 (1) has not been fulfilled in the present case, but it is equally true that this non-fulfillment has escaped notice of either the court or the plaintiff respondent leading to granting relief to the defendant-appellant. It may be pointed out that the plaintiff- respondent cannot be said to be prejudicially affected if the case is determined on merits in the presence of both parties. One cannot take advantage of his own wrong when, as in the present case, by taking no objection at the right moment before the right court, one allows its machinery to function and take objection at the conclusion of the case when if goes against him and this also not by an appropriate proceedings.</u>

For the reasons stated above, appeal is allowed with costs.

End.
